News.title: Watch moment giggling driver gives cop a lift to chase down suspect – a month after white van man drove gun police
News.content:
THIS is the hilarious moment a giggling driver picks up a cop in hot pursuit of two thieving boys.

The amusing clip shows the officer in a lung busting sprint as the two alleged offenders dash across a junction.



The out of breath bobby then seizes his moment as the women approach the traffic lights and jumps in the back seat.

The woman who filmed the incident said she and her friend were driving home when they saw the chase unfold.



“He opened the door and told us to follow the suspect,” she said.

“We thought he was coming over to tell us to stop filming, but instead he jumped in and we drove after the man until the officer told us to stop.”



The driver can be heard saying in the clip before she pulls over to pick up the cop “come on then King”.

Police were seen chasing a person on foot at Western Esplanade, Southampton at around 7.30pm on July 20, 2026.



An officer then jumped in a car passing by so they could catch up to the suspect.

A video shows the policeman getting out of the car and continuing the pursuit on foot, after getting a ride.

She said the officer entered the car as they passed by and directed them to follow the suspect.



PC Toby Pitt, who attended the incident, said: “Thank you so much to the member of the public who let me catch a lift while chasing a suspect.

“It was a hot day, so I was very grateful for the aircon!

“Thankfully the suspect was caught off guard, and despite his best efforts to hide in a bush – was arrested.”

Police said officers were called just before 8pm on July 20 to reports of the theft of a moped near Harbour Parade.

A 12-year-old boy and a 15-year-old boy fled when officers arrived.



Following a pursuit, both boys were arrested on suspicion of theft of a motor vehicle and have been bailed while enquiries continue.

News.title: Heart-stopping moment huge blast rocks homes and sends massive fireball into sky as drone footage shows devastation
News.content:
THIS is the heart-stopping moment a huge blast rocks homes and sends a massive fireball into the sky as drone footage reveals the devastation.

Locals have been warned to avoid the area and to keep their windows and doors shut as over 100 firefighters battle the inferno near Rettendon, Essex.



Essex County Fire and Rescue Service said they raced to the scene of a “large industrial unit fire” in Southend Road just before 5pm this evening.

In shocking footage, a huge explosion is captured as it sends a mushroom cloud into the sky that could be seen from miles around.





Exclusive drone footage obtained by The Sun showed the whole site and multiple buildings ablaze as a tower of black smoke erupts into the air.

The explosion could be heard from Southend-on-Sea, around 15 miles away from the area.



Local residents took to social media after hearing the blast in the area, saying that they felt the shock wave from the blast in their homes.

Cllr Danielle Belton posted a video to Facebook showing a huge plume of smoke pouring into the sky from miles away.

She said: “Did anyone else hear or see the explosion a few minutes ago?

“My whole house shook, it appears to be around Rettendon Way.

“It looks extremely serious, I really hope no one is hurt.”



It currently remains unclear whether there are any casualties.

Other footage circulating online shows a family sitting in their living room when they are stunned by the blast.

A spokesperson for Essex County Fire and Rescue Service said: “We’re currently at the scene of large industrial unit fire in Southend Road between East Hanningfield and Rettendon.



“If you live or are travelling nearby, please keep your windows and doors closed.

“Please avoid the area if you can.”

The East of England Ambulance Service said they were responding to a “significant incident”.

The building that exploded is thought to be at Highlands Farm with a number of buildings and businesses in the vicinity, including a metal manufacturing company.

The Sun has contacted Essex Police for comment.

News.title: How Ukraine’s cunning tactic to blitz ‘Russia’s Amazon’ could deal fatal blow to Putin’s regime & cripple war machine
News.content:
AFTER weeks of blitzing Vladimir Putin’s oil depots with state-of-the-art drones, Ukraine has now shifted its crosshairs to Russia’s Amazon.

In another bid to bring the tyrant to the negotiating table, Kyiv is putting its foot on Moscow’s neck with a series of strikes crippling the regime’s biggest e-commerce platform.



The despot could be staring down the barrel of a mutiny by the time key elections come round in September if Ukraine keeps its foot on the gas and Moscow continues to struggle against aerial assaults, experts say.

The devastating strikes on warehouses owned by Wildberries – the country’s biggest online marketplace – have shattered Russian morale.



Over the last few days, Ukraine has destroyed or damaged a series of complexes belonging to the biggest e-commerce platform in Russia.

And the drone onslaught has thrown Russian daily life into chaos – wiping out local businesses overnight and suffocating small-scale trade.

Russia expert Mark Galeotti told The Sun: “The Ukrainians have been extraordinarily and unexpectedly successful, and this is slowly grinding away… at support for the regime bit by bit.”

And John Foreman CBE, former UK Defence Attaché to Russia, said: “The strategy… is to inflict pain inside Russia, inside the occupied territories, inside Crimea, to bring home the cost of war back to Russians.”



Russia analyst Natia Seskuria told us: “It’s a very smart strategy from the Ukrainian side… it will have a significant impact on Russian households.”

She added: “This is something new and something that we haven’t seen before, but I think the message is still the same in terms of making the war extremely costly for Russia.”



Shocking images have shown plumes of smoke billowing over several complexes across the country with several of them decimated by flames.

Dubbed Russia’s Amazon, the online marketplace has been accused by Kyiv of housing military and drone equipment that is often sent to the frontline.

On Wildberries – which is owned by Russia’s richest woman Tatiana Kim and accounts for 52 per cent of the country’s online orders – customers can purchase radios, combat gear, and body armour.

Meanwhile, electronic chips being stored there can also be used for drones and missiles.



Seskuria called the firm “one of the driving forces behind the Russian economy” that employs some 4 million people.

Ukraine has argued they are targeting the logistics hubs in an attempt to disrupt supplies to the Russian army.

But they are also trying to frustrate millions of Russians who rely on the retailer everyday.



Galeotti said: “It’s essentially part of the wider campaign to really bring the war home to ordinary Russians and essentially make their lives harder.”

He added: “Frankly all across the country this did seem to be a war that was happening a long way away – and obviously things will change now.”

The attacks are “making people feel that the war is much more real and present for them”, he added.

Foreman agreed, saying it the move has brought the cost of war back to Russians.

Describing the online retailer, he told us: “You can buy body armour on there, you can buy electronics, can buy navigating, national creation equipment… so I think it’s a legitimate target.”



Seskuria said: “The feeling of insecurity is on the rise within Russia because there is a consistency when it comes to Ukraine’s attacks.”

She also warned of the potential uproar Putin may face down the line if Ukraine keeps up its strategy.

“Some Russians through their social media… are blaming the local governments for not being able to prepare the citizens to for these kind of attacks,” she said.



“This is something quite unusual for Russians, and that’s why I think Ukraine’s strategy has had so much impact because it shifts the narrative within Russia.”

Furious locals hitting out at the Wildberries strikes have claimed losing their livelihoods.

One woman went viral in a Putin-bashing post on Telegram, saying: “I am a mother of a disabled child, I’ve built the business myself…

“I’ve lost 1 million roubles (£9,500)… We’re already getting screwed over from every direction as it is.”

Another cried: “When will this f**k all end?



“Today at four in the morning my heart just broke. Everything I had built up piece by piece for two years just burned down.”

The significant dissent could push Putin closer to the negotiating table as he heads towards elections this year.

In September, Russians will go to the polls for legislative election – voting on who gets a seat in parliament.



But Putin’s ruling United Russia could face a crisis if living standards continue to spiral.

Galeotti said although the result will be “whatever the presidential political swing spin doctors want to announce”, it could still show, in some ways, how the population is feeling.

If the Kremlin is forced to tamper with the results too much, it might not be seen as a strong legitimate win.

“The more you rig it, the less convincing it is, but also, the more chance it does generate protests… So you know, there is clearly caution,” the expert warned.

Foreman said September would be a “time of risk for the regime because it allows a form of dissent to be expressed about the conduct of the war”.



And although the elections will be “largely symbolic”, Putin will still be trying to clamp down on public opinion to avoid future rebellion, Seskuria said.

“If the state of economy continues to deteriorate and at the same time the dissatisfaction among the population rises, this may lead Putin to think about the options,” she noted.

“And I think when it comes to the options, there aren’t many choices that he has.”



Although the attacks may not spark a full-blown revolt among the Russian population, experts emphasised that the latest campaign was having a undeniable impact.

Galeotti said: “None of this is without cost… I don’t want to downplay it.

“All of this has costs for ordinary Russians and also for big Russian business and the Russian state.”

Foreman said the strikes were a genius move as Wildberries represents a sizeable chunk of Russia’s economy

“The e-commerce sector in Russia is massive… it represents maybe eight and half to nine percent of Russian growth domestic product (GDP).



“90 per cent of Russians use these platforms.”

He speculated: “If we took out Amazon, [if it] was taken offline tomorrow, imagine the damage of that to small, medium-sized enterprises.”

Foreman also said the Wildberries attacks most affected those who have already been suffering economic impacts of war for the last four year.

But these new wave of strikes are like the final nail in the coffin.

“People trying to make money, trying to make a living through buying and selling stuff, and then suddenly that’s taken away,” he said.



Galeotti said the aim of the attacks was to “puncture” the deal between Putin and his population: Don’t protest and you won’t be impacted by the war.

He warned that although the latest tactic had been hugely successful, there is still some way to go before the world sees Russians marching in the streets.

Foreman agreed this week’s campaign had been largely effective in disrupting life in Russia.

He said: “On the battlefield, it’s been pretty static on and off for three or four years, but opening up this direct campaign against the Russian economy has proven more successful.”

Speculating on what Ukraine could target next, Foreman said data centres or communication nodes could be on the cards.



“There are clever people inside Ukraine trying to work out where’s the best places to target inside Russia which had the biggest payoff in terms of slowing the Russian war machine down and also… putting dilemmas on top of Putin.”

Seskuria said: “I think for now it’s fair to say that the momentum is more on Ukraine’s side.

“Russia has been reputationally quite damaged in the sense that they are unable to do anything about the successful Ukrainian long-range drone attacks.

“And if Ukraine wants to wants to proceed in its current pace, I think they have a good potential to significantly damage Russian critical infrastructure.”

Before the first Wildberries attack last weekend, Ukraine had been on a campaign of targeting Russian energy infrastructure – blowing up oil hubs in a bid to paralyse Putin’s economy.



The strikes sparked mass fuel shortages and massive lines at gas stations – as well as outrage among countless residents due to the soaring cost of living.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ukraine has also been blitzing Crimea – the Russian-occupied territory which was annexed in 2014 – in an attempt to isolate the peninsula from the mainland and stir unrest.

News.title: Woman robbed of £700 Lego set & pulled to the ground while riding train as cops share CCTV of man they want to speak to
News.content:
FIND HIM Woman robbed of £700 Lego set & pulled to the ground while riding train as cops share CCTV of man they want to speak to

A WOMAN has been robbed of a £700 Lego set, as cops release an image of a man they want to speak to.

The victim was sat in the vestibule of a train with her personal belongings when the train pulled into Hayle railway station, West Cornwall, at around 3.45pm on July 6.

As the doors opened a man took hold of an Amazon box belonging to the victim that contained a £700 Lego Technic crane set.



The victim managed to grab the other side of the box but was then pulled onto the floor and almost out of the train doors onto the platform.



She suffered bruising to her chest and back as a result.

The man then ran off along the platform and into the car park at Hayle station.

British Transport Police believe the man in the image could have information that may help their enquiries.

Anyone who recognises him is asked to text BTP on 61016, or call 0800 40 50 40, using the reference 417 of 6 July.

Information can be given anonymously to Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Britain hit harder than Europe by Trump’s trade war despite first shipment of tariff-free Scotch whiskey heading to US
News.content:
THE FIRST shipment of tariff-free scotch whisky will head to the US within 48 hours – but Britain is hit harder than the EU in Donald Trump’s trade war.

The US President agreed to lift the levies after King Charles‘ state visit to America earlier this year and the agreement has now come into force.



The industry supports 41,000 jobs in Scotland and a further 25,000 across the UK, the Scotch Whisky Association say.

Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said: “This historic shipment demonstrates why trade deals with our largest economic partners matter.”



But it comes as 10 per cent tariffs are being imposed by the US on 60 countries that haven’t taken action on importing goods made with forced labour.

They will replace the temporary 10 per cent levies which came to an end on Friday having been declared illegal by the US Supreme Court.

The White House has imposed 10 per cent levies on Britain and the EU. However, the UK must then pay duties on top, whereas Brussels levies are all-inclusive.

The trade deal struck with the US means pharmaceuticals, steel and aluminum are protected from these changes.

But William Bain, from the British Chambers of Commerce, said: “There will be concerns about the loss of the UK’s competitive advantage over the EU and other countries which have secured a more favourable deal in other goods sectors.”

Charlotte Brumpton-Childs, GMB national secretary, said: “The EU now has a better trading relationship with the US than we do – which undermines the so-called ‘special relationship’.



“Once again, the president’s knee-jerk actions will gain nothing, hurt US business and take dollars out of people’s pockets.”

Manufacturing group Make UK said: “The continued application of a 10% tariff underlines the importance of maintaining momentum in UK-US trade discussions under the new Government.

“Manufacturers need certainty, stability and the removal of unnecessary barriers to trade so they can remain competitive in an increasingly challenging global market.”

Confidence picking up in business, bank survey shows by Ryan Sabey CONFIDENCE levels across SME and mid-market firms is continuing to improve on last month, a survey shows. Company chiefs welcomed cost pressures easing despite optimism overall remaining below long-term average, the NatWest Tracker reveals. Figures show 37 per cent of firms now expect their export sales to rise in the next 12 months but 15 per cent are anticipating a drop. Firms are hoping to invest in overseas market and AI as a route to growth. Output growth for manufacturers in the mid-market recorded their fastest pace since May 2022. Sebastian Burnside, NatWest’s Chief Economist, said: “Manufacturing businesses have faced a lot of headwinds in recent years, from supply chain uncertainty and changing tariffs to the latest energy shock, so the growth they’ve reported in June is both encouraging and desperately needed. “Businesses across all sectors have been grappling with higher costs this year. If the modest fall in pricing pressure shown last month can continue, then it could help growth momentum to build in the second half of the year.”

A government spokesperson said: “There is no negative change to the tariff rate facing UK businesses as a result of this announcement.

“Our agreement with the US remains in place, and today we see an improvement to our trading terms with zero tariffs on whisky and medical technology.



“We take forced labour very seriously to ensure that in global supply chains UK businesses are not complicit.

“The US has recognised the steps the UK is taking, which is why there are no additional tariffs for the UK under this announcement.”

News.title: What does drought actually mean? The definition explained and where in the UK it has been declared
News.content:
WITH millions of households already facing hosepipe bans, environmental authorities have declared drought status in parts of the UK.

Here is everything you need to know about what a drought actually means, who gets to decide it, and if restrictions apply.



What does drought actually mean in the UK?

In simple terms, a drought occurs when a prolonged period of low rainfall creates a severe shortage of water affecting public supplies, farming, or nature.

The last major drought declarations happened last year in August 2025, when parts of South East Wales and multiple regions in England were placed under drought status.



Which criteria have to be met?

Official drought status can only be triggered by the UK’s regional environmental watchdogs.

These are the Environment Agency in England (advised by the National Drought Group), Natural Resources Wales in Wales, SEPA in Scotland, and NIEA in Northern Ireland.

Unlike a heatwave – declared when an area tops a certain temperature threshold for three consecutive days – there is no single trigger to officially declare a drought.

Agencies instead track key indicators like rainfall totals compared to monthly averages, river flows, reservoir capacities, and the frequency of wildfires.

When a combination of these factors shows that the local environment is under severe stress, the watchdog officially moves an area from “prolonged dry weather” into “drought” status.

Does it mean any new rules or restrictions?

An official drought declaration by an environmental agency does not automatically trigger mandatory rules or turned-off taps for households.



But the public is urged to save water to take pressure off local water sources.

You are also advised to avoid open flames, BBQs, or campfires in dry countryside areas to prevent wildfires.

Water utility companies may introduce consumer restrictions like hosepipe bans based on local reservoir stocks and consumer demand.

Where has drought been declared?

Official drought status has been declared in north Wales and the Upper Severn region following record-breaking dry spells and weeks without significant rain.

The Welsh zones now in drought include Clwyd, Dee, North and South Gwynedd, Upper Severn, and Ynys Mon (Anglesey).



Parts of north Wales have received less than 2% of their expected July rainfall, with many locations seeing no significant rain since July 6.

Although rain is finally forecast for some areas of the UK this weekend, with Northern Ireland, northern England and north Wales expected to see around 5-10mm of showers.

In England, large southern and eastern areas remain in prolonged dry weather status after receiving just 3% of average July rainfall. They include:

Devon, Cornwall, and the Isles of Scilly

East Anglia (including Norfolk, Suffolk, and the Cam & Ely Ouse catchments)

Hertfordshire and London

Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire

Solent and South Downs (Hampshire, Isle of Wight, and Sussex)

Thames (London, Thames Valley, and Home Counties)

Wessex

West Midlands

Multiple hosepipe bans are already in place, impacting 23million customers.

News.title: Rapist on run who attacked woman at knifepoint jailed in his absence after being accidentally freed from prison
News.content:
FIEND CAGED Rapist on run who attacked woman at knifepoint jailed in his absence after being accidentally freed from prison

A RAPIST on the run who attacked a woman at knifepoint has been jailed in his absence after accidentally being freed from prison.

Bernadin Dedic, 48, lured the woman to a basement in Ealing, West London, and raped her multiple times.



He was remanded in custody last year but was mistakenly set free from HMP Wormwood Scrubs after a court official wrongly told the prison that he had been granted bail.

Within hours, Dedic fled the UK on the Eurostar and returned to his native country of Bosnia.



The fiend gave a string of excuses for not returning to face justice – including claims he had a heart attack, was involved in a skiing accident and had a fear of flying.

Dedic was convicted in his absence of four counts of rape, two counts of sexual assault by penetration and causing a person to engage in sexual activity without consent.



He was also found guilty of threatening a person with a knife in a private place and making a threat to kill.

Dedic has now been jailed for 18 years in his absence, with Judge Hannah Duncan saying he is “refusing to return to the UK for his sentencing.

Isleworth Crown Court heard the predator carried out the attack shortly after separating from his partner.

He drank four bottles of red wine and snorted lines of cocaine before luring the woman to his basement.



Prosecutor Simon Sandford said: “When downstairs, she turned towards the stairs and saw him, holding a red-handled oriental kitchen knife.

“He stepped towards her, took hold of her and said he would kill her and then kill himself.

“She was extremely frightened but tried to calm him down. He said if she screamed, she wouldn’t be heard.”

Dedic was accidentally set free from prison on February 6 after a court official mixed up digital case files and mistakenly recorded he had been granted bail.

The notice was then sent to the prison, which led to Dedic’s release



Dedic claimed he wanted to come back to stand trial but was struggling to obtain a visa.

His UK passport was seized by the Metropolitan Police during the rape investigation but after being set free from prison, he used his Bosnian passport to secure a seat on the Eurostar.

A senior judge, police officers and Border Force agents attempted to bring the fiend back to the UK for his trial but Dedic claimed he could not travel as he had a knee injury so the trial was delayed until June.

But the rapist again failed to show – this time insisting he suffered a heart attack in Sarajevo – so the case went ahead without him.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Following his accidental release, HM Courts and Tribunals Service (HMCTS) launched an investigation.



A spokesperson said: “We understand the distress errors such as this can cause to those affected and instances like this have exposed deep-rooted issues across the broken justice system the Government inherited.”

News.title: Do hosepipe bans apply if you are on a water meter?
News.content:
MILLIONS of households across Britain are facing strict hosepipe bans following a dry spring and weeks without proper rainfall.

More than 23million people across England and Wales are currently subject to Temporary Use Bans (TUBs) as water companies struggle to cope with soaring demand.



Suppliers including Thames Water, South East Water, and Anglian Water have brought in restrictions, asking households to turn off the hose to protect water levels.

For the millions of households fitted with a water meter, that raises a question:



If you’re paying for every drop you use, do the hosepipe ban rules still apply to you?

Do hosepipe bans apply if you are on a water meter?

Yes, absolutely. Hosepipe bans apply to every residential customer within an affected region, regardless of how you pay your water bill.

Whether you pay an estimated flat rate through unmetered charges or have a smart water meter tracking every litre, the legal restrictions are the same.

When a water company issues a hosepipe ban, using a hosepipe connected to the mains supply for domestic tasks becomes illegal for everyone in that area.

Ignoring a ban is an offence that can lead to prosecution in a magistrates’ court and a fine of up to £1,000.

Having a water meter fitted to your home offers zero protection against a fine if you are caught breaking the rules.



Why do restrictions still apply?

It’s easy to see why metered customers might feel aggrieved.

If you are paying per unit of water, it feels logical that you should be allowed to spend your money as you see fit.

But hosepipe bans are not about financial fairness – they’re about water scarcity and network capacity.

When local reservoirs and rivers dry up, paying for water does not generate more rain to refill those natural sources.

If metered households continued using hosepipes simply because they were willing to foot the higher bill, local supplies could run low, putting drinking water at risk.



Ultimately, the ban is a conservation measure to protect public health and the environment, not a financial penalty.

Does having a water meter exempt you from any rules?

Having a water meter does not exempt you from any hosepipe ban rules.

Exemptions to hosepipe bans do exist, but they are based on personal health, mobility, or safety, and not on whether your water is metered.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

If you’re on a meter and want to maintain your garden during a ban, you can still water your plants using a traditional watering can or bucket filled from the tap.

You are also free to use harvested rainwater from a water butt or re-use greywater from your bath, shower, or washing-up bowl.

News.title: PlayStation Network down updates: Servers latest as users hit by global outage
News.content:
Video game giant Sony has confirmed that all PlayStation services are 'experiencing issues' amid thousands of reports from users worldwide

Gamers around the world, including thousands in the UK, have reported issues with the PlayStation Network, with many saying they are unable to connect to the server.

Video game giant Sony has confirmed that all PlayStation services are "experiencing issues". It added that it is working to resolve the problem as soon as possible and thanked users for their patience but did not give an estimate as to when services may be up and running again or suggest why the outage may have occurred.

Tens of thousands of network problem reports have been logged in the UK on outage-tracking website Downdetector.

One frustrated UK user wrote on Downdetector: "Can't load any digital games at all bought or free. Can't connect to servers to verify licences, doesn't matter what I try to load - I get the same message every time."

News.title: Westminster Bridge live: Multiple casualties in horror police boat crash on Thames
News.content:
Police boat was travelling at 'high speed' before 'slamming into wall'

A couple from the United States said they heard "an explosion" when a police boat travelling at "high speed" struck Westminster Bridge on the River Thames today, injuring five officers.

Jim Bagley, from Gloucester, Massachusetts, told the Press Association: "We were standing in line to get onto the city cruise hop on, hop off tours, and we saw two police boats coming up the river.

"One was an orange boat that went under the bridge and left a great big wave, and then there was a black boat that came up behind it, the police boat.

"It looks to me that he got stuck in the wake of the other boat that had just passed through the bridge and slammed into the wall on the opposite side.

"We didn’t see it happen, but we heard the explosion… the next thing we saw was three people in the water, coming down the river."

He added: "We were wondering why they were under way at high speed to begin with."

Katherine Bagley said: "They were both in pursuit of something farther down the river, but they never… the second boat never got to it because it crashed into the bridge with a big bang."

News.title: 'Babymoon' nightmare as new mum left stranded in Tenerife after newborn baby arrives five weeks early
News.content:
'Babymoon' nightmare as new mum left stranded in Tenerife after newborn baby arrives five weeks early

Chantelle Ali, 33, had been enjoying the last day of her holiday with her partner when she started experiencing contractions five weeks early - the mum was then left stranded in Spain with her baby

View 5 Images Chantelle Ali on holiday

A British woman's 'babymoon' turned into a nightmare after she was left stranded in Tenerife after going into labour five weeks early.

‌



Chantelle Ali, 33, had been on the final day of her holiday with her partner Ben Major when she started experiencing contractions at just 35 weeks. Hotel staff rushed her to a hospital and Chantelle endured a full day in labour. The Brit gave birth to her son Rico at 7.08pm on July 12, but they remain on the Spanish island nearly a fortnight on.

‌



Chantelle and Rico have been unable to return home due the lengthy process to obtain an emergency travel document for the baby.

‌



Brits struggle to get medical help abroad - for one key reason READ MORE :

View 5 Images Baby Rico was born five weeks premature

The mum, from Gloucester, said she has been living out of a carrier bag in an apartment in Playa de las Américas ever since, as her suitcase is stranded at the airport. Having fled their package holiday hotel a day before they were due to fly home, Chantelle's suitcase remains stranded at the airport, and she said it will cost £150 to retrieve it.

She said: "It has been a highly emotional and mentally draining experience. Not just to have a baby prematurely but in a foreign country is very scary. Google Translate saves me basically. There are a few nurses who can speak English but there are obviously a lot that can't.

‌



"It is always worrying because you don't know if you are getting all the correct information. We love Tenerife and we come out here all the time. I don't think I want to see Tenerife for a while."

View 5 Images Ben Major and Chantelle Ali on holiday

Chantelle revealed her waters started leaking two days before the birth, but with so little time left on the trip, she planned to see doctors once back in the UK. The couple had been enjoying a boat trip on Saturday but after returning to their hotel Chantelle began experiencing contractions.

‌



She assumed these were Braxton Hicks - contractions that are false labour pains - but when it did not stop she made her way down to reception and asked staff to call her an ambulance. She was taken to Our Lady of Candelaria University Hospital.

Chantelle said: "The contractions were getting stronger and stronger so I ended up taking myself down to reception and telling the poor young Spanish lad behind the reception desk that I was having a baby. It was the worst labour out of all my kids, it was the most painful.

View 5 Images Baby Rico in the hospital

‌



"It was the worst 48 hours ever. I had just given birth to a premature baby and my partner had to go. I was just left here in a foreign hospital on my own. It was quite scary."

Rico was due to be delivered via C-section back in England, but now holds a Spanish birth certificate. Born five weeks premature, he experienced some breathing difficulties and was placed in the ICU receiving oxygen, where he continues to remain.

Ben was forced to fly back to the UK the following day to arrange childcare for their two other children and ensure their dog was left with a family member before making his return.

‌



View 5 Images Chantelle showing her baby bump while on holiday

The hospital was far from the tourist area, with Chantelle revealing it is an hour's bus ride from where they collect their shopping and supplies. The hospital stay is covered by her insurance, but all other expenses must be met by the family themselves, including a £400 a week apartment and transport costs.

To bring Rico home, the family must provide both their passports, birth certificates, MATB1 form, proof of flights, photos of the baby, hospital documents, and proof he was premature. They currently have no indication of when this might happen.

Article continues below

Chantelle, who got in touch through Sell Us Your Story, said: "It is a lot of paperwork. When I was first told all of this I was very overwhelmed. Each day is a step closer to home that is what I keep thinking."

News.title: 'Southport killer Axel Rudakubana's move from prison is another cruel blow to families of murdered kids'
News.content:
'Southport killer Axel Rudakubana's move from prison is another cruel blow to families of murdered kids'

"Ministers must guarantee that he receives only the medically necessary treatment and is returned to prison as soon as doctors permit. Compassion for mental illness cannot come at the expense of justice"

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

The transfer of Southport killer Axel Rudakubana from prison to Broadmoor will feel like another cruel blow to the families whose children he murdered.

‌



Alice da Silva Aguiar, Bebe King and Elsie Dot Stancombe were robbed of their lives. Eight other children and two adults were attacked. Their loved ones now deserve answers about why this decision was made, particularly so close to the second anniversary.

‌



Mental illness is real, serious and must never be dismissed. Broadmoor treats patients whose conditions require specialist care under intense security. Yet there must also be honesty about the differences between hospital and prison.

‌



Reports that Rudakubana could receive benefits or enjoy greater freedoms will understandably create anger and the impression that his life has improved while his victims’ families serve a sentence without end. His 52-year minimum term remains.

Ministers must guarantee that he receives only the medically necessary treatment and is returned to prison as soon as doctors permit. Compassion for mental illness cannot come at the expense of justice.

'A welcomed start'

Protecting those whose only income is the state pension from paying income tax is a welcome start.

‌



Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor John Healey are right to prevent people who have worked all their lives from being dragged into the tax system simply because the triple lock pushes their pension above the frozen £12,570 allowance.

To many, Britain currently feels like a country where almost every part of life carries a government charge - energy, housing, transport, childcare, parking and from April even pensions in death. Fiscal drag has quietly forced millions to pay more tax without ministers formally raising a single rate.

But Mr Burnham must now go further. Families and pensioners need breathing space from a system that keeps taking more while offering less security in return.

Article continues below

'Extraordinary discovery'

For two years, Dave Green and Andrea Urmston worked side by side, never knowing they were brother and sister.

Their extraordinary discovery brought him back to the mother who had never stopped missing him.

Families can be separated by circumstance, but love has a remarkable way of finding the road home.

News.title: Horror 'murders' of mum and two daughters referred to police watchdog
News.content:
Horror 'murders' of mum and two daughters referred to police watchdog

EXCLUSIVE: The Independent Office for Police Conduct is examining what action was taken when Nothabo Zandile Tshuma, 42, contacted Bedfordshire Police, before she was bludgeoned to death with Natalie, 15, and Nala, five

View 3 Images Nothabo Zandile Tshuma, 42, Natalie, 15, and Nala, five, were discovered on July 6 (Image: Bedfordshire Police/PA Wire)

Police are being probed by a watchdog over contact officers had with a mum shortly before she was murdered, along with her two daughters.

The bodies of Nothabo Zandile Tshuma, 42, Natalie, 15, and Nala, 5, were discovered on July 6 after concerns were raised that they had not been seen for several days. They were victims of "blunt force trauma".

Nothabo's husband and the children's father Ndodana Mkhanyisi Tshuma, a British citizen of Zimbabwean heritage, has been charged with three counts of murder.

The 45-year-old, also known as Mark, was arrested in Kensington, Johannesburg, South Africa, after leaving Britain two days before the bodies were discovered in Great Denham, Beds. He was remanded in custody by Johannesburg magistrates court and work has begun to return him to Britain.

View 3 Images Ndodana Mkhanyisi Tshuma appears in a court in Johannesburg (Image: AP Photo/Themba Hadebe)

Mum and two children found dead at Great Denham home are pictured after police name suspect on run READ MORE :

Man charged with triple murder after wife and daughters found dead at Great Denham home READ MORE :

Bedfordshire Police confirmed today that officers had previous contact with Zandile. As a result, it referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct.

An IOPC spokesperson said on Friday: “We have started an independent investigation into contact Bedfordshire Police officers had with Zandile Tshuma and her daughters Natalie and Nala, prior to their tragic deaths in the Great Denham area of Bedfordshire earlier this month.

“On 7 July, we received a mandatory referral from the force relating to contact officers had with the family in June. We also received a voluntary conduct referral concerning a police constable on 8 July.

“Our thoughts remain with the family and friends of Zandile, Natalie and Nala, and all those affected by their deaths. Our investigation is in its early stages and further updates will be available in due course.”

View 3 Images Ndodana Mkhanyisi Tshuma is arrested in South Africa (Image: eNCA via AP)

Det Insp Lee Martin, senior investigating officer, said previously: "This case has attracted a huge amount of media coverage and we are aware of international reports circulating which contain some speculation about this case.

"With three murder charges authorised by the Crown Prosecution Service, proceedings around this case remain active and we are not able to provide any further detail at this stage. We continue to work with the CPS and international partners as the case progresses."

Article continues below

The South African Police Service said Tshuma was traced and arrested "through swift operational co-ordination and intelligence-led policing".

Tshuma's LinkedIn profile says that he studied management information systems at Solusi University in Zimbabwe before attending the University of Plymouth and City St George's, University of London.

Zandile was an associate director specialising in investigating financial crimes such as money laundering and fraud.

News.title: Moment murderer Vickram Digwa tells his mum to take the knife used to kill Henry Nowak
News.content:
Moment murderer Vickram Digwa tells his mum to take the knife used to kill Henry Nowak

Newly released footage shows the moment killer Vickram Digwa told his mum to 'take this' before she moved the knife he used to stab Henry Nowak

Vickrum Digwa asks mum to take his knife away after stabbing Henry Nowak

This is the moment murderer Vickram Digwa told his mum to take the knife he used to stab and kill Henry Nowak.

‌



New footage has been released by the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) after Digwa's mother, Kiran Kaur, was jailed for three years last week for assisting an offender. The 53-year-old was found guilty by jurors at Southampton Crown Court in May, after taking the weapon back to the family home on the night of the murder, on December 3 2025.

‌



In the video, Digwa can be heard talking to his mum in Punjabi asking her to take away the weapon. The clip was taken on Digwa's phone and was pointed to the ground.

‌



View 4 Images Mugshot of Kiran Kaur (Image: Hampshire Police/PA Wire)

A transcript released by the CPS revealed how Digwa told Kaur: "Take this", which they say was referring to the knife.

During sentencing, on July 17, Judge William Mousley KC said when Digwa told Kaur to take the murder weapon away, "by then you knew or believed that he had stabbed and injured Henry".

‌



View 4 Images Screengrab of the video which shows the ground and the mum's dress

The judge also told Kaur: "A responsible parent would have challenged their son over their actions and encourage them to do the right thing."

The mum took the murder weapon home and put it with a "larger collection of ceremonial and other weapons in your son's bedroom", Judge Mousley said. He added that this would have helped to conceal its use because she wanted him to "avoid being caught".

‌



View 4 Images The murder weapon used by Digwa (Image: CPS/PA Wire)

The judge said her actions at Belmont Road before and after taking the dagger away "added to your son's pretence that he had done nothing wrong and that he was the victim", before adding the mum's role added to the "degradation of Henry being arrested when he was dying".

Following the sentencing of Kaur, Mr Nowak's family shared a statement and said they will "never give up in our campaign for justice for Henry".

Article continues below

View 4 Images Henry Nowak died after he was stabbed in Southampton (Image: Family Handout/PA Wire)

It added: "Our focus is on making sure the ongoing investigations leave no stone unturned as we fight for the full truth about what happened last December, and we continue to urge the Government to deliver the changes our wonderful son deserves."

Digwa, 23, was jailed for life with a minimum term of 21 years on June 1 for the murder of the 18-year-old finance student, after falsely claiming Mr Nowak had racially abused him.

News.title: Man describes trying to save mother and daughter who drowned off Essex beach
News.content:
A day-tripper has told the BBC how he dived into the sea in an attempt to save a mother and daughter who drowned off an Essex beach.

Craig Bowe, 42, battled the incoming tide at West Mersea, near Colchester, three times after hearing screams on Wednesday evening.

The kitchen fitter, who was on a day trip from Hertfordshire to celebrate his daughter's 10th birthday, managed to haul Shally and Samiha Rahman from the waves and also helped a seven-year-old boy onto a lifeboat.

Despite his efforts, the pair - aged 41 and 15 - died in the desperate attempt to bring the boy to shore.

The boy, who became stranded during a family day out from Barking, east London, was airlifted to hospital and remained there in a critical condition on Friday.

Three others were taken by ambulance to another hospital after the incident unfolded at about 17:35 BST.

Bowe, from Northaw, sprang into action after hearing a man screaming in the water and seeing bodies floating.

"When I got there, the first two people I saw were actually face down, so [it was] more serious than I initially thought," he told the BBC.

Bowe pulled Shally Rahman to shore where bystanders began administering CPR. He then dashed back out to sea to rescue her daughter.

Having done so, he then returned to the water to help load the seven-year-old boy and another child, who were about 150 yards (137m) out at sea, onto a lifeboat.

"I helped sort of shoo him onto the boat, because he was face down too... but the seven-year-old was not in a good way," said Bowe, who was helped by an unnamed man.

"The waves were hitting me in the face. The current was definitely stronger."

News.title: 'Extremely significant' bomb in car intercepted on way to NI, Irish police say
News.content:
A car containing an "extremely significant" bomb has been intercepted in the Republic of Ireland as it was being driven across the border for an attack in Northern Ireland, gardaÃ­ (Irish police) have said.

The vehicle was stopped in County Monaghan on Wednesday during an operation targeting dissident republican activities.

BBC News NI understands police in Northern Ireland's main theory is that the bomb was set to be used to attack a police station north of the border.

A woman in her 20s has been charged and is due to appear in court in County Meath on Friday evening, while a man in his 40s remains in custody.

Police sources in Northern Ireland believe the New IRA was likely responsible.

The vehicle was stopped on the N2 near Carrickmacross at about 15:00 on Wednesday.

Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly confirmed on Friday that officers had found an explosive device.

Irish broadcaster RTÃ reported that gardaÃ­ sources said the bomb contained a power unit, a detonator and military grade explosives.

News.title: Andy Burnham's first week pledges - how much do they add up to?
News.content:
Andy Burnham is ending his first week as prime minister by working out of Manchester in the new No 10 North for the first time.

He spent this week making a series of spending announcements mostly aimed at tackling the cost of living, including capping bus fares.

BBC Verify has looked at Burnham's first week of spending commitments, how much they cost and how the government says they will be paid for, which comes to about Â£1.5bn.

Here's how that breaks down and what could later be coming down the line.

News.title: Angela Rayner rules out rent controls in England
News.content:
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said Prime Minister Andy Burnham is not looking at bringing in rent controls in England.

She told BBC Breakfast that changes made through the Renters' Rights Act, which came into effect in May, were "already having a significant impact on the market".

She added that controls which had been implemented in some areas of the UK over the past few years had not "necessarily brought rents down".

In 2023 when he was the mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham called for freezes to private sector rents until the cost of living crisis was over.

But Rayner told the BBC on Friday: "I don't think that rent freezes, rent controls, is a way forward at the moment.

"Three years ago, Andy called for that because there was a significant crisis in the rental market.

"We implemented between then the Renters' Rights Act which is giving renters more power and control."

Temporary rent controls were introduced in Scotland in October 2022 but expired last year.

Under new legislation, ministers in Holyrood will be able to designate certain places in Scotland as rent control areas - expected to come in by 2027.

Councils will be able to cap rent increases on some properties at a maximum of 6%.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said he wants to see rent controls brought in for all rented property in England.

Responding to Rayner's interview, he described Burnham as "continuity Starmer", posting on X: "The new prime minister talks a lot of about helping with the cost of living crisis. This is the one single measure that would help the most and save billions. All talk."

Jeremy Corbyn, who pledged to bring in rent controls during the 2019 general election when he was the Labour leader, described Rayner's announcement as "extremely disappointing".

"There is no hope of ending homelessness if we do not stand up to vested interests and take action against extortionate private rents.

"We need rent controls, and we need them now."

Sir Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, has also long called on the government to implement a cap.

But Gareth Bacon, the Conservative's shadow housing minister, said rent controls would be "disastrous" and "intensify the damage done by Labour's agenda that has driven landlords from the market and reduced choice for renters".

"Labour are clearly divided. Burnham's pick for housing secretary has disowned a policy he himself has repeatedly backed," he said.

The term rent controls describes a range of measures a government can implement - from capping price increases to freezing them for a period of time.

Landlord groups say they may exacerbate the housing crisis by putting owners off renting out property.

The Renters' Rights Act was brought in to give more stability and security to the 11 million people who rent from private landlords.

Under the legislation, fixed-term tenancies have been banned and it is now significantly harder for landlords to evict tenants.

Rents can also only be increased once a year to the property's "open market rent".

News.title: NBA superstar LeBron James to join Philadelphia 76ers
News.content:
LeBron James has announced he will be joining the Philadelphia 76ers next season for what he says will be his final contract in the NBA.

The 41-year-old, the highest points scorer in the history of the league, left the Los Angeles Lakers after eight years last month.

The Cleveland Cavaliers, Golden State Warriors, Minnesota Timberwolves and Miami Heat were also rumoured to be in the running for the four-time NBA champion.

"I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energise a new fanbase and start this incredible journey one last time," James said on X., external

James has won an NBA title with all three teams he previously played for. He won two with Miami, who earlier this week mistakenly posted a link to an 'introductory press conference' for James.

A Heat spokesperson told Reuters, external the video was posted in error by staff who were preparing for the possibility of James rejoining the team he played for between 2010 and 2014.

Either side of that Miami stint, James had two spells with Cleveland, who drafted James in 2003 and are based near his hometown of Akron, Ohio.

"Miami I'll forever love and Northeast Ohio will always [be] home," James added.

James helped the Cavs become NBA champions in 2016 and joined the Lakers in 2018, claiming another NBA title two years later.

He has been named the NBA's Most Valuable Player four times, all between 2009 and 2013, and has been an NBA All-Star the last 22 seasons running.

News.title: Officers hurt as police boat hits Westminster Bridge
News.content:
Five Metropolitan Police officers have been injured after a police boat struck Westminster Bridge in central London.

The Met said the incident occurred at about 15:40 BST and involved a boat from the Marine Policing Unit which was carrying armed officers.

In a statement, it said "a number of officers entered the water, but were recovered" adding it was waiting for an "update on the extent of their injuries".

No members of the public are thought to have been involved or injured in the crash.

An eye witness, Jim Bagley, who was visiting London from the US, described seeing two police boats coming up the river.

"One was an orange boat that went under the bridge and left a great big wave, and then there was a black boat that came up behind it, the police boat," he said.

"It looks to me that he got stuck in the wake of the other boat that had just passed through the bridge and slammed into the wall on the opposite side.

"We didn't see it happen, but we heard the explosionâ¦ the next thing we saw was three people in the water, coming down the river."

He added: "We were wondering why they were under way at high speed to begin with."

News.title: Faisal Islam: The UK's Trump trade deal no longer looks world-beating
News.content:
It has been a long road for President Donald Trump as he looks for a justification to erect a tariff wall around the US, including against key allies.

From the opioid crisis to illegal migration, then the need to bring manufacturing back to America's shores, the list goes on.

Through Trump's second term, there has been a new justification almost every month for the trade levies he is seeking to place on allies.

Some have been overturned by the courts, others by economics and some even by their own logic. And so, Trump has now turned to effectively accusing dozens of trade partners of trading in goods that have been produced using forced labour.

These are "tariffs in search of an authority", as one industry figure put it. The forced labour line shores up President Trump's tariffs against a challenge from Congress or the courts.

In practice, the levies are curiously similar by country to a previous round of tariffs imposed supposedly for completely different reasons.

The good news for the UK is that the regime effectively remains the same as before.

What has changed is that our nearest neighbours in the European Union now have a much better deal than before, and in turn are in a better situation than the UK.

While the UK and the EU each appear to have a 10% rate, the EU's is a flat rate, while the UK's will apply alongside other tariffs, in a range of goods including footwear and textiles.

The government has struck effective side deals on medicines, steel, aluminium, cars and, with the help of King Charles, whisky.

At the end of this process however the overall trade-weighted effective tariff rate for the EU (8.5%) could end up a bit lower than the UK's (6.8%).

It should not matter that much, but the help given by doing the first deal, and by post-Brexit trade freedoms, looks to have been short-lived.

The British Chambers of Commerce trade expert William Bain points to the competitive advantage for EU exporters into the US in some sectors.

The EU has secured better treatment because it has passed a ban on forced labour goods, which the UK has not.

This is not an accusation on the use of forced labour in supply chains. It is about the passing of specific legislation, mirroring the US ban on products that have used forced labour in supply chains.

News.title: PlayStation Network down, leaving thousands of gamers unable to play
News.content:
Gamers have been unable to connect to the PlayStation Network, leaving some unable to play digital games for several hours.

According to Down Detector, which tracks outages, tens of thousands of people have reported problems globally, external with the service - although some reported they were able to get back online since.

The outage, which affects gamers' ability to launch games, apps or network features on their PlayStation, has prompted some to highlight their concerns around Sony's plans to no longer release new PlayStation games on discs from January 2028.

Sony's status page, external currently reads all services are "experiencing issues" and it was "working to resolve the issue as soon as possible".

The BBC has approached PlayStation for comment.

"Can't play digital games till you fix it. Yet I can put my disc in and play. The all digital future looks great," read one comment on X, external.

Sony said in a blog post earlier this month, external that new games would still be able to be bought in shops, but they would come with a digital code.

The problems began to appear around the same time as an alert from Amazon Web Services that some servers were facing issues, however this has since been resolved, external.

News.title: Southport killer Axel Rudakubana appears to be manipulating the system, families' lawyer says
News.content:
A lawyer for the families of the children murdered by Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has said his transfer from prison to a psychiatric hospital may be an attempt to "manipulate the system".

Rudakubana, 19, was given a life sentence for the murder of three children - Alice da Silva Aguiar, 9, Bebe King, 6, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, 7 - and attempted murder of eight other children and two adults.

On Thursday, he was moved from HMP Belmarsh to Broadmoor psychiatric hospital in Berkshire.

Prisoners who are considered to present a risk to staff, inmates or themselves because of mental disorders can be moved to hospital under the Mental Health Act.

Next Wednesday marks two years since Rudakubana carried out the attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class on 29 July 2024.

Lawyer Chris Walker, who represents the three bereaved families, said they "don't believe the merits" of the transfer on the basis of a mental health issue and is calling for more information from ministers.

"In my mind this is a new event, this is something which occurred whilst he was at prison, and we at this stage don't believe the merits of it in terms of him because I've seen no evidence at all until today which suggests he has a significant mental health disorder," Walker told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

He added: "We do have an evil person but being evil does not mean that you're suffering with psychosis of some sort.

"We need to know is this a single event, is this a recurring event, is this him playing the system and we need those answers."

The Prison Officers' Association told the BBC that Rudakubana was transferred due to a deterioration in his mental health.

Walker added in a separate statement that the news would "devastate" the families at any time but "the fact that this has occurred as we approach the second anniversary in our view is another move by AR who would appear to be attempting, once again, to manipulate the system".

He continued: "We have been given the barest of details and whilst we are supporting the families through this we are urgently seeking a meeting with the appropriate authorities to understand the situation before commenting further."

A lawyer for the families of the attack's survivors said they did not want to give "notoriety" to Rudakubana and that attention should be focused on supporting the children around the anniversary.

Nicola Ryan-Donnelly of Fletchers Solicitors said: "The focus of public outrage should not be on moves that this perpetrator has made, it should be examining how we are two years on from this attack and some of these girls are still not receiving the proper psychological care and support that they should be to recover from this."

Prior to Rudakubana's sentencing last year, his defence lawyer told the court no psychiatric evidence could suggest a mental disorder contributed to his actions.

The court also heard how Rudakubana presented as having high functioning autism and did not have any associated learning disabilities.

Stan Reiz KC added that his client had appeared to have been a "normal child" until he reached 13, adding: "However, he did make a transition from a normal, well-disciplined child to someone who was capable of committing acts of such shocking and senseless violence."

Rudakubana was deemed mentally fit to be detained, interviewed and stand trial. His late guilty plea meant his mental health was not discussed in detail in court during a trial.

He was given a 52-year prison sentence in January 2025 but the judge was unable to impose a whole life order due to Rudakubana being 17 when he carried out the attack. He will likely never be released.

News.title: Mega dinghy carries record 165 migrants to UK
News.content:
A record 165 migrants reached the UK in a single boat, the Home Office has confirmed.

The number broke the previous record from July, when 128 crossed the Channel from France in one vessel.

Border Security Command was pictured towing a mega dinghy - estimated to be the same size as a standard bus at 13m (42ft) long - when it arrived in Dover on Thursday afternoon.

A Home Office spokesperson said the crossing served as a "stark reminder that criminal gangs have no regard for the safety of those they claim to help".

"The reality is clear and lives are being lost in the Channel," they added.

A total of 162 people died, external in the busy waterway between 2018 and 2025, according to the University of Oxford's Migration Observatory.

This rises to 257 when considering other migration-related deaths in the area, such as accidents involving people trying to board lorries bound for the UK, it added.

News.title: Fifty women tell BBC they were pressured into having sex with strangers
News.content:
Warning: This story contains details of sexual acts

Fifty women have told the BBC they were pressured or coerced by their partners into having sex with strangers.

They got in contact following an investigation which told the story of a woman who said she had been pressured into having sex with more than 100 people she did not know.

Many of the women who came forward said they had sex through swinging despite not wanting to, either because they feared the consequences of refusing or felt they had to keep their partners happy.

They spoke of deep, long-lasting trauma.

"I remember many nights of my partner keeping me up all night screaming at me, threatening me, and attempting to gaslight me into believing this was something I wanted," said one woman. "It was never what I wanted."

Another told us: "I felt like I had been given away. I felt used. I felt so dirty."

Most encounters were arranged via the website FabSwingers, say the women, which claims to have more than half a million UK active monthly accounts.

Six women told BBC News they had been raped by men met through the site.

One said her partner had forced her to have sex with more than 90 men through FabSwingers. On one occasion, he held her down by the ankles, she told us.

Sixteen said intimate photos of them had been uploaded to the website without their permission.

News.title: Chris Mason: What Burnham's first week in power tells us about his agenda
News.content:
"We are on borrowed time if we don't get a move on," Angela Rayner, the former deputy prime minister who is back in the cabinet this week as housing secretary, told the BBC's Today programme on Friday.

It has been quite the week at Westminster. Sir Keir Starmer's departure as prime minister on Monday seems rather a while ago.

The fledgling Burnham administration has been seeking to find its feet and make a decent first impression at the same time, as many try to do in the first days in a job.

There has been an early pattern in these early days: an early morning nugget of news dropping from No10.

On Thursday, it was business rates in England; on Wednesday, it was bus fares in England and on Tuesday, it was a VAT cut on electricity bills.

Today, the prime minister is assembling what Rayner calls "a pride of mayors" among others for a meeting of what is known as the National Economic Council at the new No 10 North in Manchester.

Andy Burnham claims his new base in Manchester represents the beginning of "the biggest rebalancing of power our country has seen, external" and he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years".

His early announcements have been considerably more piecemeal than that â he says his "10 year plan for Britain" will come later in the year.

It is worth remembering there was talk from both Boris Johnson and his allies and from Sir Keir Starmer about their plans for the decade ahead â both fizzled out rather more quickly than that.

So how should we assess how much politics has changed, or not?

The early evidence - and let's be frank, it is only that given we are just a few days in - points to Andy Burnham being both more sharp and more nimble than his predecessor in setting out what he is attempting to do and trying to point to early examples of what that might look like, with the announcements of the last few days.

With the tinkering of how the government is run, like the creation of the Office of Prime Minister, and the establishment of No 10 North, he's made it clear that the arteries of power flow very much to and from him.

He hopes he can overcome the critique of Sir Keir Starmer and others, that one of the frustrations of being prime minister can be pulling levers and nothing actually happens.

News.title: Chris Brown pleads guilty to affray over nightclub attack in London
News.content:
US singer Chris Brown has pleaded guilty to affray over what prosecutors called "a vicious and unprovoked attack" in a London nightclub in 2023.

Police said CCTV showed that Brown, one of the world's biggest R&B stars, hit the victim on the head with a glass bottle several times, and that the man was then chased, pushed to the floor and kicked.

The 37-year-old star had been due to face a trial on more serious charges, which he denied - assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm, and having an offensive weapon, namely a tequila bottle. However, those charges have now been dropped.

Affray, which is defined as using or threatening violence towards someone and making them fear for their safety, is punishable by up to three years in jail. Brown will be sentenced in October.

News.title: Hero swimmer helped two children during beach tragedy
News.content:
Witnesses say a heroic day-tripper managed to haul two children back to shore during an incident where a mother and daughter drowned.

Beverly Smit, 60, described the unnamed rescuer swimming out to sea three times as the tragedy unfolded in West Mersea, near Colchester, on Wednesday evening.

Shally Rahman, 41, and Samiha Rahman, 15, were trying to rescue a seven-year-old boy from the water when they got into difficulty and died.

Essex Police said the group, from Barking, east London, were all related to each other and the boy remained in hospital, fighting for his life.

Recalling the moment the "Good Samaritan" sprang into action, Smit said: "They were calling for help and the children and adults were out there.

"He swam out, I think, three times. Two of the children he brought back were not in good condition.

"It's not an easy swim when the tide's coming in - you're swimming against the tide. The water [on Wednesday] was particularly quite cold."

News.title: Heat health alerts in effect for parts of UK as rain returns for some this weekend
News.content:
Yellow heat health alerts came into effect across central and southern England on Friday morning with temperatures forecast to reach 30C (86F) in places.

The alerts, issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), cover the East and West Midlands, eastern England, London, south-east England and south-west England and are valid from 09:00 BST on Friday until 09:00 on Sunday.

The UKHSA warns that heat is expected to cause minor impacts for health and social care services, with an increased risk to life for vulnerable people.

It comes as parts of the UK prepare to see much-needed rain this weekend - although amounts are expected to be relatively small, especially in the south.

A drought was officially declared for large parts of north and mid-Wales on Thursday.

The rest of Wales, along with much of central, southern and eastern England, is in "prolonged dry weather" category - one stage below a drought - and the Sottish Environment Protection Agency said much of eastern Scotland has moved into 'water scarcity' status

Hosepipe bans are in force for millions of the customers across eastern and southern England.

News.title: Dad who murdered four-week-old son jailed for 18 years
News.content:
A man who murdered his four-week-old son after drinking up to nine pints of beer on a night out has been jailed for life with a minimum term of 18 years.

Tony Bartlett returned to the family home in Chard, Somerset, on 16 July 2022 and shook baby Atticus in what the sentencing judge described as "a sudden fit of anger".

The 39-year-old caused serious injuries to his son's spinal cord and ribs, as well as brain damage so severe he never regained consciousness or the ability to breathe independently. Atticus died seven days later.

Bartlett, who was convicted after a trial at Bristol Crown Court earlier this month, was jailed for life with a minimum term of 18 years.

Warning: This story contains details which readers may find distressing.

The trial heard the former postman, from Axminster in Devon, had gone to a pub and comedy club with his then-partner Evelyn Ballentyne on the night Atticus was fatally injured.

It was their first evening out since their son's birth.

After they returned home, Ballentyne went upstairs and left Bartlett alone to feed Atticus.

News.title: More than 100 firefighters tackling blaze at industrial unit after ‘large explosion’ in Essex

U.N. human rights chief Volker Türk faces a vote Friday for a second four-year term but is running into opposition from critics and some countries for his criticism of Israel's attacks in Gaza and his approach to China’s crackdown on its Uyghur minority.

Secretary-General Antonio Guterres quietly nominated the Austrian lawyer for a second term. After private consultations but no public discussion, the 193-member General Assembly scheduled a vote on his reappointment for Friday afternoon.

Former head of Human Rights Watch Ken Roth called it “a stealth procedure” to avoid scrutiny by civil society and the public.

The job of the U.N. rights chief, by its nature, is tricky: It requires speaking out against rights violations by the governments of the countries that make up the membership of the world body. For instance, Türk has sharply criticized Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Some suggest an extension for Türk until the end of the year

Türk's term expires on Oct. 11, and Russia’s U.N. Mission said it has proposed extending his term just until Dec. 31 — the day Guterres’ second five-year term as secretary-general ends.

Russia called Guterres’ effort to give Türk four more years as U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights “unprecedented.” None of his predecessors have served two full terms since the job was created in 1993.

An extension just until the end of the year would leave the choice of a new human rights chief to the next secretary-general. Six candidates are vying to be the new U.N. chief.

Guterres sent letters to regional groups at the United Nations earlier this month informing them of his intention to reappoint Türk. The African group had no objection, but the Latin American countries had several, including Nicaragua, Argentina and Paraguay.

Israel's Foreign Ministry called Guterres' action to get a second term for Türk the U.N. secretary-general's “latest moral failure,” saying on social media that the choice should be left to his successor.

“After years of bias against Israel, the answer is accountability — not rewriting the rules,” the ministry said.

Guterres is ‘following the rules’ on the reappointment, UN says

U.N. spokesman Stephane Dujarric, says Guterres is following the 1993 resolution that established a U.N. high commissioner for human rights and allows for a second term.

“The secretary-general is doing things in a very transparent manner, following the rules and his authority,” Dujarric told reporters Friday. “Consultations were had with member states prior to this and with regional groups.”

Türk “is ready to serve” a new term, rights office spokesperson Ravina Shamdasani said. She noted the job calls for the “promotion and protection of human rights everywhere, and as a part of this, he sees it as his role to engage with all states.”

As human rights chief, the longtime U.N. functionary who worked for Guterres at United Nations headquarters in New York, Türk has expressed concerns on issues in China as diverse as the fate of detained individuals — like artist Gao Zhen, lawyer Yu Wensheng and media mogul Jimmy Lai — and counterterrorism and assimilation practices that affect ethnic minorities including the Uyghurs in the regions of Xinjiang, Inner Mongolia and Tibet.

Critics insist he could have done more to publicly follow up on a report issued by his predecessor, former Chilean President Michelle Bachelet, that said China’s discriminatory detention of Uyghurs and other mostly Muslim ethnic groups in Xinjiang may amount to crimes against humanity.

Türk also has stopped short of joining independent U.N. rights experts who have accused Israel of genocide against Palestinians during its war against Hamas in Gaza. Israel vehemently denies those claims.

Critic focuses on approach to China's treatment of Uyghurs

Roth called Türk “a disaster” and said “the biggest stain on Turk’s reputation is his utter abandonment of the Uyghurs.” He called them victims of the most severe state persecution that Türk has ignored.

The Chinese government denies the Uyghurs have been or are being persecuted. It maintains its policies in Xinjiang rooted out terrorism and religious extremism after sporadic bouts of violence rocked the region in previous decades.

Türk has used both private engagement with Beijing and public advocacy to support human rights in China, his office said. Roth called that “an admission that he is doing nothing, that he’s putting the plight of the Uyghurs on the deep back burner, and is just pretending to care.”

Roth said Türk has a major problem because the job of U.N. human rights commissioner “should be about stirring up public pressure, and you do that by being tough, provocative, timely.”

He “has succeeded in making a powerful position largely innocuous,” talking about issues in a way “that makes people’s eyes glaze over,” Roth said.

___

Associated Press writers Jamey Keaten in Geneva and Farnoush Amiri in New York contributed to this report.

News.content:

British sprinter and Olympian CJ Ujah has denied playing a part in an alleged cryptocurrency fraud.

The athlete, who competed at the 2016 and 2021 Olympic Games, appeared among nine others before Chelmsford Crown Court on Friday.

The group are accused of being part of an organised crime group linked to a scam.

The scam was said to have involved phone calls to multiple victims from people purporting to be police officers and cryptocurrency companies.

Victims are reported to have been tricked into sharing important security details before discovering funds stored in their crypto wallets had been stolen.

open image in gallery Ujah and eight other defendants pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to defraud ( PA )

One of the victims is alleged to have lost more than £300,000.

A series of co-ordinated search warrants were carried out across Kent, Essex and London on April 29 as part of an investigation by the Eastern Region Special Operations Unit (ERSOU).

Ujah, whose name appeared in the court list as Chijindu Ujah and eight other defendants pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to defraud.

Another defendant, Joseph Umoru, will enter his plea at a later date.

A 12-week trial was set for Chelmsford Crown Court from May 24 next year.

The next court hearing will be held at the same court on September 9.

One of the other defendants, Brandon Mingeli, denied a further count of converting criminal property.

Mingeli pleaded guilty to two counts of possession of a false identity document.

Ujah, 32, of Enfield, north London, became only the fifth Briton to break the 10-second barrier for the 100 metres, running 9.96 seconds in 2014.

He won 4x100m relay gold at the world championships in London in 2017.

At the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, he raced in the 4x100m final but tested positive for two banned substances, which led to his team being stripped of their silver medal.

He was subsequently cleared of intentionally taking prohibited substances.

The other defendants are Brandon Mingeli, 25, of Thamesmead, south-east London; Louis Richards-Miller, 24, of Greenwich, south-east London; Joseph Umoru, 24, of Abbey Wood, south-east London; Adedeji Kujore, 24, of Erith, Kent; Taiwo Yusuf, 24, Kehinde Yusuf, 24, Jayden Nakayama, 25 – all from Greenwich; Samantha Gyabaa, 23, of Hackney, east London; and Jami Durston, 28, of Chelmsford, Essex.
