World.title: Wildfires trigger mass evacuations across France and Spain
World.content:
In France, 67,000 residents fled as wildfires swept through the tourist peninsula of Cap Ferret on the Atlantic coast.

 

The main blaze, active since Wednesday near Cap Ferret (60 kilometres from Bordeaux), has consumed 125 square kilometres. Around 1,500 people escaped the peninsula by sea, arriving in Arcachon aboard water taxis and ferries.

In total, 44,000 people were evacuated in the Gironde department, where 53 homes and a campsite were destroyed and 42 firefighters injured, while 23,000 were evacuated in the neighbouring Landes department due to an uncontained 25-square-kilometre blaze further south.

"It’s quite impressive and even frightening," said Laurent Moretti, a resident of Arès. "An evacuation on this scale has never happened before. All we really hope is that the firefighters can quickly get it under control."

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez stated that France has 32 active wildfires, with over 50,000 hectares burned since January, nearly triple last year's total.

In Spain, the government declared a national emergency for wildfires for the first time. A heatwave bringing temperatures above 39°C and high winds has fanned multiple blazes.

Two major fires west of Madrid merged into a single blaze, charring 30 square kilometres and prompting the evacuation of 18,000 people. Nearby in Ávila, a blaze consumed 90 square kilometres, forcing 1,500 people to flee.

Authorities later ordered the evacuation of 7,000 more people from two new localities west of Madrid. In total, around 40,000 people in the Madrid region have been evacuated or told to remain indoors. Firefighters continued attempting to extinguish Spain’s second-largest recorded fire in Guadalajara, which has destroyed 320 square kilometres over the past week.

Spanish police arrested one man in Castilla y León for starting a fire using farm machinery during a ban, with a second person under investigation.

Wildfire analyst Raúl Quílez noted that climate change and rural land abandonment have left villages exposed, creating a "perfect cocktail" for severe blazes.

International assistance and broader impact

Both nations have requested European Union assistance. France will receive aerial reinforcements from Croatia, Portugal, the Czech Republic, and Slovakia. Spain is receiving four water-dumping aircraft deployed by Italy and Greece, along with support from the Copernicus satellite system.

Wildfires also continue to affect Sicily, where temperatures over 40°C resulted in scattered evacuations and claimed the life of a firefighter in Caltanissetta.

World.title: Wildfires up 57% in Europe in just four years, WHO warns
World.content:
This summer, wildfires have broken out in France, Germany, Greece, Spain and Portugal, with firefighters killed while battling blazes in France and Italy. From the start of the year until 22 July, 1,254 fires have been detected in Europe, emitting over 8.31 million tonnes of CO₂.

 

Concerningly, wildfires are becoming more frequent and intense in Europe, WHO Europe said on Friday. Portugal and Spain have each reported a 100% increase in wildfires this year compared with the same period in 2025. Since 2022, the number of wildfires has risen by 57% across the WHO European Region. Last year alone, around 2.2 million hectares burned, while 254,388 hectares had already been destroyed by 22 July this year, according to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS).

Percentage Increase in Reported Wildfires WHO Europe

And it is only going to get worse.

“As climate change drives a warming world, we need to prepare for more frequent and intense wildfires,” WHO Europe chief Hans Henri P. Kluge said.

Fires not only destroy livelihoods, force evacuations, disrupt healthcare systems and claim lives, but also take a toll on human health even miles away.

“The health impacts extend far beyond the flames,” said

Wildfire smoke can travel hundreds of kilometres, worsening air quality far from the fire zone. It contains a hazardous mix of pollutants, such as PM2.5, NO2, ozone, aromatic hydrocarbons and lead. When fires burn homes or buildings, they can also release toxic chemicals from electronics, furniture, plastics and paints.

“Smoke can travel long distances, worsening heart and respiratory conditions and affecting mental health, particularly among older people, children, pregnant women and those with chronic diseases,” Kluge said.

He called on governments to ensure timely “wildfire, weather and air-quality alerts, clear health advice, and accessible primary and emergency care.”

“People living in or travelling through affected areas should follow official advice, move away from active fires when it is safe, avoid unnecessary travel, and wear a well-fitting protective mask if they must go outdoors near wildfire smoke,” Kluge said.

World.title: The church reshaping Spain's history: did Moors and Christians once live together in peace?
World.content:
A hill in the northwest of Murcia is forcing historians to rethink some of the most entrenched ideas about the early centuries of al-Andalus. Excavations at the Cerro de la Virgen de Calasparra have brought to light an early Christian church that not only survived the Muslim conquest of the year 713, but remained in use for almost two centuries more.

 

The study (source in Spanish), published in the scientific journal 'Salduie' by researchers David Martínez and Rubén Fernández, documents the existence of a temple founded around the first half of the 5th century that appears to have retained its religious character at least until the 9th century. If this chronology is fully confirmed, it would be one of the strongest pieces of evidence for the continuity of Christian worship on the Iberian Peninsula during the early years of Moorish rule.

The church was identified thanks to a series of survey and excavation campaigns carried out in the area since 2021. Archaeologists describe it as a single-nave building with a tripartite chancel, a layout they see as characteristic of certain "late antique" churches.

"This represents an architectural model with notable parallels in Visigothic churches such as Santa Cristina de Lena," the authors of the study point out, in reference to this church in Asturias. They also note that the sacristies and apses show parallels with some "parochial and episcopal" churches in Syria, a connection that reflects the use of similar architectural models around the Mediterranean in Late Antiquity.

Much more than a matter of time

Radiocarbon dating places the construction of the building between the years 410 and 440 AD. This is supported by ceramic and stratigraphic analyses that back the hypothesis of a prolonged occupation of the site. The site had already attracted researchers' attention in previous campaigns, when a unique bronze early Christian lamp in the shape of a Eucharistic dove was found, considered at the time an exceptional piece in the European context.

However, the most significant aspect of the new study is not the age of the temple, but its survival as such after the Muslim conquest of the peninsula. Traditionally, many historical accounts have presented the arrival of Moorish troops at the beginning of the 8th century as a relatively sharp break with Visigothic traditions. The Calasparra finds, however, sketch out a more complex reality.

The researchers argue that there is no evidence that the church was converted into a mosque, or that it immediately lost its religious function. In fact, they state that "the record, with the presence of storage containers and cooking ware, should not be understood as evidence of a desanctification of the church or of its conversion into Islamic dwellings", the study notes.

The typological and stratigraphic study of the ceramics points to a continuation of the church's liturgical character well into the 9th century David Martínez y Rubén Fernández Authors of the study

"On the contrary, such materials should be read as indicators of continued use of the space for community practices that included both worship and resource management," they maintain. This interpretation is reinforced by the central conclusion of the paper: "The typological and stratigraphic study of the ceramics points to a continuation of the church's liturgical character well into the 9th century."

The research also places this phenomenon in the context of the kūra of Tudmīr, the administrative entity that emerged after the pact signed in 713 between the Muslim authorities and the Visigothic nobleman Theodemir. That agreement allowed numerous Christian communities to retain, for a time, part of their political, religious and economic structures in exchange for paying taxes.

Taxation itself is another key to the site. Among the materials recovered are scales, weights and other objects linked to economic control and the collection of taxes. One of these weights even bears an Arabic inscription that can be translated as "justice belongs to God".

Christian faith, Muslim taxes

The presence of these objects shows that the Cerro de la Virgen played a role that went far beyond the strictly religious. Its strategic position, commanding important communication routes and nearby agricultural resources, turned it into a centre of territorial and economic organisation. In other words, the Christian community that used the church also took part in the fiscal mechanisms of the new Andalusi power.

The authors sum up this situation in a forceful statement: "The hill was a Christian community subject to the taxes of the Islamic state and forced to insert itself into regional fiscal and commercial circuits."

For the researchers, the case of Calasparra helps to explain more clearly how the islamisation of peninsular society took place. Far from an immediate replacement of populations or institutions, the process seems to have been marked by decades of adaptation, coexistence and gradual transformation.

They explain that the Christian population "gradually became trapped between two converging dynamics: on the one hand, the growing capacity of the Andalusi state to reorder the territory and ensure fiscal extraction; on the other, islamisation also operated as a path towards social and legal accommodation".

The study concludes that the disappearance of these Christian communities was not necessarily due to episodes of destruction or expulsion by the Moors, but to a slow process of integration into the new Andalusi society.

"The ecclesiastical hierarchy was unable to sustain the advantageous agreements reached at the time of the conquest, while growing centralisation and fiscal efficiency and the urban pull of Córdoba eroded the productive base of churches, monasteries and Christian elites," Martínez and Fernández state in their study.

More than 13 centuries later, the ruins of the Cerro de la Virgen thus offer a new window onto one of the most decisive periods in the history of the Iberian Peninsula. And they suggest that the transition between the Visigothic world and al-Andalus was, at least in some territories, far more gradual, negotiated and complex than had been assumed for decades.

World.title: Latvia to ban books, newspapers and video games from Russia and Belarus
World.content:
Latvia’s parliament approved law tweaks restricting the import of a range of Russian and Belarusian consumer goods not already covered by EU sanctions, in a move aimed at further cutting economic ties with Moscow and limiting the spread of Kremlin propaganda.

 

“To ensure the security of Latvian society… and to provide general support to Ukrainian society, the importation of certain industrial goods into the Republic of Latvia from the Russian Federation and the Republic of Belarus is prohibited,” the amendments to Latvia's law (link in Latvian language) on Support for the Civilian Population of Ukraine read.

The tweaked law prohibits imports of goods originating in Russia and Belarus that are not already subject to EU sanctions, tariffs or other trade restrictions — in what appears to be one of the first national bans in the EU on a broad range of Russian and Belarusian consumer goods beyond the bloc's sanctions regime. The restrictions will also apply to goods imported via third countries if their country of origin is Russia or Belarus.

The ban, which was approved on the same day as the EU agreed its latest sanction package, covers products that lawmakers say can be used to spread propaganda and disinformation, including books, newspapers and video games, as well as sporting goods, toys, clothing and footwear.

"These amendments are the latest tool to systematically reduce economic ties with Russia and Belarus while maintaining our unwavering support for Ukraine in its fight for freedom and independence,” said Raimonds Bergmanis, Chairman of the Defense, Internal Affairs and Corruption Prevention Committee responsible for the progress of the bill in the Latvian Parliament.

Imports of the newly targeted goods from Russia and Belarus totalled €12.5 million in 2025, accounting for 6.5% of Latvia's remaining imports from the two countries and just 0.05% of Latvia's total imports.

Cutting the last ties

The proposal was drafted by Latvia's Foreign Ministry and fast-tracked through parliament as part of the government's broader effort to eliminate remaining trade links with Russia.

"Latvia has already significantly reduced economic ties with Russia, but our goal should be a complete policy of refusal with regard to the goods of the aggressor state,” Minister of Economy Viktors Valainis said at the end of May, following the ministers' meeting on restricting trade with Russia. At that meeting, the Foreign Ministry was instructed to prepare the legislation approved by parliament this week.

The final list of products covered by the ban will be adopted by the Cabinet of Ministers. The law will enter into force the day after it is promulgated, with the import restrictions set to remain in place until 1 July 2027.

Foreign Minister Baiba Braže has repeatedly argued that Latvia should end its remaining economic ties with Russia by the end of 2026 and has called on other EU member states to adopt similar measures.

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

Spotlight on Africa is produced by RFI's English language service. This episode was mixed by Erwan Rome.

World.title: Russia hits drone demonstration near Kyiv, killing 10
World.content:
Ukraine says 10 were killed and around 100 injured in the strike, a day after Zelenskyy met with officials from US arms giant Raytheon. Meanwhile, in St. Petersburg, another Wildberries warehouse came under drone fire.

Russia struck various sites in Ukraine on Friday, including a defense event on the outskirts of Kyiv thought to be showcasing aerial defense technologies like drones.

Sometimes fatal attacks elsewhere in the country disrupted power supplies in five separate regions.

Meanwhile, Ukraine again struck facilities belonging to Russia's largest online retailer, Wildberries, this time in President Vladimir Putin's hometown of St. Petersburg.

And in the skies over Romania, NATO jets downed a stray drone on Friday morning, with no immediate reports of casualties or damage.

Across the Atlantic, the White House said President Donald Trump and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy would hold talks on Tuesday of next week, almost four and a half years after Russia's full scale invasion.

The strikes came soon after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held talks with representatives of US weapons manufacturer Raytheon, which makes the mobile Patriot missile interceptor SAMs Image: State Emergency Service of Ukraine

What happened in Ukraine?

Acting regional military administration head Ruslan Oliinyk said the strike hit the grounds of a privately operated military training site that was hosting an event at the time. The site is some 20-30 kilometers (12-18 miles) from central Kyiv, in the Bucha district.

Attorney General Ruslan Kravchenko called the attack a war crime, saying that 10 people were killed and around 100 more were injured.

The surrounding area was also struck repeatedly, with Zelenskyy posting images of destruction and rescue efforts from the wider Kyiv region.

He said, "Interceptors for Patriot systems are the number one priority," a reference to the air defense systems made by US arms giant Raytheon, which had sent a delegation to Kyiv on Thursday.

Russia's Defense Ministry also acknowledged the attack online, saying it had used "high-precision long-range weapons" to target "a demonstration of unmanned aerial vehicles [UAVs or drones], including promising ones, of Ukrainian and foreign production, used to strike civilian targets in Russia."

Russia's Defense Ministry claimed that at the time of the strike, leading defense industry officials and Ukrainian military members were at the site, saying these people were "directly planning and carrying out strikes on Russian territory."

Five people were reported killed in the eastern region of Slovyansk on Friday. The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, bemoaned one such strike that she said hit "Latvia's Honorary Consulate" in Slovyansk, saying, "We will summon Russia's envoy to the EU over today's strikes," and thatshe would propose further EU sanctions to target Russia's "military-industrial complex."

Ukraine's energy company Ukrenergo reported damage to power plants in five separate regions, saying around 150,000 people were left without power in the Chernihiv region alone after an attack on a facility there.

Smoke billowed over Vladimir Putin's hometown St. Petersburg on Friday after the latest strike on Wildberries online retail warehouses Image: REUTERS

What happened in Russia?

The latest Ukrainian drone strikes to target warehouses of the online retail giant Wildberries struck in St. Petersburg, Vladimir Putin's powerbase for decades, on Friday.

Company founder Tatyana Kim said facilities came under attack in St. Petersburg, in the adjacent Leningrad region, and also in occupied Ukraine in Simferopol, a city in illegally annexed Crimea.

Large plumes of smoke were visible rising over central St. Petersburg on Friday morning.

Ukraine has struck a series of Wildberries facilities in recent days, causing large fires. It describes the sites as logistics hubs and says it provides components that Russia uses for military equipment like drones. Analysts also speculate that it might be an attempt to make ordinary Russians feel the consequences of the war and sense that their government cannot safeguard their interests.

Wildberries facilities have been repeatedly struck on an almost daily basis this week Image: AFP

What happened in Romania?

Romania's Defense Ministry and later NATO also said on Friday that Alliance aircraft had shot down a stray drone that had entered Romanian airspace.

Bucharest's Defense Ministry said a Romanian F-16 fighter engaged the drone and neutralized it "over an unpopulated area in the vicinity of Padina, Buzau County."

It described a flight path entering its airspace around Sulina, a town bordering the southwestern tip of Ukraine, across the Black Sea from occupied Crimea. It headed west and inland, approaching Buzau. After tracking the drone for a little over an hour, a Romanian Air Force jet shot it down just after 11 a.m. local time, the ministry said.

Several incidents of stray drones straying into NATO members, more typically in the Baltic but also sometimes further south, have taken place this year. Ukraine tends to blame Russia for scrambling the drones' navigation systems and causing them to encroach on other countries' airspace.

World.title: US floats AI 'kill switch' to stop rogue AI models
World.content:
A rogue AI agent has sent a "wake-up call" about the perils of the fast-evolving technology, sparking calls to provide a US government kill switch. But what exactly does that mean, and what are the issues with it?

Lawmakers in the US have called for an AI kill switch after an Open AI agent in testing went rogue and hacked a tech startup earlier this week.

Congressman Ted Lieu, a Democrat, and Congressman Nathaniel Moran, a Republican, introduced a bill named the "AI Kill Switch Act" on Thursday.

The move came a day after Open AI CEO Sam Altman admitted to a "significant security incident" in which an Open AI agent had escaped its testing environment, reached the internet and broke into tech startup Hugging Face to try to fulfill its task. In other words, Open AI lost control.

Hugging Face is an open-source repository for sharing AI models used largely by developers and researchers. The company's co-founder, Thomas Wolf, called the incident a "wake-up call” and "very different" from the usual cyberattacks.

"This will be one of the most common types of cyberattacks we see", he told the BBC, adding that most firms are not aware that the "game has changed."

Can Germany and Europe hold their own in AI race? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the wake of the attack there were some unsubstantiated claims that the incident was a PR stunt to raise the profile of Hugging Face. Regardless of the truth of the matter, the incident has brought into even sharper focus the threat posed by AI without clear guardrails.

What is an AI kill switch?

There are different types and levels of kill switch, according to what's gone wrong. What politicians Lieu and Moran want is to ensure the US Department of Homeland Security has the authority to order a private company to shut down an AI model or tool in an incident like what happened this week, when control is lost.

"It is imperative that these AI systems have kill switches so we can keep this technology from causing catastrophic harm, and that the federal government has the clear authority and process to shut down rogue AI models," said Lieu.

Rather than a physical switch, this would involve any compromised AI company disabling or throttling a number of technical processes to shut a rogue agent, or program, down.

The US government has generally welcomed AI advances. The Pentagon said earlier this year that the US military is fast becoming an "AI-first fighting force," after signing new and expanded contracts with many of the sector's biggest names. In 2025, the Trump administration launched an"‘AI Action Plan" which he said would "remove red tape and onerous regulation" around AI development.

Why is an AI kill switch needed?

Companies including Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic and Samsung have already agreed to show US authorities new AI tools and capabilities before release. In theory, this should mean that a kill switch is not needed in products released to the public.

But the commitment is voluntary and does not mandate a kill switch. Neither would that mechanism stop a product in testing, like OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol, which was involved in this week's incident.

The rapid rise of AI has posed serious questions over its regulation, with technology able to move much faster than lawmakers. There are also concerns that models may, at some point, become sophisticated enough to bypass a kill switch.

How the US is merging artificial intelligence and warfare To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The bill in the US is an attempt for a government to take some form of control over a largely unregulated technology in which power is largely concentrated in a few private companies. However, even if the AI Kill Switch Act is successful, it will still rely on the cooperation of profit-driven private companies.

What other AI safeguards are US authorities now considering?

As well as the kill switch capability, the proposal in the US seeks "incident reporting and [to] preserve forensic records so we actually learn from failures instead of only hearing about them after the fact."

At the same time, but separately to the kill switch act, a bipartisan group of six US lawmakers has proposed legislation that ​would require developers of the most powerful AI models to submit them for independent security audits. The auditors would be overseen by a new role in the US Department of Commerce, which would also accredit the auditors.

World.title: Europe wildfires: Many flee by boat as fires spread, merge
World.content:
Tens of thousands hopped onto cars and boats to escape southwestern France's wildfires. In the Madrid region, authorities declared a national emergency as at least two fires merged.

Wildfires continued to rage through parts of France and Spain on Friday, forcing tens of thousands to evacuate and authorities to ask European Union neighbors for help.

French authorities ordered the total evacuation of the tourist Cap Ferret peninsula off the Atlantic coast, with many boarding boats to flee.

In Spain, two fires converged near the capital, Madrid, with authorities declaring a national emergency, the first over a wildfire.

Heat waves fuel wildfires across southern Europe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What do we know about France's Cap Ferret fire?

Over 60,000 people evacuated the area in and around Cap Ferret as the blaze consumed some 100 square kilometers (38 square miles) of land.

Authorities sent boats to help with the evacuation, with many others using small water taxis.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told local television that a fire that erupted in Saumos, north of Cap Ferret, was the largest so far this season in France. It was threatening to cut off the only road out of the peninsula.

"It's quite impressive and even frightening," the Associated Press quoted Laurent Moretti, a resident in the town of Ares, as saying. "An evacuation on this scale has never happened before. All we really hope is that the firefighters can quickly get it under control."

Tens of thousands had to evacuate the tourist area of Cap Ferret as wildfires continued to rage Image: Stephane Mahe/REUTERS

Some 1,500 of those who fled the peninsula arrived in the city of Arcachon by sea. They were met with coffee, fruit and water in a reception area prepared by town officials.

In the Gironde department, Nunez said 40,000 people have been evacuated, with 23,000 more in the Landes department.

French President Emmanuel Macron said the country will receive EU reinforcements to help put out the blaze, after calling for the neighbors' help.

At least 2 fires merge in Madrid

As Spanish authorities declared a national emergency over the wildfires, two fires converged despite the deployment of over 2,000 personnel and 10 aircraft in an effort to control the blaze, according to Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska.

Some 40,000 people evacuated or confined due to Madrid region wildfires, officials have said. Over 19,000 people were ordered to evacuate from towns in the mountains west of Madrid, where many of the capital's residents sport second homes. The area is densely populated.

Only emergency vehicles were allowed on roads near the blaze, the AFP news agency reported. Police set up checkpoints to prevent unauthorized access.

Nicanor Sen, the government representative for the Castile and Leon region, told reporters a third fire in nearby Avila province was about to also merge with the other fires, or may have already done so.

Residents had to flee to shelters in the area west of Madrid to escape the fires Image: Pierre-Philippe Marcou/AFP

"I've lived here for 36 years and I've never seen anything like it. ​Nor did I expect it. I thought they were going to get it under control last night, but it was already late, and it was all out of control," local resident Javier Martin told Reuters.

Spanish authorities declared a national emergency on Thursday in the Madrid region and the Avila province.

"We are experiencing a dramatic situation, not just in several Spanish regions but also in neighboring countries," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez wrote on X.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

World.title: Niger still seeks stability, after 3 years of military rule
World.content:
The military government in Niger had promised social, security and economic improvements when it took power in 2023. Three years down the line, there are mixed reviews on its performance.

The military seized power in Niger on July 26, 2023. General Abdourahamane Tchiani , who became head of state, justified the coup by citing the poor security situation, which he said persisted despite international support.

In the weeks that followed, the military government announced a transitional period that was to last a maximum of three years.

However, the political promises made upon taking office have not been fulfilled. The transitional government continues to hold all the reins, and the security situation in the Sahel country remains fragile.

In the Tillabery region in southwestern Niger, attacks by jihadists are on the rise. Thousands of people have been forced to flee their villages, plunging the region into a severe humanitarian crisis.

Niger's military government has struggled to end an Islamist insurgency despite promises to do so Image: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty Images

"Today, attacks on the armed forces and the civilian population are significantly more frequent and violent than they were three years ago," Maiga, a resident of the city of Tera, which has a population of 30,000, told DW. Maiga wished to remain anonymous for security reasons.

"Life used to be better despite the insecurity; the weekly markets operated normally and supplies arrived regularly," he said, adding that at the moment entire villages had fled and schools are closed.

The independent conflict monitor ACLED has also said the the security situation has deteriorated since the 2023 coup.

According to the organization, the Tillaberi region remains the main hot spot for clashes between two rival Islamist groups, Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin and the so-called Islamic State in the Sahel Province (formerly ISGS). This rivalry has resulted in numerous casualties among soldiers and civilians.

In 2025, nearly 1,200 deaths were recorded in the region. For Heni Nsaibia, a staff member at ACLED, these figures attest to the scale of the security crisis affecting Niger.

The most recent major attack, on July 17, claimed the lives of at least 16 soldiers, according to Niger's state media, ANP. Fifteen terrorists were killed in that attack, ANP said.

"The situation in Niger has worsened, particularly in the Tillaberi region, where the death toll is the highest in the central Sahel," Nsaibia told DW.

Insecurity taking a toll on civilians

"We live in makeshift shelters and are defenseless against the elements; we take on small odd jobs to survive," a woman told DW.

"I used to be able to live with dignity from my work, but right now it's very difficult; even [portable] drinking water is a problem for us," added a local herder.

Young Nigeriens are torn between disappointment and optimism: In the youth assemblies, known as "Fadas," the topic continues to spark discussion. Some — like Fadila — believe that the situation is gradually stabilizing after the turmoil of the first few years.

There was much optimism in Niger after the military took over power three years ago Image: AFP/Getty Images

"For a while, it wasn't easy at all: Salaries weren't paid on time, food supplies… that wasn't easy. But for some time now, things have been going pretty well overall," Fadila told DW.

General Tchiani has emphasized that young people can once again participate in politics. "Before the coup, young people were excluded from decision-making bodies." But in the meantime, he said, an advisory commission has been established that includes young people. "So that means the concerns of young people are now being taken into account in decision-making bodies."

Just two days after the ouster of President Mohamed Bazoumin 2023, junta leader Tchiani announced plans to combat corruption and boost the economy.

But three years later, the people of Niger are no better off, noted Tahirou Garka, a close ally of Bazoum. He is the spokesperson for the G25, a movement advocating for a return to constitutional order in Niger.

"They have failed economically and socially," he said, referring to the military government. "People are struggling to find drinking water; there is no water, no electricity, no fuel."

What is the Alliance of Democrats for the Sahel? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, Hamani Oumarou of LASDEL, a social sciences research institute based in Niamey, takes a different view. According to him, the socioeconomic situation has improved for a large portion of Niger's population, especially for those who are not part of the middle class or the elite.

"Households with low incomes have more money left over to feed their families," Oumarou told DW. However, Niger is also forced to import food at certain times of the year, which leads to a sharp rise in prices.

Rebuilding ties with ECOWAS

Along with Mali and Burkina Faso, Niger is a founding member of the lliance of Sahel States (AES), which was formed in 2023 after all the three countries withdrew from the West African regional organization ECOWAS.

The AES has distanced itself from Western partners and is seeking closer ties with Russia.

Pape Ibrahima Kane, an expert on international organizations, now hopes for a rapprochement between the AES member states and their longtime allies in West Africa.

The military leaders of the Sahel Alliance support one another militarily and economically, but still face political sanctions by the African Union Image: Mahamadou Hamidou/REUTERS

He sees a positive sign in the fact that former Guinean Prime Minister Lansana Kouyate was elected chief negotiator for ECOWAS a few days ago. According to Kane, Kouyate seems to have been accepted by the AES.

"We are at the beginning of a promising process, as both sides are truly on the same page when it comes to starting talks," he told DW.

For him, economic negotiations should also play a role. Niger depends on access to the port of Benin and on its electricity supply from Nigeria and Benin, both of which are ECOWAS member states.

Reliou Koubakin and Ali Abdou contributed to this article.

This article was originally written in German.

Correction, July 24, 2026: A previous version of this article stated that Lansana Kouyate is Guinea's current prime minister. This has been corrected, and DW apologizes for the error.

World.title: UNESCO adds Lebanese, West Bank sites to endangered list
World.content:
Israel has rejected the listing of a Lebanese castle and an occupied West Bank archaeological site. UNESCO added both sites to its World Heritage in Danger list in the context of Israeli activity.

The United Nations cultural agency on Friday updated its list of World Heritage in Danger, with locations including a Lebanese castle that Israeli forces recently captured as well as an archaeological site in the occupied West Bank, amid Israeli objections.

The decision was made during a UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) meeting in South Korea's Busan.

Members agreed that five castles in Lebanon's Mount Amel, including Beaufort Castle, and the West Bank's Sebastia would both go on the agency's World Heritage List and List of World Heritage in Danger.

The decision came after reviewing the nominations on an emergency basis, citing ongoing conflicts in the Middle East.

Israel's Foreign Ministry had urged the committee to reject the designation efforts, calling the nominations a "weaponization of cultural heritage."

Israeli forces occupied Lebanon's Beaufort Castle in May Image: Stringer/REUTERS

What do we know about the UNESCO-designated sites?

Beaufort Castle is a Crusader fortress also known as Qalaat al-Shakif. Israeli forces captured the fortress in May amid their military operations in southern Lebanon as part of the fight against Iran-backed Hezbollah militants.

The mountainous area where Beaufort and the other five Jabal Amel listed castles are located has come under repeated Israeli bombardment during the war.

UNESCO said the fortresses had sustained damage and faced ongoing threats from the conflict "serious enough to justify resorting to an emergency procedure."

Lebanese Culture Minister Ghassan Salame told the French AFP news agency that only two of the castles were "within the Lebanese government's reach" and accused Israel of having already destroyed Shamaa Castle and of threatening to demolish Beaufort.

Salame described the UNESCO listing as a "remarkable achievement in the effort to protect these important Lebanese historical landmarks."

Israel seizes strategic castle in Lebanon in deep incursion To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Meanwhile, Sebastia, the other site added on Friday, lies near the West Bank city of Nablus. It is thought to be the ancient Israeli and later Roman city of Samaria, with archaeological remains spanning the Iron Age, Roman, Byzantine and Islamic periods.

Israel still uses the name Samaria to refer to the northern West Bank.

Israeli authorities have developed an interest in the site in recent years, in 2025 taking control of around 200 hectares of Palestinian land nearby for what it calls preservation and development purposes.

The site is important to the Palestinian tourism industry and threatened by the recent Israeli actions, including an Israelis-only road, a fence and entry fees.

"The integrity of the site is currently threatened by an expropriation project aimed at subdividing the property and creating the 'Samaria' (Shomron) National Park," UNESCO said.

Sebastia is thought to be the ancient Israeli and later Roman city of Samaria, with archaeological remains spanning the Iron Age, Roman, Byzantine and Islamic periods [FILE: Feb 12, 2026] Image: Zain Jaafar/AFP

Sebastia's nomination to the UNESCO list was first submitted by the Palestinian delegation to UNESCO in 2012. It argued the site remains largely undeveloped under Israeli control and requires additional conservation despite attracting tourists.

Adel Naim Daoud Atieh, a member of the Palestinian delegation to UNESCO, said the World Heritage designation rewards the perseverance of Sebastia's residents "who have protected this extraordinary site through generations, despite occupation, restrictions and repeated attempts to separate them from their own heritage."

How has Israel responded?

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar slammed UNESCO for the listings, calling that of Samaria in particular an attempt at "erasing and denying the Jewish connection to this land."

A member of the Israeli delegation, attending the Busan meetings as an observer after Israel withdrew from the organization in 2019, said it was a "shame politicization has ruined UNESCO and led to mockery of history."

In a statement on Tuesday, the Israeli Foreign Ministry accused the Palestinian delegation of waging a "hostile, one-sided campaign" at UNESCO by falsely portraying Sebastia as an area facing an emergency.

Addressing the listing of the Lebanese Beaufort Castle, the Israeli Foreign Ministry alleged that Hezbollah turned it into a military stronghold by building tunnels beneath the site and launching rockets from the area.

Sebastia is an important site for the Palestinian tourism industry that is threatened by the recent Israeli actions, including an Israelis-only road, a fence and entry fees [FILE: Nov 20, 2025] Image: Nasser Nasser/AP Photo/picture alliance

At Friday's meeting, a Lebanese delegate said the castles have been used "only for cultural and tourism purposes" since Israel's withdrawal from southern Lebanon in 2000 and accused Israeli media of circulating images of tourist facilities as military tunnels.

Israel's withdrawal from UNESCO was owed to what it called bias against it, accusing the UN agency of downplaying its historical ties to the Holy Land.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

World.title: Highs and lows as Bayreuth Festival turns 150
World.content:
The Bayreuth Festival's 150th anniversary has been clouded by controversy surrounding German-Jewish speaker Michel Friedman. Yet it offers an opportunity to celebrate, including with an AI-enhanced Ring cycle.

The last weekend in July marks the beginning of the Bayreuth Festival, which is celebrating its 150th anniversary this year. The event regularly attracts international opera fans and distinguished guests, especially German politicians. This year, attendees include the current chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and his predecessor, Angela Merkel, who regularly attends.

The first Bayreuth Festival opened on August 13, 1876, after years of disputes over funding Richard Wagner's ambitious project. Philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche, a friend of Wagner who was also a guest at the festival, praised the event, calling it "the first circumnavigation of the world in the realm of art."

In August 1876, the Bayreuth Festival Theater was the site of the festival's inauguration Image: Archives Snark/Photo12/picture alliance

Special anniversary program

The anniversary program is diverse and includes a new staging of Richard Wagner's landmark work, "The Ring of the Nibelung,” using artificial intelligence, along with a new production of the opera "Rienzi," Wagner's first major success, composed at age 29.

These two productions have replaced the festival management's original plan to stage all 13 of Wagner's finished operas during the anniversary year, which was deemed financially unfeasible.

The opening ceremony on July 25 is expected to be spectacular. It features a major work by Wagner's idol, Ludwig van Beethoven — Symphony No. 9. Notably, in 1872, Wagner conducted this very symphony at the Margravial Opera House in Bayreuth during the ceremonial laying of the foundation stone for his Festival Theater.

Despite a few compromises, the anniversary program appears promising and innovative, fully aligned with Wagner's credo of "Children, create new things" ("Kinder, schafft Neues!").

Still, a shadow has been cast over the festival in the run-up to the opening: the initial exclusion and subsequent re-invitation of the German-French journalist Michel Friedman, who is Jewish.

There was controversy over the initial cancellation of a speech by Michel Friedman, who is Jewish Image: Bernd Wüstneck/dpa/picture alliance

The 'Friedman Affair'

At first glance, the scandal appeared to be a planning mishap. Friedman had been invited to the memorial event titled "Silenced Voices," ("Verstummte Stimmen") which was scheduled for the second day of the festival. It honors the many Jewish artists whose work at Bayreuth was ended by antisemitism, persecution and murder.

Friedman, a prominent voice on Jewish life and a former president of the European Jewish Congress, was to speak about antisemitism and the festival's efforts to confront its Nazi past.

"Especially in the year of its 150th anniversary, the Bayreuth Festival is aware of its historical responsibility regarding Richard Wagner's antisemitic views, and the festival's subsequent connections, along with those of certain members of the Wagner family, to National Socialism," stated an official release by the Bayreuth Festival.

Due to insufficient security measures, it was suggested that Friedman postpone his commemorative speech to a later date — a mishandling which seemed to suggest that Bayreuth was trying to avoid confronting a history marred by antisemitism.

Following an apology from the festival management, Friedman will now be attending after all. The event will feature musical works by the Jewish composers Gustav Mahler and Pavel Haas, who died in the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration camp, as well as Wagner's "Siegfried Idyll."

Festival director Katharina Wagner will deliver the opening address on July 25 Image: Karl-Josef Hildenbrand/dpa/picture alliance

On the festival's website, Katharina Wagner, the festival director and great-granddaughter of the composer, expressed her delight in welcoming Friedman to the festival.

A first for Bayreuth: Wagner's 'Rienzi'

This year's special premiere is Wagner's opera "Rienzi," which will be performed at the Bayreuth Festival for the first time. Wagner composed it in the style of French "Grand Opera." But he didn't believe it aligned with the repertoire of operas he would present in his festival theater in later years.

Captivated by the literary adaptation of a true 14th-century story, the rise and fall of the Roman leader Cola di Rienzo, who fought against the aristocracy, Wagner chose it as the subject for an opera.

He was not alone in his interest; "Rienzi" was also among Adolf Hitler's favorite works. "What Hitler appreciated about 'Rienzi' was, of course, the figure of the self-made man who rises to become the sole ruler through his charisma," said Sven Friedrich, the director of the Richard Wagner Museum in Bayreuth.

How does populism fuel fantasies of omnipotence? This is the question posed by the two directors of 'Rienzi,' Alexandra Szemeredy and Magdolna Parditka Image: Christina Figge

The decision to premiere one of Hitler's favorite operas during this significant anniversary year has sparked debate. Nonetheless, Hungarian directors Alexandra Szemeredy and Magdolna Parditka are committed to updating "Rienzi" for contemporary audiences.

"That's why we're not focusing solely on this specific dictatorship but rather exploring the boundaries of how a state can gradually evolve from populism into an authoritarian regime," they said in a statement.

Sensational AI Ring set to surprise audience, creators

The festival is eagerly anticipating the new productions of the opera cycle "The Ring of the Nibelung." This opera explores themes of power, greed and intrigue. According to legend, whoever seizes gold from the Rhine will possess ultimate power. Wagner built his opera house in 1876 specifically for this 16-hour mammoth work.

Stage designs created using artificial intelligence are set to take audiences by surprise Image: Marcus Lobbes/Bayreuther Festspiele

Artistic director Katharina Wagner aims to break new ground with this anniversary production by incorporating AI. As curator Marcus Lobbes explained, "we'll be working with image layers partly generated in real-time, creating holographic 3-D spaces."

The team has chosen archival footage of Ring performances from 1876 to 2024 for the AI to analyze for the projections. "The entire composition aims to evoke a sense of a vast, resonant image," said Lobbes. The creators have promised a "visually effervescent cosmos of light, texture, history, and association."

There will be unexpected moments, not only for the audience but also for Lobbes' team, as they discover what the AI ultimately produces. The Bayreuth Festival takes place from July 25 to August 26.

Edited by: Sarah Hucal

World.title: Can Pakistan-administered Kashmir elections calm tensions?
World.content:
Pakistan-administered Kashmir heads to the polls after weeks of deadly protests over seats reserved for displaced people from India-administered Kashmir. One local group has called for the elections to be boycotted.

The first phase of local elections in Pakistan-administered Kashmir is scheduled for Monday, July 27, amid calls for a boycott from the recently outlawed Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a grassroots alliance of civil society groups.

The JAAC has been demanding the abolition of 12 seats in the regional assembly reserved for people displaced from India-administered Kashmir and living in Pakistan. It argues that only residents of Pakistan-administered Kashmir should be eligible to contest regional elections.

The dispute escalated after the Supreme Court of Pakistan-administered Kashmir ruled that the refugee seats are constitutionally protected and cannot be abolished without a constitutional amendment.

The regional government outlawed the JAAC in June under anti-terrorism laws, citing threats to public order, and detained dozens of its supporters.

The ban came amid rising tensions over the refugee seats and ahead of violent protests sparked by the group's campaign to scrap them.

The unrest has left around 30 people dead since June, according to local estimates cited by Reuters news agency.

India and Pakistan both claim Kashmir in its entirety, but each country only controls a section of the territory, making the Muslim-majority region a longstanding flash point between the nuclear-armed neighbors since their independence from Britain in 1947.

Protests cast shadow over vote

Since early June, Pakistan-administered Kashmir — known locally as Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) — has witnessed weeks of protests and sit-ins. While the dispute over the refugee seats has become a major issue, JAAC has also campaigned for broader economic and governance reforms.

Following the unrest, authorities split polling into three phases, with voting in Mirpur set for July 27 and elections in the protest-hit Poonch division postponed until August 10.

Voting in the regional capital, Muzaffarabad, has been delayed until August 2 over security concerns. The JAAC continues to stage a sit-in in Rawalakot, near the Line of Control with India.

Demand for fair representation

A major question is whether the elections can restore public confidence or merely offer a temporary pause in public anger.

"We are just asking for fair representation, which is our right," Ali Raza, a 22-year-old student protester in Rawalakot, told DW. "The local people who live here should have the right to choose their representatives, not the refugees who settled here from India."

"The election is a major opportunity for the people of AJK to choose their representatives," said Shazia Marri, the central information secretary of the Pakistan People's Party, which currently rules the region. "The people want their rights protected, their issues addressed and a government that delivers on its promises."

Unrest keeps flaring up in Pakistan-administered Kashmir To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, JAAC leaders argue that elections alone cannot resolve the issues that brought thousands of people onto the streets.

"Our movement is not replacing one government with another over time; we need our rights, but there are just political slogans in the campaigns," one JAAC official told DW under condition of anonymity.

Imran Khan, a geopolitical expert and former director of the US Institute of Peace Pakistan, expects the movement to continue post-elections.

"While elections in AJK are important on their own merit and for the continuity of the political process, they will not address the political grievances and demands of the people who are supporting JAAC," Khan, no relation to Pakistan's former prime minister, told DW. "The protest is outside the assembly. They no longer trust those institutions fully."

Has JAAC changed Kashmir's political landscape?

Analysts have said the JAAC protests marked a significant shift in Pakistan-administered Kashmir's politics by bringing together citizens across party lines around economic and governance issues rather than traditional political rivalries.

For analyst Khan, JAAC is a dominant political force to reckon with in quite significant parts of Pakistan-administered Kashmir.

"They have more street credibility than mainstream politicians and parties despite the allegations of foreign backing and funding. For now, they have disrupted the status quo politics in AJK," Khan said, noting that the Pakistani establishment has the means and methods to break up such political movements.

Experts caution that rebuilding trust will require more than campaign promises.

"[The] next government in AJK will be very weak, as it will be sandwiched between pressure from both the Pakistani establishment that controls AJK through administrative and security framework and the sentiment on the street, which is very pro JAAC," argued Khan.

He added that the next government would have "little credibility and limited room to govern unless it reaches an understanding with JAAC to ease political tensions."

But Marri of the Pakistan People's Party believes trust is rebuilt by listening to people's concerns, delivering practical solutions and empowering elected institutions.

Will protests return if reforms stall?

If key grievances remain unresolved, analysts warn that another wave of protests cannot be ruled out.

"It is too early to say that more waves of protests will be seen, but JAAC has the potential to become a lasting political force," said Khan, who suggested the group risks being weakened by internal divisions and pressure from the establishment.

"For now, both sides are treading carefully, with JAAC relying on mass support and the establishment avoiding a full crackdown while buying time," Khan added.

Kashmir tourism struggles post Pahalgam attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

While the vote will determine who governs Pakistan-administered Kashmir, it is unlikely to resolve the broader constitutional dispute over Kashmir or eliminate long-standing frustrations with the region's governance.

"Governments must listen to public concerns and address them through dialogue and effective governance. Stability comes from listening to people, respecting the law, and delivering results," Marri added.

For Raza, the Gen Z protester, "the world has changed, and we have seen governments toppling through student protests in the neighboring countries; we won't stop, and protests will continue until our rights have not been given to us."

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: Última hora de los incendios forestales, en directo | El incendio en Madrid se encuentra en su “momento álgido” y está ya “fuera de capacidad de extinción”
World.content:
El incendio en Madrid se dirige hacia El Escorial: la UME intenta frenar el avance del fuego | Ya son ocho los municipios evacuados en Madrid y más de 40.000 los afectados, entre desalojados y confinados | La Guardia Civil detiene a una persona por el origen del fuego en Ávila mientras crece el temor a que se una al de Madrid

El incendio que afecta al suroeste de la Comunidad de Madrid se encuentra en su “momento álgido” y está ya “fuera de capacidad de extinción”, según ha reconocido el consejero de Medio Ambiente, Agricultura e Interior, Carlos Novillo, tras la reunión del Cecopi. Los tres frentes que afectaban a la región ya se han fusionado en un único incendio, que ha obligado a evacuar Chapinería, Navas del Rey, Colmenar del Arroyo, Fresnedillas de la Oliva, Robledo de Chavela, Aldea del Fresno, Navalagamella y Zarzalejo, mientras San Martín de Valdeiglesias, Pelayos de la Presa y Villa del Prado permanecen confinados. El delegado del Gobierno en Madrid, Francisco Martín, ha elevado a más de 45.000 los afectados, entre evacuados y confinados, y no ha descartado que la cifra siga creciendo, ya que “las pavesas vuelan kilómetros y el fuego está saltando en grandes distancias”, lo que complica aún más la extinción. Martín ha alertado además de que el fuego se dirige ahora hacia El Escorial, por lo que “la gran misión” del operativo es proteger ese municipio y, después, San Lorenzo de El Escorial, para lo que la UME trabaja ya en establecer una línea de defensa. En Ávila, la Subdelegación del Gobierno ha ampliado las medidas de protección, con el confinamiento de Cebreros y Navaluenga y la evacuación de Hoyo de Pinares y Burgohondo hacia la capital. Por último, la Guardia Civil ha detenido a una persona e investiga a otra como autores del incendio de Burgohondo, cuyo origen sería una imprudencia grave por el uso de maquinaria pesada en una zona donde estaba prohibido.

EL PAÍS ofrece de forma gratuita la última hora de los incendios. Si quieres apoyar nuestro periodismo, suscríbete.

World.title: Blood on Her Tongue: A modern vampire tale not for the squeamish
World.content:
Johanna van Veen’s gothic horror Blood on Her Tongue offers up a classic vampire tale with some modern contemplations.

The book follows Lucy Goedhart as she is called to the ominously named Zwartwater (black water) estate, where her sister has taken ill. In 1887, there isn’t much in the way of medical treatment, but Lucy’s sister Sarah isn’t fighting off a regular illness.

Sarah has become obsessed with a body found in the bog of the vast estate and since interacting with the 300-year-old corpse she has become increasingly incoherent, struggles with taking care of herself and has developed an insatiable hunger.

As Lucy tries desperately to save her sister, she finds that her sister’s husband, her sister’s doctor and childhood friend, and several other characters who are present at the remote manor house all have their own interests and motivations – some as dangerous as whatever condition is plaguing Sarah.

The book is not for those easily bothered by gore. The title – Blood on Her Tongue – is a pretty good indication of what is to come. Van Veen does not shy away from the horror elements, including two separate scenes of eyeball gouging.

Like any good horror novel, the macabre monster is not the scariest part. The threats Lucy faces are from the men surrounding her sister. Her brother-in-law attempts to seduce Lucy while badgering her to send Sarah away to an asylum.

Sarah’s doctor expresses his own interest in Lucy, pushing his vision of the future while supposedly devoting himself to his patient. The mores of 19th-century upper-class society may be the biggest piece of villainy of all.

In the tradition of Dracula, Blood on Her Tongue tells its story through letters, journal entries and newspaper clippings. The personal correspondence adds to the claustrophobia of the work, with everyone limited to an isolated house, but the media reports remind the reader that the world outside does exist.

The work is the second book from Dutch author Johanna van Veen. It was published in 2025 in English and became a USA Today bestseller. Her first book, My Darling Dreadful Thing, was nominated for the Bram Stoker Award for best horror novel. Van Veen grew up in the Netherlands as a triplet, something that influenced her writing about the sisters Lucy and Sarah.

If horror is your thing, Blood on Her Tongue will creep you out and keep you turning the pages.

You can get your copy at the American Book Center.

World.title: Thousands cross finishing line as Nijmegen Vierdaagse ends
World.content:
The 108th edition of the Nijmegense Vierdaagse (four-day march) ended on Friday, with tens of thousands of walkers being welcomed with flowers by well-wishers.

British walker Simon Brownlee crossed the finishing line ahead of the rest of the walkers for the 27th time, local media reported. Brownlee, who completed the distance before 10am, told local broadcaster Omroep Gelderland that the walk “felt like home”. “I’m happy it is over and I can now relax,” he said.

Wheelchair participant Ronald van Dort was the very first person to finish, picking up his seventh medal for completing the event.

Over 45,000 walkers from 70 countries took part in this year’s series, which is proving increasingly popular among the young. Ten years ago, 7.5% of the walkers were aged 21 to 30, but this year their number rose to over 20%.

This year the event was marred by a fatal shooting just outside the area where the Vierdaagsefeesten, the street festivities accompanying the annual four-day marches, were taking place. One man has been arrested.

The shooting, and other crowd problems, led the organisers to cancel performances by urban scene artists such as Ronnie Flex and Lil’ Kleine because their presence was “attracting the wrong sort of people”, the AD reported.

World.title: Dozens of women forced into prostitution by Romanian gang
World.content:
Dozens of women may have been forced into working as prostitutes in Amsterdam’s red light district by a Romanian gang, Dutch police confirmed on Friday.

The statement follows a joint Dutch and Romanian campaign against human trafficking in the area earlier this month. Seven men were arrested during a string of raids on July 14 – four in the Netherlands and three in Romania. All were Romanian nationals.

Shortly after the arrests, police issued a video interview with one of the victims speaking Romanian, which has led more women to come forward and has resulted in other information reaching the police, the statement said.

Police now say they have spoken to several victims and say they believe more women have been trafficked. They too are said to be Romanian.

The women were lured to Amsterdam with the promise of high earnings but found themselves forced into working in brothels and handing over their earnings to the gang. They were also forced to pay “rent” for their rooms.

None of the men had jobs but were big spenders, buying expensive clothes and cars and gambling heavily, the statement said. The gang also treated part of the red light district as their “personal kingdom”.

Four men remain in custody in the Netherlands, one of whom was extradited from Romania. Another man may also be extradited soon, RTL said. They are all suspected of human trafficking and forming a criminal organisation.

According to the Parool, two of the suspects are half brothers aged 44 and 45 who have earlier convictions for trafficking in women in Romania.

More arrests have not been ruled out.

A year ago, Dutch and Romanian police arrested 13 people in a joint investigation into human trafficking and the forced prostitution of Romanian women, mainly in and around Amsterdam.

World.title: Singer Sophie Straat cleared of discrimination over mosh pit
World.content:
Discrimination hotlines in both the Netherlands and Belgium have concluded that Dutch singer Sophie Straat did not discriminate when she asked “all white men to step back” during two of her recent performances.

Last month at the Best Kept Secret festival in Beekse Bergen, Straat — real name Sophie Schwartz — asked for space for women, queer people and people of colour in the “mosh pit”, an area in front of the stage where fans dance chaotically.

She made the same request on Monday during a performance in Ghent, Belgium.

The Dutch discrimination hotline Discriminatie.nl said it received hundreds of complaints but maintains that Straat’s comments do not amount to discrimination against white men based on their colour or gender.

“The call only concerned one short, one-off mosh pit for these groups,” said the hotline. “Therefore, visitors were not refused entry to the concert.”

Belgian authorities reached the same conclusion after receiving some 200 complaints following her performance in Ghent.

“Although the statement may be perceived as polarizing or offensive, in this context it must be seen as a symbolic and artistic expression,” a spokesperson for the Belgian discrimination hotline Unia told the Flemish broadcaster VRT.

“According to the case law of the European Court of Human Rights, artistic and political expressions enjoy broad protection under freedom of expression, even when they provoke, shock or offend.”

Hate messages and death threats

Straat wrote on Instagram earlier this month that she has received “a wave of sexist, antisemitic hate messages and (death) threats, some more explicit and creative than others”.

She has also questioned where the left-wing media has been in all this, saying the public narrative is being controlled by the right.

The singer, who was raised in a Jewish home in Amsterdam’s de Pijp neighbourhood and is known for her protest songs, has said she never wanted to exclude anyone but rather wanted to make room for people who feel unsafe in a mosh pit.

World.title: Youngster arrested for participating in sadistic online network
World.content:
Police have arrested a young man from Noord Holland who they suspect of being part of the sadistic online Com network “764”.

The public prosecution department reported the arrest on Thursday, saying the suspect encouraged underage girls to cut themselves and write his online name on a wall with their own blood—so-called “bloodsigns”.

He also is said to have prompted them to write his name on their bodies with a marker, known as“fansigns”. Both are practices within the Com movement—short for The Community—for members to gain prestige.

The suspect himself, who was also charged with aggravated assault, exploitation of underage girls and possession of images of sexual child abuse, was a minor at the time of the alleged crimes. Because of that, no further details are being released.

The Com network consists of various chat groups where members recruit vulnerable young people and force them to commit acts including assault, sexual abuse and murder.

The members, from all corners of the globe, then share images of these acts online in private chat groups, using such platforms as Telegram and Discord.

According to NOS, at least 70 Dutch people are involved in this movement known as “nihilistic extremism” because the incitement to commit such extreme violence doesn’t have a clear ideological motive.

The phenomenon is especially attractive to young men.

World.title: Dangerous drivers face extra surveillance under points system
World.content:
The police and justice ministry officials are working on a system which would see traffic offenders being given points for dangerous driving – which will lead to persistent offenders coming under extra surveillance.

Motorists who have collected six points for using a mobile phone while driving or not wearing a seatbelt would come under the tougher regime, RTL Nieuws reported on Friday. No start date has yet been set.

The points will be awarded in addition to regular fines. The number of points will depend on the seriousness of the offences and speeding tickets recorded by camera will not be included.

The new system is being devised in an effort to tackle persistent offenders who do not change their behaviour despite being fined multiple times, RTL said. Last year, almost 30,000 people would have had at least six points if the new system had been in existence.

“Research shows that people who don’t stick to the rules are often responsible for accidents,” Achilles Damen from the public prosecution department told the broadcaster.

The privacy implications of monitoring specific individuals are still being assessed, RTL said.

World.title: Ajax beat Vojvodina in Conference League qualifier, Twente lose
World.content:
Ajax kicked off their European football campaign with a 4-1 win over Serbian club Vojvodina in the second qualification round of the Conference League competition in Novi Sad on Thursday evening.

The simple win sets the Amsterdammers up in a strong position ahead of the return match next week. If Ajax win again, they will meet either Irish side Shelbourne FC or Estonian club Nõmme Kalju in the third qualification round for the third-tier European competition.

The Amsterdam goal total included one for 16-year-old debutant Mohamed Abdalla, who became the youngest player to score for a Dutch club in Europe.

There was disappointment for FC Twente, who are hoping to qualify for the group stage of the Europa League. They lost 1-2 at home to Hungarian side Ferencváros and will have to pull out all the stops during the away leg next week to remain in the competition.

If they do lose, Twente will move down to the qualification rounds of the Conference League.

PSV Eindhoven and Feyenoord have qualified directly for the Champions League while NEC is taking part in the qualification competition. AZ, as winners of the KNVB Cup last season, will take part in the Europa League competition.

World.title: Unilever backs London for food division secondary listing
World.content:
Unilever’s food division, which is being sold to US sauce and spice producer McCormick, will have a secondary listing on the London stock exchange, despite an intensive lobbying campaign to list in Amsterdam.

Unilever itself has been based in London, and listed there, since 2020.

Unilever said in a statement that the secondary listing is separate to McCormick’s plans to establish an international headquarters in the Netherlands and maintain Unilever Food’s R&D facilities and operations in Wageningen.

This “reflects its commitment to the European market and the critical role the Netherlands will continue to play in the combined company”, the statement said.

Economic affairs minister Heleen Herbert said in a reaction to the sale when it was announced in March that the cabinet had already discussed developments with Unilever and would talk to the new owner “such as about a listing on the Amsterdam stock exchange”.

Unilever’s ice cream arm, spun off in 2024, is listed on the Amsterdam stock exchange as the Magnum Ice Cream Company and is headquartered in the Dutch capital.

The sale of the food arm means there is nothing left of the original Dutch part of Unilever, which was set up in 1930 through the merger of the Dutch Margarine Unie and British soap maker Lever Brothers. Unilever now focuses on personal care and household cleaning products.

Keeping dogs and cats chained up at home will be banned in Poland from next year, after President Karol Nawrocki signed into law a bill prohibiting the practice. His decision ends a long-running dispute over the issue, after Nawrocki last year vetoed a previous proposal to ban chaining because it also included what he argued were excessive and unrealistic additional measures on minimum kennel sizes for dogs. Zawetowana w listopadzie 2025 r. ustawa łańcuchowa była źle przygotowana i przeregulowana, ponieważ nakładała na obywateli obowiązki, których wielu nie byłoby w stanie spełnić. Dzisiaj otrzymujemy ustawę lepszą, z pozytywnym głosem takich podmiotów jak rolniczy samorząd.… pic.twitter.com/h7kIAI77KR — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) July 24, 2026 The new law bans owners from tethering dogs and cats at home. Animals must be kept either inside the house, in a fenced garden or, if that is not possible, in a kennel “large enough for the animal to move freely and satisfy its natural needs”. Dogs kept in kennels must be provided with daily exercise outside of it. Dogs and cats can still be put on leashes in certain situations, such as when they are being walked, but also during transport, while participating in shows, performances or training, if they are at vets or groomers, or if they represent a danger to humans or other animals. Now that the bill has been signed by Nawrocki, it will be published in the official Journal of Laws (Dziennik Ustaw), after which it goes into force 12 months later. The new measures represent a successful second attempt to introduce a leashing ban. A previous bill was approved by parliament last September. However, in December, Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, announced that he was vetoing it. The president argued that, “although the intention – protecting animals – is just and noble, the law itself was poorly drafted”. In particular, he said that elements introducing minimum sizes for dog kennels were unrealistic and would “harm farmers, breeders and ordinary rural households”. After an attempt by parliament to overturn the veto failed, legislators went back to the drawing board and, following discussions with the president’s chancellery and animal rights groups, drafted a compromise bill that was approved by parliament earlier this month. The bill received support from the current ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, as well as most MPs from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the main opposition party. The far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) voted against it. Thousands of people have protested in Warsaw against President @NawrockiKn's veto of a law that would have banned the chaining up of dogs Parliament will vote on Wednesday on whether to overturn Nawrocki's veto, which would require a three-fifths majority https://t.co/0GRup2sppb — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 15, 2025 “We now have a better law, with positive feedback from entities such as the agricultural chamber,” said Nawrocki today. “It demonstrates that the pressure of the presidential veto makes sense. My previous decision to refuse to sign this bill forced the government and parliament to work harder.” However, although Nawrocki said the new law would no longer entail “rigid and costly requirements” for kennels, his office noted in a separate statement that the legislation requires the agriculture minister to issue a regulation establishing “minimum kennel area, taking into account the dog’s size”. It remains unclear if and how that would differ from the requirements Nawrocki previously vetoed. The presidential chancellery also noted that the law itself already outlines that kennels must be made of “wood or wood-like material with thermal insulation”, must be insulated from the ground, and must have openings on at least two sides to allow light and air to enter. A dog who throws a ball to passers-by from a balcony above one of Poland’s most famous streets and waits for them to throw it back has become a star. Police officers and rangers have stepped up joint patrols in Poland’s mountainous Tatra National Park during the peak summer season, following a spate of rule-breaking including swimming in the park’s lakes and ponds, driving cars and going off marked trails. Meanwhile, national park authorities have repeated warnings that bathing, littering and breaking other rules can damage the park’s fragile ecosystem. Local police officers have joined Tatra National Park rangers on patrols on popular tourist routes. On one such patrol last week, officers focused on education and prevention, reminding visitors not to leave marked trails or litter and explaining how to behave safely and responsibly in the mountains. They also checked that organised groups were accompanied by qualified mountain guides, as required by law. Fines for such offences range from 50 zloty (€11.55) to as much as 1,000 zloty (€231) in the event of environmental damage or multiple offences. Police said that all visitors encountered during the patrol were complying with the park’s regulations. However, they added that similar patrols would continue on a regular basis. The Tatra National Park, home to Poland’s highest peaks, and the nearby mountain resort of Zakopane are among the country’s most popular holiday destinations, with crowds taking to park trails in the summer season. The park, the most visited of Poland’s 23 national parks, welcomed a record 5.3 million visitors in 2025 and offers 275 km of marked hiking trails, including high-altitude routes that connect at several points with the adjacent national park in Slovakia. 🚨 Ukraiński Influencer wjechał nielegalnie samochodem na Morskie oko 🗣️: Jesteśmy pierwszymi ludźmi w historii, którzy wjechali samochodem nad Morskie Oko. To było jedno z miejsc, do których chcieliśmy dotrzeć podczas tej podróży i wszyscy znajomi oraz przyjaciele mówili, że… pic.twitter.com/tA9shZ6Rqk — Pigułka 💊 (@informacyjnie) May 23, 2026 This season has already seen a number of high-profile cases of transgressions of the park’s strict rules. In May, a Ukrainian social media influencer sparked outrage after driving a sports car along a road closed to traffic to Morskie Oko, a picturesque lake nestled between the mountains. As a result, he was banned from entering Poland and other Schengen Area countries for five years. Tourists have also been filmed entering Morskie Oko and other protected lakes and ponds, which is not permitted in the national park. This month, a group of young Dutch tourists were filmed bathing in Przedni Staw Polski in the Valley of the Five Lakes, one of the Tatras’ best-known hiking destinations. Witnesses repeatedly warned the group that entering the lake was prohibited, but they ignored the warnings, reports Gazeta Wyborcza. Park authorities have responded to such incidents by reminding visitors of the reasons for the strict rules. “Tatra ponds are incredibly delicate ecosystems. Cosmetics, UV filters, insect repellents, and bacteria entering the water can have a long-lasting impact on its chemical composition and the organisms living in the lakes,” they warned. A national park in Poland’s southern mountains has completed testing of an electric bus that could replace horse-drawn carriages carrying tourists to a famous lake.
