World.title: Polish opposition PiS party set to split, with over 30 MPs being expelled
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. More than 30 MPs from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party, have effectively resigned after refusing to sign a loyalty pledge, party leader Jarosław Kaczyński has announced. The dispute centres around a more moderate faction in the party aligned with former prime minister and deputy PiS leader Mateusz Morawiecki, who is one of those now set to be expelled from the party. They have for months been unhappy with PiS’s move in a hard-right direction. 💬 Prezes PiS Jarosław Kaczyński @OficjalnyJK. 👉 Udostępnij pic.twitter.com/bycjE0Yq0f — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) July 24, 2026 “Around 30-something…of our group’s MPs have resigned,” revealed Kaczyński at a press conference on Friday. He added that their departures would be formalised at a meeting of the party’s political committee scheduled for Tuesday next week. Kaczyński’s announcement came after a deadline expired at midnight on Thursday for its MPs to sign a pledge of loyalty to the party that included a commitment not to be members of any external political associations. That measure was aimed in particular at an association called Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) founded by Morawiecki in April. The former prime minister had always insisted that his organisation was intended as complementary to PiS, rather than a rival to it. However, many figures in the party saw it as an attempt by Morawiecki to create a separate centre of power, and potentially to use the association as a launchpad for creating his own party ahead of the autumn 2027 parliamentary elections. The right-wing opposition PiS party has threatened disciplinary action, including exclusion from electoral lists, against dozens of its MPs who have joined a new internal group led by former PM @MorawieckiM and intended to appeal to more moderate voters https://t.co/y62Cm361U2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 17, 2026 After PiS issued a resolution on Wednesday last week requiring that its parliamentarians pledge to withdraw from any such associations, most of its 186 MPs quickly complied. However, a group of between 30 and 40 who are part of Development Plus refused to do so. “Everyone knew what they were supposed to sign, and knew the consequences of not signing,” said Kaczyński on Friday. “And so they made the decision they did.” “In this situation, we cannot view the [Development Plus] association as anything other than a component of a plan…to split our party,” he added. However, although its supporters will now leave PiS, “we want to part ways without any animosity”, said Kaczyński. At the time of writing, Morawiecki himself had not commented on Kaczyński’s announcement. One of his allies, Piotr Müller, clarified that no one in Development Plus had resigned from PiS membership. They had simply not signed the declaration requested by PiS. Earlier on Friday, before Kaczyński’s announcement, Morawiecki told broadcaster wPolsce24 that an unnamed “group of schemers” in the party was trying to turn Kaczyński against him. He expressed hope that “people will come to their senses”. Morawiecki revealed that, at a meeting with Kaczyński on Thursday, he had “proposed a framework for the association’s operation that would not only not contradict the party’s activities, but would actually support its actions”. Meanwhile, Kaczyński said he had proposed a compromise of his own, whereby the association’s activities would be suspended until after next year’s elections. But neither side was willing to accept the other’s demands. Budujmy razem szerokie środowisko prawicy, bo cel jest jeden – silna Polska! pic.twitter.com/tb9czS8DAK — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 24, 2026 If the expulsion of Morawiecki’s supporters is confirmed, it will mark a major shake-up of Poland’s political landscape. PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right, including periods leading governments in 2005-2007 and 2015-2023. However, since losing power at elections in 2023, when the party won 35% of the vote, PiS has seen its average support in polls fall to around 23-24%, the lowest level in 14 years. Meanwhile, it has been challenged by the rise of the far right, where two parties, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), now together poll a similar combined level of support to PiS. In response, Kaczyński in March named a hardline figure, Przemyszław Czarnek, as PiS’s candidate for prime minister in next year’s elections. Czarnek was seen as someone who could appeal to far-right voters, while also potentially working with the far right if a coalition was needed after the elections. Support for PiS has fallen to its lowest in 14 years, as the party grapples with internal division, the rise of far-right challengers, living in President Nawrocki's shadow, and the unpopularity in Poland of PiS ally Donald Trump, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/QRScBpEQQG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 2, 2026 However, there has been no rise in support for PiS since Czarnek was named, prompting growing concern from more moderate figures within the party, led by Morawiecki. They argue that PiS has wrongly disowned many of the successes of its time in office before 2023, and they fear that its rightward shift damages its chances of winning over more centrist voters. Morawiecki, who was an international banker before joining PiS to become finance minister and then prime minister, wants the party to focus on more technocratic issues, such as economic development, rather than the culture wars. That has led to frequent public sparring between his supporters and others in the party. In April, PiS threatened disciplinary action against members of Development Plus. Kaczyński and Morawiecki then reached an agreement that allowed the association to continue. But that uneasy truce has now fallen apart. World.title: Polish president renews bid for referendum on EU climate policy
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has submitted a second request to parliament for a nationwide referendum on whether Poland should continue implementing the European Union’s climate policies, which he argues are too costly. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, first proposed a referendum in May. But it was rejected by the Senate, the upper house of parliament, where the more liberal government has a majority. Senators argued that the proposed referendum question was “absurd”. The president has now submitted a revised proposal featuring a simplified question and again proposed holding the referendum on 27 September this year. Nawrocki’s originally proposed question was: “Are you in favour of implementing EU climate policy, which has led to an increase in citizens’ cost of living, energy prices and the cost of running business and agricultural activity?” However, following criticism in the Senate that the question was clearly intended to elicit a specific answer, this time he has proposed a more neutral one: “Are you in favour of Poland implementing the European Union’s climate policy?” “I’m looking for compromises, looking for solutions,” said Nawrocki on Thursday while announcing the new referendum bid. “The Senate wasn’t satisfied with the [previous] question”, so “we prepared a different one…[that] does not suggest anything”. However, the president has also proposed that the ballot paper would include information on what answering “yes” or “no” would mean in practice. Voters would be told, for example, that maintaining EU climate policy would result in, among other things, “Poland bearing costs estimated at 3.5 trillion zloty by 2040”, “burdens on agriculture”, “increasing costs for industry” and “obligations for owners of buildings”. By contrast, voting “no” would mean “negotiating exceptions and exemptions for Poland with the relevant EU bodies that will protect Polish industry and citizens from the burdens of climate policy”. Poland's right-wing opposition wants to withdraw from the EU Emissions Trading System, saying it makes Poles "a cash machine for absurd leftist climate policies"@PStrzalkowski explains what costs ETS really brings, and what prospects there are for reform https://t.co/UxpMWpG1pE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 4, 2026 Under Poland’s constitution, the president may call a referendum with the approval of a majority of senators in a vote where at least half of all members of the 100-seat chamber are present. The ruling coalition of Prime Minister Donald Tusk controls 63 seats in the Senate, making approval of proposals brought forward by Nawrocki, who often clashes with the government and regularly vetoes its bills, unlikely. While the government is generally pro-EU, it has also been critical of Brussels’ green policies, arguing that they place too great a burden on Poland. After the European Commission last Friday unveiled changes intended to soften the impact of the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS), the EU’s flagship climate policy, they were welcomed by the Polish government as a step in the right direction. Dzisiaj robimy milowy krok w zmianie systemu ETS. Po raz pierwszy Komisja Europejska proponuje rozwiązania, które łagodzą, a nie zaostrzają wpływ systemu na gospodarkę i obywateli. To efekt konsekwentnych działań Polski i zbudowania silnej koalicji państw w UE. Dzisiejsza… pic.twitter.com/5AMd9KCBVa — Ministerstwo Klimatu i Środowiska (@MKiS_GOV_PL) July 17, 2026 However, in his written justification for the new referendum proposal, Nawrocki wrote that, while he had “given the government time” in its push for ETS reform, the final result was simply “technical adjustments” that postpone some elements but do “not change the direction” or ultimate outcome. “ETS will remain an increasingly expensive, increasingly extensive system, and increasingly burdensome for the Polish economy,” wrote the president. The national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), which is the main opposition and supported Nawrocki’s bid for the presidency last year, wants Poland to unilaterally withdraw from ETS. Government figures warn, however, that there is no way to do so without either accruing enormous fines or leaving the EU entirely. When in power, PiS launched a revolution in Poland's energy transition. But now, in opposition, it has disowned those achievements and returned to an emphasis on coal. This could be a missed opportunity to win back centrist voters, writes @OrzelBartlomiej https://t.co/8cGvubn7N2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 29, 2026 Nawrocki’s new referendum proposal was met with criticism by figures from the ruling coalition. “There is no possibility of one country suspending part of EU law,” wrote Stanisław Gawłowski, a senator from Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO) party. “This referendum is pure fraud.” Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, also from KO, wrote that, “as the Brits have learned, the Europhobe’s dream world, in which one enjoys all the privileges of EU membership without any obligations, does not exist”. However, Nawrocki’s initiative was welcomed by Przemysław Czarnek, deputy leader of PiS, who wrote that, “on such fundamental matters as climate policy, Poles should decide, not Brussels bureaucrats”. Zaproponowane przez @NawrockiKn pytanie referendalne jest wybiórcze. World.title: Poland appoints new human rights commissioner
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The government’s majority in parliament has chosen Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram as Poland’s new human rights commissioner. She will take office after the five-year term of the incumbent, Marcin Wiącek, expires today. Gregorczyk-Abram is a prominent lawyer and activist, who is particularly well known for opposing the overhaul of the judiciary by the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. PiS, which is now the main opposition party, strongly opposed her election, arguing that she is politically aligned with the current, more liberal government. Gregorczyk-Abram herself, however, has pledged to “put all my beliefs and views aside” when she takes up the new role. Senat wyraził zgodę na powołanie Sylwii Gregorczyk-Abram na Rzecznika Praw Obywatelskich. pic.twitter.com/gz3rwGy3hi — Senat RP 🇵🇱 (@PolskiSenat) July 22, 2026 The commissioner for human rights (widely known by its Polish initials, RPO) is appointed by a resolution of the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, with the consent of the upper-house Senate. Candidates must meet certain requirements, including not belonging to any political party and having legal expertise and relevant experience. As well as acting as a watchdog for human rights, the RPO also has the power to submit motions to the Constitutional Tribunal to assess the constitutionality of laws and to file so-called cassation appeals to the Supreme Court and Supreme Administrative Court against rulings by lower courts. Poland’s human rights commissioner has written to the government expressing concern that a "temporary" ban on asylum claims by most migrants who irregularly cross the border from Belarus remains in place after more than a year https://t.co/9SA2TypQdK — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 28, 2026 Gregorczyk-Abram was last month nominated as a candidate to be the new RPO by the main ruling party, Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO), along with one of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica). PiS proposed a rival candidate, Adam Borowski, a veteran of Poland’s anti-communist struggle in the 1980s. However, critics argued that Borowski, an activist and former PiS election candidate, does not appear to have the requisite legal knowledge and experience. In a Sejm vote last Friday, the ruling coalition supported Gregorczyk-Abram, who won 233 votes to Borowski’s 177. On Wednesday, her candidacy was also supported by the Senate, with 59 votes in favour and 25 against, confirming that she will become the new RPO. Gregorczyk-Abram is best known as one of the founders and leaders of the Free Courts (Wolne Sądy) initiative launched in 2017 amid a wave of protests against the then-PiS government’s efforts to take greater control over the judiciary. Free Courts was prominent in efforts to defend the rule of law. Many of its leading figures are now associated with the current ruling coalition: Maria Ejchart is a deputy justice minister, while Michał Wawrykiewicz is a member of the European Parliament representing KO. In April last year, Gregorczyk-Abram was made chairwoman of a commission established by the current government to look into cases of abuse of power against civil society under the former PiS administration. In September, her commission published its first findings, in which it said that public media outlets under PiS control had “carried out systematic repressive and defamatory actions against activists, non-governmental organisations, and civil society”. Poland's public media “carried out systematic repressive actions against activists, NGOs and civil society” during the rule of the former PiS government, a report commissioned by the new government has found https://t.co/S2MO9KGssC — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 26, 2025 PiS argues that Gregorczyk-Abram’s previous activity makes her unsuitable as a suitable candidate for RPO, which is meant to be a non-partisan role. They also point to claims that she was involved in a group of legal figures that discussed the Tusk government’s controversial takeover of public media in December 2023. “[She] is a discredited and extremely politicised person who should be brought to justice, and not receive the laurels of the commissioner for human rights,” former PiS justice minister Marcin Warchoł told the Do Rzeczy weekly last month. After a Sejm committee hearing on Gregorczyk-Abram’s candidacy earlier this month, former PiS deputy justice minister Sebastian Kaleta criticised her for ignoring questions over her alleged “role in the illegal takeover of public media”. World.title: President to swear in new judge to Poland’s disputed constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has agreed to swear in a new judge to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), ending weeks of doubt as to whether the opposition-aligned president would accept the judge appointed by the government’s parliamentary majority. Although Sławomir Patyra will now be accepted onto the court, four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year continue to be excluded after Nawrocki refused to receive their oaths and the TK’s chief justice, also aligned with the opposition, blocked them from taking office. W najbliższy wtorek 28 lipca Prezydent Karol Nawrocki działając na postawie art. 4 ust. 1 ustawy o statusie sędziów Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, przyjmie ślubowanie od prof. Sławomira Patyry i tego samego dnia wręczy powołania czterem nowym sędziom Sądu Najwyższego. W przyszłym… — Zbigniew Bogucki🇵🇱 (@BoguckiZbigniew) July 22, 2026 Under Polish law, when a vacancy emerges among the 15 positions on the TK – for example when a judge’s nine-year term expires – the lower house of parliament, the Sejm, chooses who should fill it. However, to take office, the judge must swear an oath before the president. In April, after the Sejm had chosen six candidates to fill vacancies on the court, Nawrocki took the unprecedented step of inviting only two of them to be sworn in. He argued there were doubts over the legality of how all six had been chosen, but decided to accept two to ensure the TK had the necessary quorum to function. Those two have been able to take up their seats on the court, but the other four remain in limbo. Although they arranged their own private swearing-in ceremony without the presence of Nawrocki, the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, has refused to accept them. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the quartet be allowed to take up their positions. But the TK – where judges appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government retain a majority – issued its own ruling endorsing Nawrocki’s right not to swear in the new judges. On 11 June, the Sejm then chose another judge, Patyra, to fill a newly opened vacancy on the court. In his case, the legal doubts Nawrocki had expressed regarding the previous appointments, which in some instances were made more than a year after the vacancies had arisen, did not seem to apply. Yet for weeks the president refused to confirm whether he would swear him in. That prompted Patyra to write to Nawrocki in early July and then again this week, asking the president to indicate a date on which he could take his oath. Patyra himself has also made clear on which side of the dispute he stands. In an interview with news website Onet in May, he accused Nawrocki and Święczkowski of “blatantly unlawful actions” in deciding which TK judges can and cannot take office and suggested that the police should intervene. Sędzia TK prof. Patyra po raz kolejny zaapelował do Prezydenta o wyznaczenie mu terminu na złożenie przysięgi. Ignorowanie sędziego TK przez Prezydenta jest kolejnym przykładem psucia państwa. To pokazuje, jak bardzo siły anty-demokratyczne boją się odbudowy niezależnego TK.… — Dariusz Mazur (@_Dariusz_Mazur) July 21, 2026 Finally, on Wednesday this week, Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, announced that Nawrocki had invited Patyra to the presidential palace on Tuesday next week to take his oath. Speaking to Polsat News, Bogucki said that, in the case of Patyra, initially “there were some doubts, but the president dispelled them”, without specifying what they were. In the end, they concluded that “we had a fundamentally clean situation here” and Patyra was chosen “in accordance with all procedures”, unlike the six new judges chosen by the Sejm in March to fill longstanding vacancies. “It was not President Nawrocki or the current opposition who destroyed and are destroying the tribunal; it is the government that is doing it,” he added. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Germany has deployed soldiers to Poland to help reinforce defences on NATO’s eastern flank in response to the threat of Russia. While Poland already hosts various allied forces, the presence of German troops is particularly symbolic given the two countries’ difficult history. “United, we will prevail,” wrote the General Staff of the Polish Armed Forces (SGWP), announcing the deployment. “This is what allied cooperation looks like in practice, which translates into greater military readiness and strengthens NATO’s defensive potential.” Polscy i niemieccy żołnierze razem wzmacniają granicę z Rosją. Takie rzeczy możliwe tylko za Tuska ☺️ pic.twitter.com/oNBME2gBsv — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 22, 2026 Last December, the Polish and German defence ministries revealed that a “mid-double-digit number” of German troops would be deployed from mid-2026 until the end of 2027 to support implementation of Poland’s East Shield operation, which seeks to bolster defences along the borders with Belarus and Russia. They said that the German personnel would mainly engage in engineering work, such as digging trenches, laying barbed wire and constructing anti-tank barriers. Today, Poland’s SGWP confirmed that “several dozen” German troops, including “highly specialised engineering forces” along with their equipment, had since June been temporarily deployed to “support the Polish armed forces in expanding defence infrastructure on NATO’s northeastern flank”. It emphasised that the East Shield project is “purely defensive in nature” and comes in “response to threats stemming from, among others, Russian aggression against Ukraine”. While the armed forces did not reveal the location of the deployment, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk indicated in a social media post that it was on the Russian border. Poland has a 210-km frontier with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. German public broadcaster Deutsche Welle reports that the activities of the German sappers are focused in particular on improving defences around the so-called Suwałki Gap, a strategically important stretch of land around the Polish-Lithuanian border between Belarus and Kaliningrad. “Together, we are ensuring Europe’s security,” said Lieutenant General Alexander Sollfrank, the Bundeswehr’s operational commander, announcing the deployment today. “Through our engagement in Poland, we are strengthening NATO’s defence capabilities and underscoring the alliance’s unwavering commitment to ensuring peace through unity and credible deterrence.” Poland and Germany have signed a bilateral security agreement that will see the two neighbours and NATO allies increase cooperation in areas such as military mobility, logistics infrastructure, maritime security in the Baltic Sea, and cybersecurity https://t.co/6BPX2WxvxH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 17, 2026 SGWP, which shared footage of Polish and German forces installing anti-tank barriers, said the work aims to “hinder and delay an aggressor’s actions in the event of a threat”, thereby “increasing the time for a response from the Polish armed forces and the entire [NATO] alliance”. It also seeks to “create conditions for the efficient reception, deployment and use of NATO forces on Polish territory”. SGWP welcomed “the involvement of the German contingent as a practical expression of allied solidarity and the result of consistently developing military cooperation between Poland and Germany”. It also noted that the cooperation would help the two sides improve their ability to operate jointly, including “developing the competencies necessary for conducting a joint defence operation”. However, it emphasised that the current deployment is focused on training and engineering, with no combat component, and that the German troops are unarmed. SGWP also emphasised that the East Shield operation remains entirely a Polish national programme. The leaders of eight countries on the EU's eastern flank have met in the first summit of its kind to discuss closer security cooperation. Finland and Poland announced that they would jointly lead an initiative, Eastern Flank Watch, to bolster defences https://t.co/fxRHpkM6w9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 The deployment of German troops to Poland comes shortly after the two countries signed a defence cooperation agreement in which they pledged to increase cooperation in areas such as military mobility, logistics infrastructure, maritime security in the Baltic Sea, and cybersecurity. The agreement is a sign that the two countries now stand “shoulder to shoulder, as equals”, declared German defence minister Boris Pistorius. Poland is also currently seeking a new permanent US military base on its territory, after President Donald Trump recently pledged to boost American troop numbers. Last week, Tusk also announced that Poland will host military exercises involving France and the UK this autumn. Poland will host military exercises later this year with France and the UK to prepare for providing future security guarantees to Ukraine, says PM @donaldtusk. Poland’s climate and environment ministry has inaugurated the first of 11 planned “community forests” around large cities, with the aim of giving residents a place for recreation and contact with nature while also helping to fulfil the government’s pledge to reduce logging. Plans for the forests were announced in 2024, and the first has now been established around Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city. Ten other major urban centres, including Warsaw, Kraków, Poznań and Łódź, are set to follow. Dotrzymujemy słowa. Powołaliśmy pierwsze lasy społeczne w Polsce, to lasy ochronne wokół Wrocławia. Kolejne miasta przed nami. @MKiS_GOV_PL pic.twitter.com/RxhsMZShj9 — Paulina Hennig-Kloska (@hennigkloska) July 21, 2026 “This is a historic moment and the beginning of a new approach to forest protection – with residents in mind first and foremost,” said climate and environment minister Paulina Hennig-Kloska at an inauguration ceremony outside Wrocław on Sunday. “Community forests are places where residents can relax, play sports and simply spend time close to nature,” she added. “At the same time, they are crucial to our security and quality of life: they retain water, regulate the climate, purify the air and protect the soil.” An area covering 13,000 hectares (32,124 acres) has been designated as a community forest around Wrocław. Forest management there will now be aimed at “maximising the forest’s social functions”, says the ministry, while timber harvesting is also restricted. The area will be divided into three zones, including “natural forests”, where nature will be left to take its course, and “near-natural forests” with minimal intervention. However, the largest zone, amounting to over 8,000 hectares, will be “social forests”, which the state forestry agency says “will be managed in a way that ensures the comfort of those who use the forest and its benefits related to wellbeing, physical exercise and recreation”. Hennig-Kloska noted that, in the latter area, educational trails as well as hiking and cycling paths would be established. However, given that such facilities already exist in many forests, it remains unclear how the new community forests will differ. The ministry is now conducting consultations and analysis on establishing community forests around ten other designated urban centres: Bielsko-Biała, Tricity (Gdańsk-Gdynia-Sopot), Katowice, Kielce, Kraków, Łódź, Poznań, Szczecin, Toruń-Bydgoszcz and Warsaw. On Sunday, Hennig-Kloska said that the “next in line” to have their community forests established are Kielce and Bielsko-Biała, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Shortly after coming to power in December 2023, the current government announced that it would halt planned logging in some forests. The former Law and Justice (PiS) administration had faced criticism for overseeing an increase in logging, especially in Białowieża Forest. The current government also launched plans to create Poland’s first new national parks in over two decades. However, PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki last year vetoed that move, arguing that it would “block the economic development of the region” and threaten Poland’s security. World.title: Prague Compared to 11 European Cities: Housing, Jobs, Transport,
World.content:
A new report from the Prague Institute of Planning and Development (IPR) compares life in Prague with 11 other European cities, following a typical resident’s day—from housing and commuting to work, education, and leisure.

Based on verified data collected directly from partner cities, the study highlights both Prague’s strengths and its biggest challenges.

Prague Has Some of Europe’s Least Affordable Housing

The report found that Prague has the least affordable owner-occupied housing among the cities compared.

Buying an apartment requires more than 13 years of gross salary, placing Prague alongside cities such as Barcelona, Munich, and Amsterdam. Unlike many Western European cities, Prague also lacks relatively affordable rental housing.

Renting a 60-square-meter apartment costs around 40% of the average salary in Prague. By comparison, the same apartment would consume about 28% of average income in Munich and just 14% in Vienna.

Strong Job Market, But Lower Incomes

Prague continues to have one of the lowest unemployment rates in Europe, making it relatively easy to find work.

However, real incomes remain below those of most Western European capitals. Workers in Munich earn roughly 50% more than those in Prague, while wages in cities such as Copenhagen have grown steadily over the past decade.

Although Prague residents now work fewer hours than they did ten years ago—less than 39 hours per week on average—they still work around three hours more each week than people in many Western European cities.

Public Transport Is One of Prague’s Biggest Strengths

Prague ranks among Europe’s top cities for public transport.

Around 70% of residents use public transport regularly, while 87% report being satisfied with the service. The city’s extensive tram, metro, and rail networks make commuting easy, and the system stands out for its reliability, dense coverage, and affordability.

A monthly public transport pass costs less than 1% of the average monthly income, making Prague one of the most affordable cities for public transport after Barcelona.

Car Ownership Continues to Rise

Despite having one of Europe’s best public transport systems, Prague continues to see a steady increase in car ownership.

Together with Warsaw and Bucharest, Prague is one of the few cities in the study where the number of registered cars is still growing significantly. By contrast, cities such as Stockholm, Copenhagen, and Vienna have between one-third and one-half fewer cars per capita and a much higher share of electric and hybrid vehicles.

The report warns that increasing car ownership contributes to traffic congestion, road accidents, poorer air quality, and greater pressure on public space.

World.title: Meet the Four Prague Pizzerias Recognized in 50 Top Pizza Europa 2026
World.content:
Prague’s growing pizza scene gained international attention after four local restaurants were recognized in the 50 Top Pizza Europa 2026 guide.

The biggest success went to Pizza Nuova, which secured 30th place among the best pizzerias in Europe outside Italy. While the restaurant slipped a few places compared with last year’s ranking, it remains the only Czech establishment to appear in the guide’s main European list.

Located near Prague’s Kotva department store, Pizza Nuova has built its reputation on authentic Neapolitan pizza made with premium Italian ingredients. The restaurant also holds certification from the Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana, an organization that promotes traditional Neapolitan pizza-making standards.

Prague’s recognition extended beyond a single restaurant. Three additional venues received the guide’s Excellent Pizzerias distinction, awarded to restaurants that consistently demonstrate outstanding quality.

This year’s recipients are Da Pietro, Sasy The Original, and Diskotéka in Prague’s Dejvice district.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Pizzeria Da Pietro Praha (@dapietropraha)

Diskotéka is one of this year’s notable newcomers. Shortly after opening, the restaurant attracted attention for its distinctive interior, centered around a large silver pizza oven designed to resemble a disco ball.

Alongside its food, the venue hosts DJ nights and combines a traditional pizzeria with a relaxed social gathering space.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Diskotéka Pizza (@diskoteka.pizza)

The annual 50 Top Pizza rankings are compiled by anonymous inspectors who visit restaurants without prior notice. Their assessments go well beyond the pizza itself, taking into account ingredient quality, dough preparation, baking technique, service, beverage selection, atmosphere, and the overall dining experience.

World.title: Czech Women Earn About CZK 109,000 Less Per Year Than Men
World.content:
Czech women earn significantly less than men on average, with the annual difference estimated at CZK 109,000.

New figures based on Eurostat data show the country’s gender pay gap remains above the EU average.

Across the EU, employed women earn an estimated CZK 93,800 less annually than men on average. The European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC), which converted the hourly wage gap into annual earnings, estimates that the combined difference across the bloc amounts to more than CZK 8.65 trillion every year.

Czech Republic exceeds the EU average

According to Eurostat, women across the European Union earned 11.1% less per hour than men in 2024. In practical terms, women received CZK 88.90 for every CZK 100 earned by men. The figures cover companies with at least ten employees.

Applying that methodology, the ETUC estimates that women in the Czech Republic earn roughly CZK 108,700 less per year than men, placing the country above the EU average.

Only a handful of member states recorded larger estimated annual gaps. Finland ranked highest at around CZK 183,500, followed by Austria (CZK 165,600), Germany (CZK 146,200) and Sweden (CZK 123,600).

At the opposite end of the scale, Luxembourg was the only EU country where women earned slightly more than men on average. There, women’s hourly earnings exceeded men’s by 0.8%, equivalent to roughly CZK 11,500 annually in their favor under the ETUC model. Estonia recorded the largest percentage gap in the bloc, at 18.8%.

Different methods produce different figures

National Czech statistics paint a somewhat different picture because they rely on a different methodology.

Data from the Czech Statistical Office shows that in 2025 the median gross monthly wage reached CZK 41,068 for women and CZK 47,648 for men. That represents a monthly difference of CZK 6,580, or just under CZK 79,000 over a full year.

The discrepancy does not mean either calculation is incorrect. Eurostat measures average gross hourly earnings, while the Czech Statistical Office compares median monthly wages. Because the indicators measure different aspects of income, the results cannot be directly compared.

Eurostat uses an unadjusted gender pay gap, which reflects a range of labor market factors, including differences in occupations, industries, management roles, work experience, career interruptions, age and the balance between public and private sector employment.

World.title: Spicy, Not Spicy: How This Chef Is Bringing Authentic Chinese Street Food to Prague
World.content:
At Manifesto Market, the aroma of Sichuan peppercorns and chili oil stands out among the usual mix of street food and drinks.

It comes from Lá Bù Lá Street, the more casual sibling of the restaurant Lá Bù Lá, both founded by Wen, a Chongqing native who wants to introduce Prague diners to the real flavors of her hometown.

Wen arrived in Prague in 2019 after being accepted into a Master’s program at the Prague University of Economics and Business. But studying was only part of the reason she moved. At 22, she wanted a new beginning and the chance to discover a different version of herself.

“There was something about Prague that attracted me immediately,” she says. “The architecture, the pace of life, the atmosphere of the city —

it all felt very charming. I wanted to see what kind of person I could become here.”

That decision eventually led her into the restaurant business, with four concepts launched over the years — two that closed and two that continue today.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Lá Bù Lá Street (@labula_street)

Beyond the Stereotypes

For Wen, opening a Chinese restaurant in Prague was never only about selling food. It was also about showing people that Chinese cuisine is far more diverse than many stereotypes suggest.

“China is a huge country, and every region has its own culture and food traditions,” she says. Through her restaurants, she hopes guests become more curious about where dishes come from, how ingredients are used, and how different regions eat.

She also wants Chinese food to be seen as something connected to special occasions, not only a quick meal.

“Chinese food can create beautiful memories too,” she says. One example is Chongqing chili, which is often associated only with heat. Wen says there is much more to it.

“Many people think Chongqing chili is only about being spicy. But it is also about aroma,” she explains. The same applies to Sichuan peppercorns, where the famous numbing sensation is only part of the experience.

Learning the Hard Way

Wen’s path has not been simple. Her first two projects, Chi Xiao Mian and Mi I’m, did not succeed as she had hoped, but she sees them as important lessons.

“They taught me how to work with people, how to manage a team, and how important communication is,” she says.

The experience also taught her to stay focused on her original vision. Running a restaurant requires listening to others, but also knowing when to trust your own ideas.

“Building something meaningful always requires finding a balance between dreams and reality,” she says.

A Restaurant, and Then a Street

Today, Wen runs two concepts: Lá Bù Lá and Lá Bù Lá Street. The name, meaning “spicy, not spicy,” reflects the idea that Chongqing cuisine is about much more than just heat.

The original restaurant offers a deeper introduction to traditional Chongqing dishes, while Lá Bù Lá Street at Manifesto Market has a more relaxed atmosphere.

“It is more spontaneous and more social,” Wen says. The concept is inspired by street food culture in Chongqing, where people gather, share dishes, and spend time together.

At Manifesto, surrounded by music, travelers, and international crowds, the idea has naturally evolved. Some dishes work better for sharing, while others simply encourage people to stay longer.

“For us, food tastes better when shared,” Wen says. “Passed around a table. Offered to a friend. Or quietly stolen from someone else’s plate.”

Growing Step by Step

Like many restaurant owners, Wen faces daily challenges, from managing a team to introducing unfamiliar flavors to new customers. Building a group of people who share her values has been one of the most difficult parts.

When asked about opening more locations in Prague, she says the ambition is there — but there is no rush.

“Of course, I would love for more people to discover the food of my hometown,” she says. “But I am not in a hurry.”

For now, Wen is focused on improving the restaurants she already has and building a stronger team.

“When my team and I are truly ready, we can always begin the next journey,” she says. “For now, we are happy to keep growing step by step.”

World.title: Prague and Stockholm Launch Cross-Border Public Art Project
World.content:
Visitors in Prague and Stockholm will soon be able to communicate across borders through a pair of interactive public art installations designed to exchange anonymous messages between the two cities.

The linked installations, created by the Czech initiative Praho! project and its Swedish partner Stockholm! project, will open in Stockholm on August 20 and in Prague on August 31.

The installations are designed as private spaces intended for one visitor at a time.

After entering, participants answer a series of questions before listening to an authentic audio recording left by someone in the other city. They are then invited to record their own message, creating an ongoing exchange between residents and visitors in Prague and Stockholm.

According to the project team, the concept explores what happens when anonymous thoughts become personal through the human voice.

“The installation creates a space where you first listen to someone else—and only then can you speak,” the organizers said. “We want to explore how connecting two different cities through shared experiences can foster understanding.”

The initiative is part of Art & Design Without Borders, an international collaboration supported by the Erasmus+ programme. The project brings together organizations from the Czech Republic and Sweden to promote participatory art, community engagement and new approaches to public space.

Although they work closely together, Praho! project and Stockholm! project operate as independent non-profit organizations. Their partnership reflects a shared history rather than a branch structure.

Praho! project was founded in 2021 and focuses on participatory art in public and digital spaces. Through text-based interventions and an online platform, it has collected more than 30,000 anonymous responses addressing personal experiences and broader social issues. Those contributions have since been transformed into publications, exhibitions and artistic installations.

The concept, however, began even earlier. Founder Annamarie Čermáková first developed the idea in 2019 while studying at Stockholm University of the Arts. Returning to Sweden inspired the creation of Stockholm! project in 2025.

The project extends beyond the installations themselves. Organizers will also host workshops, educational programmes, international internships and prepare a methodology guide documenting best practices in participatory public art across different European settings.

World.title: BAY55: 114 Luxury Apartments Planned for Prague’s Riverfront in Smíchov
World.content:
One of the last undeveloped riverfront plots in central Prague is set to become home to a new luxury residential project.

Developer Daramis has unveiled plans for BAY55, a development featuring 114 high-end apartments on Hořejší nábřeží in Smíchov, just steps from the railway bridge and within walking distance of the city center.

According to Daramis, BAY55 is designed to compete with premium residential developments in leading European and North American cities. The company says the project will emphasize architecture, technology, privacy and resident services alongside its prime location.

The residence will include a wellness and fitness center covering roughly 600 square meters, a private residents’ lounge and hospitality facilities.

A restaurant or café is also planned on the ground floor, serving both residents and visitors. The developer says the level of amenities is intended to match those found in luxury hotels.

Designers have also focused on balancing density with comfort. Every apartment is planned to include either a spacious balcony or terrace, complemented by integrated shading systems intended to provide greater privacy despite the urban setting.

Before construction of the residential complex can begin, significant work will be carried out along the riverfront.

The existing Smíchov embankment will be extended, creating additional public space and improving pedestrian access along the Vltava. The infrastructure upgrades are expected to become part of the wider transformation of one of Prague’s fastest-growing neighborhoods.

Daramis acquired the land from BPD Development in 2024. Although the developer has not disclosed the value of the investment, it says BAY55 represents the largest and most expensive project in the company’s history.

Costs are driven not only by the location and construction standards, but also by flood protection measures, advanced building technologies and architectural features planned for the shared spaces.

The project is currently progressing through the permitting process. If approvals proceed as expected, construction of the new embankment will begin first, followed by the residential development itself.

Completion is currently scheduled for around 2030.

World.title: From Müller to Krispy Kreme, Global Chains Are Coming to Czechia
World.content:
International drugstores, fashion retailers, discount chains and restaurant concepts are preparing to open their first locations in Czechia, adding new competition for established players.

Here are some of the biggest brands expected to enter the Czech market.

Müller

German retailer Müller is preparing to launch in the Czech Republic. The company has already established a Czech branch and website, although it has not yet announced the opening date of its first store.

Unlike traditional drugstores, Müller combines cosmetics and personal care products with toys, stationery, household goods, pet supplies and organic food.

The chain operates nearly 1,000 stores across nine European countries and will compete with established Czech market leaders such as dm, Rossmann and Teta.

Krispy Kreme

American doughnut chain Krispy Kreme is reportedly searching for a location in central Prague and could open its first Czech store soon.

Founded in North Carolina in 1937, the company became famous worldwide for its Original Glazed doughnuts and stores where customers can watch the production process.

Ochnik

Polish fashion brand Ochnik plans an ambitious expansion in the Czech Republic, with 15 to 20 stores expected by the end of 2026.

The company specializes in leather jackets, footwear, luggage and accessories. It previously considered acquiring Czech brand Kara but decided to build its own network instead.

OVS

Italian fashion retailer OVS is also preparing its Czech debut.

The company focuses on affordable clothing for the whole family and is particularly strong in children’s fashion. It is positioned between discount retailers and mainstream brands such as H&M, C&A and Reserved.

Normal

Danish discount chain Normal is preparing to enter the Czech market after establishing a local company.

The retailer sells cosmetics, household products, snacks and everyday goods at permanently low prices. Its stores are designed to encourage impulse shopping, with customers walking through a changing selection of products.

MR. D.I.Y.

Malaysian discount retailer MR. D.I.Y. has some of the biggest expansion plans among new arrivals.

The company plans to open around 20 stores in Prague and eventually grow to more than 100 locations across the Czech Republic. Its first Czech store is expected to open at Forum Nová Karolina in Ostrava.

MR. D.I.Y. sells household equipment, DIY products, electronics and stationery.

Burgermeister

Berlin burger chain Burgermeister will enter the Czech Republic as part of its European expansion.

The brand started in 2006 inside a converted toilet building near Berlin’s Schlesisches Tor station before growing into a chain with more than 30 restaurants.

It focuses on its own production, including burgers made with Irish beef and ingredients prepared in Berlin.

Dave’s Hot Chicken

American fast-food chain Dave’s Hot Chicken is preparing to compete with KFC and Popeyes in the Czech market.

The brand specializes in Nashville-style spicy fried chicken, offering chicken tenders and sandwiches with different levels of heat.

Founded in Los Angeles in 2017, the chain has expanded to more than 400 locations worldwide.

Arthur Gelato

Slovak premium ice cream brand Arthur Gelato has already opened its first Prague location on Francouzská Street.

The company focuses on handmade ice cream, fresh ingredients and unusual flavors. It plans further expansion through franchising.

Sticks’n’Sushi

Danish restaurant group Sticks’n’Sushi will open its first Prague location this autumn.

The concept combines Japanese sushi with grilled skewers and will operate a three-story restaurant on Jungmann Square with around 160 seats.

World.title: Five Things to Know Before Flying From Prague Airport This Summer
World.content:
Passengers departing from Prague Airport this summer are being advised to plan ahead as the airport prepares for its busiest travel season in years.

To help travelers avoid unnecessary delays, the airport has released a list of practical recommendations covering transport, security screening, travel documents and baggage rules.

Leave Extra Time to Reach the Airport

The biggest challenge this summer is expected to be road access to the terminals. Construction at the Aviatická–Lipská intersection may cause traffic congestion on routes leading to the airport.

Airport officials recommend using public transport whenever possible, as buses are not affected by the roadworks. Travelers arriving by car should allow extra time to reach the terminals, particularly during peak holiday periods.

Self-Service Check-In Can Save Time

Passengers can speed up the departure process by using the airport’s self-service facilities. Prague Airport now offers 31 check-in kiosks and 32 self-service baggage drop counters, available for flights operated by 18 participating airlines.

Before heading to the airport, travelers should also verify the entry requirements for their destination. Those flying to the United Kingdom, for example, now need an Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA) before departure.

Bring Physical Travel Documents

Although many travelers rely on digital wallets and electronic documents, Prague Airport reminds passengers that electronic IDs and passports cannot be used during passport control.

Travelers should carry a valid physical passport or national identity card, depending on the requirements of their destination.

Security Rules Depend on the Terminal

Passengers departing from Terminal 2 will notice a faster security process thanks to newly installed CT scanners.

The new technology allows travelers to leave electronics and liquids inside their cabin baggage during screening. In addition to the standard one-liter transparent bag containing containers of up to 100 milliliters each, passengers may also carry one extra liquid container with a capacity of up to two liters.

These updated rules currently apply only in Terminal 2. Security procedures in Terminal 1 remain unchanged.

Pack Power Banks Correctly

The airport is also reminding travelers about one of the most common packing mistakes.

Power banks, laptops and tablets must always be transported in carry-on baggage, not checked luggage. In addition, lithium batteries must not exceed 100 Wh unless specifically approved by the airline. Ignoring these rules can lead to delays during security checks or, in some cases, passengers being refused boarding.

World.title: Shocking video: police search for men travelling on the side of a train in Hungary
World.content:
Unknown individuals chose to travel on the side of a train in Érd, according to footage shared by the local police.

Uknown men travelled on the side of a train

According to a video uploaded to the official YouTube page of the Hungarian police, unidentified men travelled on the side of a passenger train departing from Érd. In the late afternoon of 1 June, they jumped onto the side of a moving train at Érd railway station. They remained there until the next stop, Érd-felső, before jumping off and fleeing the scene.

One of the perpetrators. Photo: PrtScr/Youtube

The local police are asking anyone who recognises the individuals, who were risking their lives, to contact the Pest County Police Headquarters on +36 1 236 2897, or to submit an anonymous report via the Telefontanú (Phone Witness) service on +36 80 555 111, or by calling the central emergency number 112.

They added that travelling on the side of a train can easily lead to life-threatening situations, particularly when the carriages contract. Furthermore, individuals can easily fall while the train is travelling at high speed, or be struck by high-voltage overhead wires.

Check out the video below:

Teenagers died after climbing on a freight train

In a separate incident, a 17-year-old boy and a 16-year-old girl climbed onto a freight train in Budapest and came dangerously close to a 25 kV overhead wire. Although they did not touch it, both were fatally struck by an electric arc. Such phenomena can cause death even from several metres away. This is one of the reasons why entering areas near high-voltage equipment is strictly prohibited, vaol.hu wrote.

If you missed: Epstein scandal reaches Hungary again after unexpected death of agent who hunted out Hungarian girls

Professionals working with such infrastructure are required to wear specially designed arc-rated personal protective equipment (PPE) that meets international standards.

The teenage boy died instantly at the scene, while the girl suffered severe burns over more than 70 per cent of her body and later died in hospital.

Another 16-year-old girl who was with them did not climb onto the train and was therefore unharmed. However, she was severely shocked by the incident and was taken to hospital after witnessing what had happened to her friends.

World.title: Yemeni Ambassador Ahmed Abdullah Nagi: Why the world should not allow Bab al-Mandab to become “another Hormuz”
World.content:
Bab al-Mandab Between Global Security and Human Tragedy in Yemen.

By: Ambassador Ahmed Abdullah Nagi

Chargé d’Affaires of the Embassy of the Republic of Yemen in Budapest

Bab al-Mandab is no longer merely a maritime passage connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden; it has become one of the most important indicators of stability in the global economic system. Every threat targeting this strait has direct repercussions on international trade, energy security, supply chains, shipping costs and insurance rates. With the escalating Houthi attacks on maritime navigation, the international community faces a real test: Will it act preemptively to prevent Bab al-Mandab from becoming another Hormuz, or will it merely manage crises after they occur?

Approximately 13% of global trade passes through Bab al-Mandab, along with significant part of the oil and gas exports destined for Europe and Asia. This means any sustained disruption in this passage threatens not only regional nations but the entire global economy through increased shipping and insurance costs, supply chain disruptions, and rising energy and commodity prices. Therefore, the security of Bab al-Mandab is no longer merely a Yemeni or Middle Eastern issue, it has become a shared international concern.

Ambassador Ahmed Abdullah Nagi

In this context, recent threats issued by Houthi militias claiming to impose an “embargo” on Saudi maritime navigation in the Red Sea are unjustified. These terrorist militias argue this blockade on the Saudi maritime navigation is a response to the blockade on Yemen. In reality, there is no blockade on Yemen; rather, there are restrictions on Houthi movement following their 2014 coup, specifically since 2015, under international decisions, most importantly UN Security Council Resolution 2216 of 2015.

In contrast, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia has provided unlimited humanitarian, developmental, and economic support to the Yemeni people during the worst phase of Yemen’s contemporary history. Without this support, the suffering of the Yemeni people would have intensified and worsened.

Official data indicates the continued flow of commercial and relief ships to ports under Houthi control. Since the beginning of 2026, more than 300 ships have entered these ports, including 157 ships loaded with food supplies, 104 ships carrying construction materials, and 45 ships carrying petroleum derivatives. These figures weaken the narrative of a comprehensive blockade and confirm the continuation of trade movements and humanitarian supplies.

On the contrary, military developments indicate the growing offensive capabilities of the Houthis on Yemen’s western coast, including the deployment of missiles, drones, and attack boats, in addition to reports of continued Iranian logistical and intelligence support, including the return of the Iranian ship previously known as “Saviz” to the Red Sea under a new name. This reflects that what is occurring does not represent an isolated local development, but rather falls within a broader Iranian strategy seeking to possess leverage over the most important international maritime passages.

From here emerges the comparison with the Strait of Hormuz. The world has become accustomed over past decades to dealing with threats targeting that strait as part of the security landscape in the Gulf, despite the economic disruptions they cause. Today, the international community faces the possibility of repeating the same scenario in Bab al-Mandab, but through Iranian proxies in Yemen, as the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab experience escalating threats directed against international navigation, amid the continued use of this vital maritime passage by the Iranian-backed Houthi group as a political and military pressure card. If disrupting navigation or threatening with it become an acceptable political tool, the world will face a dangerous precedent threatening one of the most critical maritime passages of the twenty-first century. The danger lies not only in the direct impact on commercial ships but in the potential establishment of a new maritime security equation in the region based on using international passages as means to impose political will and achieve geopolitical gains.

Saudi Arabia: From Crisis Management to Peacemaking Opportunities

Amid these challenges, the pivotal role played by Saudi Arabia in supporting Yemen’s stability cannot be overlooked. Since the beginning of the crisis, the Saudi role has not been limited to supporting the legitimate Yemeni Government, but has included launching one of the largest humanitarian and development assistance programs through King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Center, supporting the Central Bank of Yemen, financing the fuel needed to continue basic services, and implementing projects in the health, education, water and food security sectors. This support has mitigated humanitarian deterioration and prevented complete state institutional collapse.

Saudi Arabia also played a central role in promoting political solutions, leading—in coordination with Oman and the United Nations—intensive efforts to end the war and achieve comprehensive settlement. The Yemeni Government has shown clear flexibility in engaging with these initiatives, based on its conviction that the just peace is the only path to end Yemeni suffering and rebuild the state. However, continued military escalation by the Houthis has prevented tangible progress, highlighting the need for a more forceful international stance supporting the peace process and holding obstructing parties accountable.

Yemen: When Children Become the Greatest Victims

Maritime security cannot be separated from the humanitarian reality in Yemen. While the world focuses on ship movements in the Red Sea, millions of Yemenis suffer one of the worst humanitarian crises in modern times. War has destroyed the economy, weakened state institutions, caused essential services to decline, and pushed millions of families into poverty and displacement.

Most painfully, the primary victims of this war are the children. An entire generation has grown up in an environment dominated by fear and violence, lacking opportunities for education, healthcare, and psychological stability. These children need not only food and medicine but genuine opportunities to reclaim their lives and build their futures. If the war continues, Yemen will lose not only its present but its future as well, because state reconstruction begins with human reconstruction.

Therefore, supporting peace in Yemen should not be viewed merely as a moral obligation but as an investment in regional and international security. Each child returning to school is a step toward stability; each institution resuming operations reduces opportunities for extremism and violence; and each advance in the peace process directly reflects on Red Sea security and global trade stability.

Responsibility Beyond Protecting Maritime Passages

Protecting Bab al-Mandab cannot be achieved solely by deploying more naval vessels or strengthening military patrols, important as these are. It requires a comprehensive vision addressing the crisis’s root causes. Lasting stability begins with the Yemeni state recovering its institutions and sovereignty and supporting the legitimate Government, combined with promoting development and reconstruction efforts, in parallel with continued international pressure to ensure freedom of navigation and hold accountable those who threaten it.

Trump warns Iran over US troop deaths

Today, the international community stands before two clear choices: either taking preemptive action to prevent Bab al-Mandab from becoming “another Hormuz”, or waiting for a new reality to take hold in which global trade becomes hostage to regional crises.

Protecting Bab al-Mandab is not the responsibility of Yemen alone, but of the entire international community. It is the protection of global trade freedom, energy security, and international economic stability. At the same time, it is the protection of the future of millions of Yemenis who deserve to live in a safe and stable state, not on an open battlefield.

Yemen’s stability is the true guarantee for Red Sea security, and Red Sea security is an integral part of global security.

World.title: PM Péter Magyar launches probe concerning Orbán government’s EUR 1 billion North Macedonia loan
World.content:
Hungary’s government has launched an investigation into a €1 billion loan extended to North Macedonia, which the previous administration provided on preferential terms through the state-owned Eximbank, according to the North Macedonian news portal 360 Stepeni following an announcement by PM Péter Magyar.

Péter Magyar launched probe concerning North Macedonia loan

According to the report, the Hungarian government is reviewing four transactions linked to the state Eximbank, one of which concerns the loan granted to North Macedonia on favourable terms by the previous cabinet. The prime minister is said to believe that the conditions of the loan — a 3.25 per cent fixed interest rate and unrestricted use — were significantly more advantageous than those under which the Hungarian state itself can borrow, or those available to Hungarian businesses. As a result, suspicions have arisen that the previous government may have used financial instruments intended to support domestic enterprises for foreign political purposes.

The North Macedonian loan agreement was concluded in mid-July 2024 by Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski shortly after taking office, during a meeting with his then Hungarian counterpart Viktor Orbán on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Washington, the Hungarian news agency wrote.

If you missed: Hungarian lawyers’ circle head: former PM Orbán may soon become a suspect – can he be arrested?

North Macedonia subsequently entered into two €500 million agreements with Eximbank: the first was signed on 8 October, with a 15-year maturity, a three-year grace period and a fixed interest rate of 3.25 per cent. The second €500 million loan was signed in December 2024. According to 360 Stepeni, North Macedonia used part of the Hungarian loan to support businesses, with the remainder allocated to municipal investment projects.

Mr Magyar said the interest equalisation linked to the transaction, which is backed by a full state guarantee, imposes a burden of more than 90 billion forints on Hungary’s budget.

World.title: Breaking – Football superpower to arrive in Budapest: Real Madrid to face Ferencváros in August
World.content:
It has now been made official that the Groupama Arena will host a prestigious international pre-season fixture this summer, as Ferencváros welcome Real Madrid to Budapest on Saturday, 8 August. The encounter will form part of the Spanish giants’ Austrian training programme and is set to rank among the most high-profile summer matches seen in Hungary in recent decades. Ticket sales for the Budapest Real Madrid match will begin shortly.

Reports of the fixture had previously circulated in the press, now confirmed by Ferencváros, according to Nemzeti Sport. The record-breaking Spanish club is scheduled to play several international matches during its summer preparations, with Budapest included as one of the tour’s key stops.

Mourinho returns to the Real Madrid bench

Real Madrid’s summer preparations began in mid-July under the stewardship of José Mourinho, who has once again taken charge of the club. The side will play its first friendly at home against CD Leganés before travelling to Austria for a training camp, where it will face a number of international opponents. The Budapest fixture is expected to be one of the highlights of that programme.

First meeting in three decades

Ferencváros and Real Madrid last met in the group stage of the 1995–96 Champions League. At the Santiago Bernabéu, the Spanish side recorded a commanding 6–1 victory, while in Budapest the Hungarian champions secured a valuable 1–1 draw. Ferencváros’s goal was scored by Flórián Albert Jr, a moment that remains etched in the club’s European history.

The two sides have not met in either competitive or friendly fixtures since, making the upcoming clash a special occasion for supporters of both clubs.

Mourinho’s previous link to the Groupama Arena

Notably, the Groupama Arena’s opening match in 2014 featured José Mourinho’s Chelsea side as Ferencváros’s opponents. The Portuguese manager experienced the atmosphere of the Budapest stadium first-hand on that occasion, and reports suggest this prior connection may have played a role in Real Madrid selecting the Hungarian capital as one of its summer destinations.

Don’t Miss: F1 Events in Budapest

Ferencváros may seek league postponement

The timing of the friendly coincides with a major fixture in Hungary’s top flight: Ferencváros are due to face reigning champions ETO FC Győr away that weekend. The Budapest club is therefore expected to request a postponement of the NB I match in order to prepare for the gala encounter against Real Madrid with a full squad.

Ticket sales to begin shortly

According to Ferencváros, ticket sales will begin at 2 PM on 27 July. For the first 24 hours, only current season ticket holders will be eligible to purchase seats, after which sales may be opened to the general public, subject to availability.

The cheapest tickets will cost HUF 14,000, while the most expensive non-VIP tickets will be HUF 46,500 in sectors C4 and C5.

Demand is expected to be exceptional, as the 15-time Champions League winners rarely play in Hungary, making the Budapest fixture one of the standout events of the domestic football calendar this summer.

World.title: New details in the Hatvanpuszta zebra scandal: illegal keeping, escaped animals, and carcasses dumped in a pig pit
World.content:
László Gajdos, the minister responsible for animal welfare, has ordered a full investigation into the zebras kept at a farm between Bicske and Hatvanpuszta in western Hungary, he said on Facebook on Friday.

In the post, Gajdos said the relevant official documents reflected “total chaos” in the case, adding that “one thing is certain: there has been no responsible ownership there”. He said some of the zebras had arrived at the farm with inadequate documentation and that permits were applied for only later. The owners did not apply at all for a special licence for five of the animals, he added as per the Hungarian news agency.

Of the 17 zebras, only 10 had been registered, he said. He added that one of them, called Tihamér, had been kept illegally and that his existence only came to light after his death. He also said there had been no proper fence, and that three of the animals escaped and froze to death. Moreover, he said, the carcasses were disposed of illegally and thrown into a pit for pigs that had died of swine fever.

Screenshot from Gulyáságyú Média/YouTube

“This is not animal protection, but grave irresponsibility … we will not leave it at that,” Gajdos said. He also added that there are currently 17 adult zebras and three foals at the farm.

World.title: Hungarian lawyers’ circle head: former PM Orbán may soon become a suspect – can he be arrested?
World.content:
The head of the Lawyers’ Circle, Lóránt Horváth, said on the programme Konkrétan with Egon Rónai that he is convinced the case of the Ukrainian gold convoy lies behind the resignation of chief prosecutor Gábor Bálint Nagy, and that the affair could eventually reach Orbán himself.

Gold convoy case: are Hungarian authorities failing to investigate at full strength?

According to Horváth, while the chief prosecutor cited moral reasons for his departure, financial and economic considerations may also have played a role. He said that after his resignation there follows a 30-day notice period, after which Gábor Bálint Nagy could continue working as a prosecutor on a net salary of 2.5 million forints, whereas a removal procedure would also put his prosecutorial status and related benefits at risk. The lawyer therefore said that removal proceedings should be initiated even during the notice period, since the chief prosecutor continues to exercise full powers during that time, the Hungarian News Agency wrote.

The former premier is currently attending the Tusványos festival in Transylvania, Central Romania. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

Speaking about the gold convoy case, Lóránt Horváth claimed that the investigation had omitted steps that would have been justified in a case of comparable gravity. In his view, organised offending appears to be taking shape, and investigators should either have worked their way up to the leadership level or gathered evidence from the bottom up. Instead, he said, the chain of responsibility was “cut in the middle” and János Hajdu, the former head of the Counter-Terrorism Centre, was placed at the centre of the case. Although he was charged, Horváth said that, given the gravity of the case, detention, house searches and the seizure of IT equipment could also have been warranted.

The scandal may reach former PM Orbán

The lawyer also claimed that in cases of this magnitude, investigating prosecutors brief the chief prosecutor on a daily basis, meaning he can know about every important investigative step and issue instructions as well. In his opinion, the new chief prosecutor, while reviewing the cases of the past year, may find numerous circumstances suggesting interference in the proceedings.

Former PM Orbán in Brussels on a press conference. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

Lóránt Horváth said he believed the threads of the case lead to Orbán, and that if this is proved, it could have criminal significance. He said a political will had been tried to present as a criminal offence, but this had not fully materialised. In his view, no crime had in fact been committed, but rather an operation organised on a political order, for campaign purposes, of which the prime minister was most likely also aware. He added, however, that questioning or charging Orbán would require an incriminating statement or other evidence.

Will former anti-terrorism chief Hajdu face jail instead of ex-PM Orbán? Alleged aim of secret meeting revealed

They turned to the press deliberately

The programme also touched on János Hajdu’s testimony. Horváth said that, to his knowledge, Örs Farkas, who previously supervised the civilian national security services, had not yet been questioned, but that he could soon be heard as a suspect.

Orbán and Hajdu on the morning of the gold convoy operation. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

The lawyer also said that the Ukrainian bank had regained the seized assets, and that he himself was present at their handover. According to him, a few items remained in the money-laundering investigation, and their return had also been requested. He said that the expulsion measures imposed on those concerned had also been withdrawn, so they can once again move freely within the territory of the European Union.

Lóránt Horváth said ensuring publicity for the case had been a deliberate legal strategy, at the request of their client, because otherwise the gold convoy affair would, in his view, have been lost among the other proceedings.

World.title: German tourist drowns in popular Hungarian lake
World.content:
Hungarian police have launched an investigation after a German tourist drowned in Lake Hévíz, a popular tourist destination in Hungary. Authorities say he attempted to swim in the thermal water in a prohibited area.

According to hvg.hu, the German national entered the lake’s outflow at a restricted point. The Zala County Police Headquarters said they were notified on 22 July that a body had been found in Lake Hévíz. It later emerged that the 41-year-old man had decided the previous evening to swim in the thermal water. However, he drowned for reasons that have yet to be determined. The Keszthely Police Department is investigating the circumstances of the incident.

In other parts of the lake, swimmers may encounter hazards that are not immediately visible. “Complying with the rules is not an unnecessary obligation but serves to protect life. Unfortunately, tragedies occur every year that could have been prevented with a single responsible decision.”

World.title: Romanian director Alina Șerban’s debut film “I Matter” to premiere at Venice Film Festival
World.content:
“I Matter” (“Eu contez”), the feature film debut of Romanian director Alina Șerban (in photo), will have its world premiere at the 83rd edition of the Venice International Film Festival, taking place from September 1-12.

Written and directed by Alina Șerban, one of the few Roma female directors in the world, “I Matter” is a co-production between Romania (microFILM), Germany (2Pilots Filmproduction), and Belgium (Frakas Productions, Lemming Film), exploring themes such as overcoming fear, hope, and self-acceptance, according to the press release.

Spoken in Romanian and Romani, the film tells the story of Rebeca, a young Roma woman who is about to leave the foster care center where she grew up.

“We very rarely see Roma characters who live complex human experiences beyond stereotypes. And stories about what it means to be a girl, Roma, and part of the child protection system are almost nonexistent. Through ‘I Matter’ I wanted to build a bridge toward a deeper understanding of these experiences and, above all, to tell a story about humanity. The fact that this film is beginning its journey in Venice means a great deal to me,” said Alina Șerban.

The film was developed over more than four years together with young people from the social protection system. During this period, Alina Șerban created several documentary short films and theater performances alongside them.

The film’s cast includes Denisa Farcaș, Sorin Mihai, Angelina Pavel, Vanessa Dancea, Raisa Mihai, Juno (Alexandru Stancu), Alina Berzunțeanu, and Natalia Călin. Alongside them, 16 children and young people residing in the Casa Iosif and Casa Sara foster centers, part of the Măgurele Christian Social Ensemble in Bucharest, also appear in the film.

The Venice International Film Festival / Mostra Internazionale d'Arte Cinematografica will take place from September 2-12, 2026. “I Matter” has been selected alongside seven other titles in the Spotlight section, dedicated to audience films characterized by innovation and creativity in the way they engage with viewers. The film is competing for the Audience Award offered by Armani Beauty and the Luigi de Laurentiis Award for Best Debut, awarded by an international jury.

Winner of the Best Actress award at the German Actors’ Association Awards for her role in Gipsy Queen (2019), Alina Șerban is a graduate of the prestigious Tisch School of the Arts (New York), Royal Academy of Dramatic Art – RADA (London), and UNATC. In 2024, she was decorated by the president of Romania with the Order of Cultural Merit, in the rank of Knight.

She is the first Roma film and theater director in Romania and, for more than a decade, has developed artistic projects dedicated to children and young people from disadvantaged backgrounds, as well as Roma communities.
