World.title: Armenia’s labour market trends: Social media replaces employment agencies as jobs and wages grow
World.content:
Analysis of labour market trends in Armenia

Armenia‘s unemployment rate fell only slightly in 2025, declining to 11.8% from 13.3% in 2024. At the same time, according to the country’s Statistical Committee, wages continued to rise, with the average monthly salary increasing by 5.6% over the same period to 303,140 drams ($828).

Compared with 2021, the average nominal monthly salary has increased by 48.6%, the number of employees has grown by 22.4%, and the unemployment rate has fallen by 2.7 percentage points.

Employment remains highest in the wholesale and retail trade sectors, as well as in education and manufacturing. By contrast, employment is lower in the arts and culture, scientific research, and real estate sectors.

An analysis of online job platforms shows that employers are currently seeking couriers, waiters, accountants, assistants, sales and marketing specialists, and fundraising professionals.

At the same time, job seekers are increasingly drawn to international, foreign, and joint ventures, attracted by both higher salaries and better working environments.

“The labour market has become more coordinated”

Until 2016, Naira Piloyan ran an employment agency that helped many people find jobs and earned a reputation as a reliable partner for local organisations. Over the past decade, however, she says the labour market has changed. Employers now search for candidates through online platforms, using their own social media pages and job websites. As a result, she had to close her agency. She now works as a human resources specialist at a pharmaceutical company.

She says every medium-sized and large company in Armenia now employs HR specialists. They use online platforms and professional networks to find qualified candidates.

“I closely follow developments in the labour market. From my own experience, I can say that local professionals have become much better at presenting themselves during the hiring process. Employers have also become more selective when recruiting staff. The whole process is now far more streamlined and coordinated,” she says.

At the same time, she notes that personal connections and recommendations from friends or acquaintances still influence hiring decisions.

However, serious companies have realised that hiring unqualified staff creates a “time bomb” for their future development.

Instead, they rely on candidates’ experience, references from previous employers and personal interviews.

“Over the past few years, salaries at our company have increased by around 30% on average. Higher levels of professionalism among staff have largely driven that increase. Every employee takes professional development courses or retrains in a new field. As people gain knowledge and experience, they expect higher pay. If they don’t receive the salary they believe they deserve, they start looking for another job. That staff turnover has become a major challenge for large companies,” the HR specialist explains.

She says employers have also started investing more in their employees’ skills. Many companies now pay for foreign language courses, mainly English, as well as training abroad in manufacturing, technology and other fields.

She believes this growing coordination has improved the quality of Armenia’s labour market. When someone from another company applies for a job with her employer, she can now openly discuss the candidate’s abilities and professional qualities with HR managers at their previous workplace.

“In the past, asking someone for an opinion about a job applicant felt awkward. Now I simply send an email and receive a reply within a few days. The only real difficulty today is finding highly specialised professionals and technical staff. Problems usually arise when we urgently need to hire someone like a driver, security guard or cleaner. Candidates for these jobs tend to be very conservative. For example, if they need to stay just 10 minutes beyond the end of their shift, they often show little flexibility. Some may even leave work during the day without informing anyone.”

According to her, wages for these positions have risen by a larger percentage than salaries for many higher-skilled professions, including finance specialists and translators.

Working conditions are more attractive at foreign companies

Ilona Khachatryan is a logistics specialist. She now works for an American company and earns four times more than she did two years ago in the same role at a local firm. But salary is only part of the reason she left. She says unhealthy relations with management at her former company also played a major role. More broadly, she is critical of hiring practices and personnel management at many local organisations.

“At the company where I worked, it was extremely difficult to receive the bonuses that management itself had promised. To avoid paying them, they would even falsify hourly timesheets.

I applied for jobs at other local companies as well. I attended interviews and then waited for months without hearing back. Even if they decide not to hire you, shouldn’t they at least tell you? After all, you invest your time and effort preparing for those interviews. Foreign companies treat candidates much more fairly. They make transparent hiring decisions. If they decide not to hire someone, they explain in detail why they cannot move forward with the candidate.”

Ilona says her current employer hired her after the first interview. The company immediately explained the salary, holiday entitlement, employment rights and job responsibilities.

“Hearing the words ‘thank you for your work’ genuinely motivates me. It gives me energy and makes me work with greater enthusiasm and commitment. And when your employer also recognises your achievements, you realise just how undervalued professionals are in the local labour market.”

Analysis of labour market trends in Armenia

World.title: Azerbaijan changes status of internally displaced people: What do new rules provide?
World.content:
The status of internally displaced persons in Azerbaijan

On 23 July, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed into law amendments to the Law on the Status of Refugees and Internally Displaced Persons and the Law on the Social Protection of Internally Displaced Persons and Persons Equated with Them.

The amendments to the Housing Code provide for the creation of a Permanent Resettlement Fund in the territories liberated from occupation. Housing from the fund will be used to resettle internally displaced persons (IDPs) to the reclaimed territories and will later be transferred to them as private property.

The legislation also clarifies the grounds on which a person may lose IDP status. This applies to those who refuse housing offered by the state, as well as to those who are provided with alternative housing that meets the officially established housing standard for the relevant region instead of accommodation in their previous place of residence. At the same time, social protection measures will remain in place for three years after a person loses or voluntarily relinquishes their IDP status.

The changes are intended to strengthen the legal framework for the Great Return programme. In practice, however, they could significantly affect the lives of hundreds of thousands of people who have spent decades building their lives in Baku and other parts of Azerbaijan.

The purpose of the law and the benefits linked to IDP status

Under the previous legislation, internally displaced person (IDP) status entitled holders to a range of social benefits, including a monthly allowance of 60 manats (about $35) for each family member, state-funded tuition at fee-paying departments of public universities, and exemptions from certain government fees and utility payments.

For people forced to flee their homes in the early 1990s and who had spent decades living in dormitories, temporary housing units or other makeshift accommodation, these benefits represented a basic form of social support. The status also carried legal significance, as it formally recognised that they had been displaced against their will.

Under the new rules, the state is deemed to have fulfilled its obligations once it offers an internally displaced person permanent housing. If the person accepts the apartment, ownership is transferred to them, but they simultaneously lose their IDP status. Those who refuse the offer also lose their status and may forfeit the temporary accommodation provided to them in Baku or another city.

During a three-year transition period, only social support measures, including financial assistance and education benefits, will remain in place. The legal status itself, along with the other rights and guarantees associated with it, will cease to apply.

Freedom of choice and the problem of “any available housing”

The law refers to “alternative housing that complies with the standards established for the region of residence”. In practice, this means that internally displaced people are not necessarily offered housing in their native village or on their ancestral land.

For example, a person who owned several hectares of farmland before being displaced may now be offered a house in a newly built settlement with a plot of only 100–200 square metres. Ownership of their original land is not restored, as the state provides housing only. As a result, the concept of “returning home” is significantly narrowed.

According to dozens of families whose accounts have been shared on social media and in public appeals, many of the homes offered to them suffer from poor construction. They report leaking roofs during rainfall, flooded yards, and repeated disruptions to gas, water and electricity supplies. In some cases, applicants say they have been told verbally: “You’ve been given a house — be grateful, or you’ll lose that too.”

Similar complaints have also been submitted through official grievance mechanisms, although the issue has yet to generate wider public debate.

Life in Baku after three decades of integration

A large proportion of Azerbaijan’s internally displaced people have spent more than 30 years living in Baku and other major economic centres. Over that time, they have found employment, received an education, gained access to healthcare and established stable social networks. After losing their homes in the early 1990s, they were provided with temporary accommodation by the state, including places in dormitories, unfinished buildings and container settlements, as well as apartments in purpose-built residential complexes.

Under the new rules, however, this housing may be reclaimed once a person loses IDP status. As a result, many people face a difficult choice: accept an apartment in Karabakh and leave behind the life they have built in Baku, or lose both their IDP status and the accommodation provided to them by the state.

International human rights standards, including the UN Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement, require that return be voluntary, safe and carried out in dignity. These principles are based on freedom of choice, the provision of adequate housing and, wherever possible, the restoration of rights to former property. Under Azerbaijan’s new legislation, however, the state is considered to have fulfilled its obligations once it offers housing, while refusing that offer results in the loss of IDP status. This weakens the principle that return should be voluntary.

Official position and expert assessments

Pro-government media outlets, including Milli.az, Report.az and APA, have presented the amendments in a positive light, using phrases such as “restoring property rights”, “sustainable social support” and “providing a legal framework for the Great Return programme”.

MP Vugar Bayramov has also argued that the three-year transition period demonstrates the state’s continued commitment to social support. Official statements emphasise that the new housing is transferred into private ownership rather than provided on a rental basis, which the authorities say will encourage people to settle permanently in the region.

At the same time, independent observers and some human rights advocates argue that the changes restrict freedom of choice, fail to fully restore land rights and raise other concerns. They also point to the contrast between the urban lifestyles that many IDPs have built over the past three decades and the newly established rural settlements, as well as the risks of unemployment and inadequate infrastructure.

The status of internally displaced persons in Azerbaijan

World.title: EU’s 21st sanctions package targets Kulevi oil terminal and cryptocurrency platforms in Georgia
World.content:
Georgia in the EU’s 21st sanctions package

The European Union’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia includes an oil refinery in the Georgian town of Kulevi and several cryptocurrency platforms.

The sanctions against the Kulevi refinery, which processes and sells Russian oil, include a six-month grace period. The ban on transactions will take effect after six months unless the refinery changes its business practices.

The Kulevi refinery had previously been considered for inclusion in the EU’s 20th package of sanctions against Russia, but was ultimately removed from the sanctions list.

At the time, the EU said that “the Georgian authorities and the port operator had made positive commitments.” This was stated in a letter from the EU’s Special Envoy, David O’Sullivan, to Georgian Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili.

What does the new sanctions package include?

The EU’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia, which is expected to take effect shortly, was formally approved by the permanent representatives of the EU member states on 23 July 2026.

The sanctions are expected to enter into force on 23 July following approval by EU leaders and their publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.

The measures target sectors of the Russian economy that generate significant revenue for Moscow’s war in Ukraine, including energy, financial services and the cryptocurrency sector.

The package also imposes sanctions on more than 50 companies and organisations involved in supplying military goods and weapons to Russia.

It includes the EU’s largest-ever round of individual sanctions, targeting a total of 218 entities — 48 individuals and 170 legal entities.

It is one of the most significant expansions of the EU’s sanctions regime in the past four years.

Sanctions against the Kulevi refinery

“The package introduces the possibility of banning transactions with oil refineries listed in Russia and third countries that process Russian crude oil and petroleum products. Under these measures, the EU is imposing a ban on transactions with the Georgian oil refinery in Kulevi, which processes and trades Russian oil. The ban will take effect in six months,” the EU said in a statement.

According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, citing a source familiar with the matter, the introduction of a six-month deadline is unprecedented in EU sanctions policy.

The same source said the decision reflected Tbilisi’s willingness to meet the EU’s requirements, which became apparent during discussions over sanctions related to the port.

This means that if the Kulevi refinery continues processing Russian oil over the next six months, it will become subject to EU sanctions. The refinery’s owner, Black Sea Petroleum, announced on 1 July 2026 that it would begin full-scale processing of non-Russian crude from August or September.

According to Georgia’s National Statistics Office, domestic exports rose sharply in January 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, driven largely by exports of petroleum products.

Petroleum and petroleum products ranked as Georgia’s second-largest export category in January 2026, with exports worth $58.7 million, accounting for 12.2% of the country’s total exports.

Cryptocurrency platforms added to the sanctions list

The EU has imposed transaction bans on 14 cryptocurrency platforms based in Georgia, Panama, the United Arab Emirates, Kyrgyzstan, Belarus and the Marshall Islands.

For the first time, the EU has introduced a mechanism allowing it to impose a complete ban on transactions between EU companies and cryptocurrency platforms that help Russia circumvent sanctions.

The measure also applies to crypto service providers operating in third countries if they facilitate activities that serve Russian interests.

What does the inclusion of Georgian companies in the sanctions package mean for Georgia?

The inclusion of the Kulevi refinery in the EU’s 21st sanctions package has already sparked debate in Georgia.

“The EU’s 21st sanctions package is a national disgrace: Georgian assets are being used as cannon fodder for Russia’s war machine. By allowing the Kremlin to circumvent sanctions, those in power are betraying our sovereignty. Georgia’s place is in Europe — we will never become a loophole for Russian aggression,” Georgia’s fifth president, Salome Zourabichvili, wrote on X.

Analyst Lela Djedjelava said sanctions against such an important economic asset would have an impact on the Georgian economy.

“The consequences will become increasingly visible over time. The reality is that the Kulevi refinery is probably not the only facility that could be exposed for cooperating with Russia. If other businesses in Georgia are also hit by sanctions, it will naturally have a very negative impact on the country.”

Gedevan Popkhadze, one of the leaders of the opposition Coalition for Change, said the EU sanctions against the Kulevi refinery were the result of the Georgian government’s inaction.

“If you are not helping Ukraine, why are you helping Russia? If you do not want war, why are you acting in favour of one of the parties to the conflict? We must clearly understand that these sanctions are not a message to the Kulevi refinery itself — they are a message to Georgia’s de facto government. It should realise that claiming to be neutral is hypocrisy.”

Georgia in the EU’s 21st sanctions package

World.title: Opinion: ‘There is no longer peace in Georgia’
World.content:
Opinion on the latest events in Georgia

Professor at Ilia State University and literary critic Zaal Andronikashvili comments on the events that unfolded in Georgia on 22 July 2026, including the arrest of a journalist, a shooting in central Tbilisi, and an attack on an opposition stand-up comedian.

He writes that there is no longer peace in Georgia and blames Bidzina Ivanishvili and his Georgian Dream party.

Journalist Vakho Sanaia was sentenced to 14 days of administrative detention over satirical social media posts about members of the Georgian Dream party. A shooting took place in central Tbilisi on 22 July, leaving four people injured, including two minors. One of the minors later died in hospital. Comedian Onise Okriashvili, a critic of the government, was brutally beaten at his home. Before the attack, he had been the target of a disinformation campaign on pro-government television channels.

Zaal Andronikashvili: “It is important to find the right name for what is happening in Georgia. The situation is new, and historical parallels apply only in part.

Since at least 2019, during the ‘Gavrilov Night’ protests, Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party have done everything possible to prevent a peaceful transfer of power. Some scholars describe this as a ‘coup from above’.”

This “coup from above” is not peaceful.

Anyone who believes that Georgia is at peace today is deeply mistaken. Beyond dragging Georgia into a geopolitical confrontation on Russia’s side — at an enormous cost to the country — Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party are waging an asymmetric, hybrid civil war against the overwhelming majority of the Georgian population.

Part of this hybrid civil war consists of unlawful restrictive legislation enforced only against certain groups of citizens and against civil society as a whole.

There is also financial repression aimed at depriving opponents of the regime of their livelihoods, as well as the deliberate destruction of education and culture. Alongside this come aggression, hopelessness, and an absence of love and empathy elevated to the level of state policy.

There is micro-level violence — encouraging crime and fostering a culture of impunity that ultimately erodes trust in the law, the justice system, and the very idea of justice. There is macro-level violence carried out by the police and special forces, along with many other elements.

“I repeat: this is not peace.

It is a hybrid civil war waged by a regime that controls the police, the legislature and the country’s financial resources against the majority of Georgia’s population, especially its most active citizens. Its goal is to suppress, subjugate and ultimately enslave them.

The other side has nothing but the truth and peaceful resistance. But the truth is a powerful, almost invincible weapon — and it can never truly be defeated.

Despite this asymmetric civil war, whose domestic objective is to cement the regime permanently in power and make the current government irreplaceable, while its foreign policy goal is to sever Georgia once and for all from the European values-based community and turn it into a banana republic under a quasi-colonial regime, Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party have failed to win this unequal conflict.

Peaceful resistance is alive. The people have not been broken. They have not been intimidated.

Those who support the regime today, or choose silent complicity, should look at Russia.

People there also believed that if they kept quiet and buried their heads in a bowl of caviar, none of it would affect them. Other people’s children would die, someone else would go to prison, someone else’s life would be ruined. Perhaps someone would stop greeting them, but they could live with that.

In reality, supporting injustice always comes at a price. Injustice and lawlessness may begin by targeting only selected groups, but they very quickly spread to everyone.

By supporting injustice, you create an environment in which that injustice will inevitably reach you in one form or another.

But people are willing to ignore it until it affects them personally. There is a powerful metaphor in the Gospel of Matthew (26:52): ‘All who draw the sword will die by the sword.’ This is not really about the sword itself, but more broadly about the laws of social reality and their universal nature.

There is no peace in Georgia. Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party are responsible for that.”

Opinion on the latest events in Georgia

World.title: Russia’s state Duma passes law targeting citizens abroad, restricting property rights and passport renewals
World.content:
Russia Passes Law Targeting Citizens Who Left the Country

Russian Embassy in Lisbon, Portugal. Photo: Antonio Pedro Santos / EPA

On July 22, Russia’s State Duma approved, in its second and third readings, a bill introducing what it calls “temporary restrictive measures.” The legislation targets people living outside Russia who are deemed to be evading criminal or administrative penalties.

The restrictions will apply to anyone convicted under any article of Russia’s Criminal Code. They will also affect people facing a range of administrative charges — many of them based on provisions that Russian authorities have increasingly used to prosecute political opponents and dissenters.

The law will take effect once it is officially published.

This article is based on reporting by Novaya Gazeta Europe.

What restrictions would the law introduce?

Authorities would be able to impose the following measures on people entered into the special registry:

freeze bank accounts and other assets;

block access to banking apps and online accounts;

redirect a person’s income into a special ruble-denominated account;

prohibit the sale of real estate and vehicles;

block the registration of property and automobiles;

suspend licenses, permits and accreditations;

bar individuals from registering as sole proprietors or self-employed workers;

restrict driving privileges;

deny access to government and consular services;

prohibit notarial services and transactions carried out through a power of attorney.

Before the vote, State Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin said that Russians living abroad should be thinking about how to appear before a court.

“We are talking about people who are harming our country — extremists, traitors to our homeland. People who have spent years trying to do everything possible to destroy our state,” Volodin said.

How the registry will work

The government will create a state registry of people who are outside Russia and deemed to be evading criminal or administrative penalties. The registry will be maintained by the Justice Ministry, which already administers the country’s lists of “foreign agents” and “extremists.”

Information will be supplied to the Justice Ministry by the Interior Ministry, the Federal Security Service (FSB), the Prosecutor General’s Office, the Federal Bailiff Service and other government agencies.

To be entered into the registry, a person must meet three criteria:

have a criminal conviction or administrative penalty that has entered into legal force;

be officially deemed to be “evading” enforcement of that sentence or penalty;

be outside Russia.

The law, however, does not specify how authorities will determine whether someone is “evading” enforcement.

An interagency commission will be established to coordinate information sharing between the Justice Ministry and law enforcement bodies. It will also decide whether to impose the restrictions.

Lawyer Yevgeny Smirnov said he expects the registry to expand regularly, much like Russia’s list of “foreign agents.”

“I believe the mechanism will closely resemble the weekly expansion of the ‘foreign agents’ register. It will become a show of intimidation through the constant addition of new names,” he told Novaya Gazeta Europe.

Who could be affected?

Formally, the law applies to anyone outside Russia who has been convicted of a crime or an administrative offense and is deemed to be evading enforcement of the resulting sentence or penalty. The specific article under which a person was convicted does not matter.

In practice, however, those most at risk are people prosecuted for political reasons. According to lawyer Yevgeny Smirnov, this primarily includes journalists, politicians, human rights defenders and civic activists.

The law also applies to people facing administrative charges under six specific provisions:

failure to comply with Russia’s “foreign agents” law;

violations of regulations governing the activities of a “foreign agent”;

calls to violate Russia’s territorial integrity;

“discrediting” the Russian Armed Forces;

calls for sanctions against Russia;

participation in the activities of an “undesirable organization.”

Lawyer Anastasia Burakova said the legislation is primarily intended to intimidate Russians living abroad. Since the state cannot physically detain them, she argued, it is instead restricting their civil and property rights.

In her view, the authorities also aim to silence opponents of the war and spread fear among Russians who have left the country.

What happens to a person’s money and property?

The law allows authorities to freeze a person’s funds and other assets. Formally, this does not amount to confiscation, since ownership does not transfer to the state. In practice, however, it would make it much more difficult for people to manage or dispose of their property.

All payments, including pensions, would be redirected to a special ruble-denominated account. The rules governing access to and use of those funds will be determined later by the Central Bank of Russia. Court costs and other financial penalties could also be deducted directly from the same account.

People included in the registry would be barred from selling real estate or vehicles. They would also be unable to register ownership of newly acquired property or register a vehicle.

In addition, banks would block their access to mobile banking apps and online accounts, making routine bank transfers impossible. Banks would also be allowed to deny them loans and other forms of credit.

Lawyer Valeria Vetoshkina described the measures as a tool of financial pressure.

“It creates a paradoxical situation. A person is deprived of access to the very financial tools needed to fulfill the obligations that led to their inclusion in the registry,” she said.

Restrictions on business and employment

People included in the registry would be barred from registering as sole proprietors or self-employed workers.

If their profession requires a license, authorities would refuse to issue a new one. Existing licenses could also be suspended until the individual is removed from the registry.

The government would also be able to suspend permits and accreditations that have already been granted.

Driver’s licenses would not be revoked outright. However, the right to drive would be suspended until the person is removed from the registry.

Ban on powers of attorney and access to government services

People included in the registry would no longer be able to use an enhanced qualified electronic signature. Existing certificates could be revoked, and new ones would not be issued.

They would also lose access to Russia’s Gosuslugi online government services portal, making it impossible to submit applications, process official documents, or access federal and regional public services online.

Before carrying out any notarial act, Russian notaries would be required to check the registry. If a person’s name appears on the list, the notary would be obligated to refuse service.

The law would also prohibit anyone from carrying out transactions on behalf of a listed individual under a power of attorney. In practice, this would deprive Russians living abroad of one of the main ways to manage their property and handle legal matters in Russia remotely.

Which consular services would be denied?

One of the law’s most significant restrictions concerns Russian consulates abroad. People included in the registry would lose access to nearly all consular services.

They would no longer be able to:

obtain a new international passport;

notarize a power of attorney;

certify copies of documents or authenticate signatures;

obtain notarized consent required for legal transactions;

register a marriage or a legal name change through a consulate;

receive consular assistance if detained abroad;

rely on Russia for emergency consular assistance while overseas.

Lawyer Valeria Vetoshkina said the most consequential provisions are the ban on representation through a power of attorney and the restrictions on consular services. Those are the mechanisms that allow Russians living abroad to handle most legal matters remotely.

At present, even people held administratively liable can still obtain a new international passport through a Russian consulate. Those charged with or convicted of criminal offenses also retain access to some consular services.

Once the law takes effect, however, obtaining official documents without returning to Russia will become significantly more difficult.

Lawyer Yevgeny Smirnov described the initiative as a form of de facto deprivation of citizenship.

“Citizenship technically remains, but a person is no longer able to exercise the rights that come with being a citizen,” he said.

Lawyer Anastasia Burakova agreed with that assessment. In her view, the law would leave affected individuals in a situation approaching statelessness, as the Russian state would effectively cease providing them with documentation and legal assistance.

What is the “humanitarian allowance”?

The law provides for what it calls a humanitarian allowance. The payment may be granted if a person included in the registry has close relatives who are financially dependent on them.

Eligible relatives include parents, a spouse, or children who have no independent source of income. The allowance would be paid monthly using the person’s own frozen funds.

The decision to grant the payment would be made by the interagency commission, while the amount would be set by the Russian government in coordination with the Central Bank.

When would the restrictions take effect?

The restrictions would come into force the day after a person’s name is added to the registry.

In theory, a person could be removed from the registry in several circumstances:

if a court overturns or revises the underlying decision;

if the person begins serving their sentence or complies with the penalty;

if the person returns to Russia;

if the person dies.

If the Justice Ministry fails to remove someone from the registry without justification, that person may file a request for review. The ministry must issue a decision within 20 working days, and its refusal can be challenged in court.

In practice, however, not all penalties can be served remotely. For example, a prison sentence cannot be served from abroad. As a result, anyone convicted and sentenced to imprisonment would have no realistic way to be removed from the registry without returning to Russia.

Administrative penalties present a different paradox. A person on the registry would face restrictions on banking services while also being barred from appointing a representative under a power of attorney. It therefore remains unclear how they would be able to pay an administrative fine and secure their removal from the registry.

What do lawyers recommend for those at risk?

The law will take effect once it is officially published. Lawyers advise people who could potentially be affected to resolve key property and documentation issues before it comes into force.

In particular, they recommend:

settling matters related to real estate and vehicles in Russia in advance;

obtaining notarized copies of Russian documents;

securing apostilles for school certificates, university diplomas, and civil status documents;

renewing international passports while they can still obtain long-validity documents;

withdrawing funds from Russian bank accounts and deposits;

obtaining apostilled certificates confirming the absence of a criminal record and their driving history.

Once a person is added to the registry, many of these steps would no longer be possible.

exchange

World.title: ‘Unsolved crimes are being passed off as suicides’: Armenian soldier’s death sparks questions
World.content:
Death of soldier in the Armenian Armed Forces

A serviceman has died at an Armenian military base. Investigators found the body of 20-year-old conscript Narek Torosyan on July 21. The Investigative Committee released only limited information after the incident. It said authorities had opened a criminal case and launched an investigation.

The committee later charged two of Torosyan’s fellow servicemen with driving him to suicide through negligence. One is a junior sergeant and the other a private. Authorities have placed both men under arrest.

The Ministry of Defence has made no public statement about the soldier’s death. Human rights activists and politicians have condemned the ministry’s silence.

Among them was human rights defender Zhanna Aleksanyan, who regularly raises concerns about human rights violations in the armed forces. She wrote on social media that Defence Minister Suren Papikyan ultimately bears responsibility for the lives of servicemen.

“The minister remains strikingly detached when soldiers die. At the end of each year, he tries to downplay the numbers, but no genuine effort exists to reduce the death toll,” she said.

According to official figures, eight servicemen have died since the beginning of 2026.

What we know so far

Armenian media report that Narek came from the town of Charentsavan and was a fourth-year student at the Russian-Armenian University. He hoped to become a sports journalist. The army drafted him in January 2026. Shortly before the incident, he had gone home on leave and visited his family. Reports also identify Chambarak as his duty station.

Authorities have not disclosed where the incident took place or what exactly happened.

According to a version published by several local media outlets, other servicemen severely beat the soldier before he took his own life.

Charentsavan Mayor Hakob Shahgeldyan also told reporters that, according to the information available to him, Narek had died by suicide. However, the mayor provided no further details.

Comments

Human rights activist Zhanna Aleksanyan wrote:

“The Ministry of Defence remains silent about the death of 20-year-old serviceman Narek Torosyan.

The minister has still offered no explanation or clarification. Did he visit the military unit to find out what happened and why? I am certain he did not. He bears responsibility for the life of every serviceman, and he is accountable to both their families and society.

I cannot accept the ‘suicide’ version circulating in the media. Journalists may learn that a serviceman has died, but they cannot know the circumstances of his death. Law enforcement agencies often leak such versions to the press. They later use those same reports to support their own conclusion that it was ‘suicide.’

And in the army, most ‘suicides’ are in fact unsolved murders.”

Tigran Abrahamyan, an opposition MP from the I Have Honour alliance, wrote on social media:

“Soldier Narek Torosyan, who died following the incident at the Chambarak military base, was my student. […]

Narek was a kind, gentle person with outstanding personal qualities. Both students and lecturers respected and cared for him.

Given the sensitivity of the case, I do not want to comment on the different versions or discuss the information available to me.

One thing is clear, however. The state has failed to ensure proper discipline, maintain a healthy psychological environment in military units, and provide effective oversight. That failure ultimately leads to incidents like this.

The authorities must carry out an objective and comprehensive investigation and take steps to prevent similar tragedies in the future.”

Mané Tandilyan, founder of the Country to Live party, said:

“Do not say that incidents like this are inevitable in the army. We must not accept such an attitude. After so many losses, it is unacceptable that we continue to lose our young people in peacetime.

How do officers demonstrate accountability? How has violence and cruelty become so deeply rooted among 18- to 20-year-olds that it repeatedly leads to deaths? What is the army doing to foster mutual respect, discipline and responsibility?

What is especially alarming is that intolerance and aggression are becoming increasingly visible in society. And yes, much of the responsibility lies with the country’s top leadership, which speaks to society in a language that fuels division, hostility and hatred. That atmosphere eventually seeps into people’s everyday relationships.

We must overcome this nightmare. Let us each begin with the people around us.”

Death of soldier in the Armenian Armed Forces

World.title: Farmers kept planting as the war raged and now they are paying for it
World.content:
Vegetable growers in north Queensland were anxious to plant their winter crops when the price of diesel jumped above $3 a litre in March.

The harvest is now underway and, although fuel prices have eased, farmers are not making the return on what they spent earlier in the year.

Bowen vegetable farmer David Richardson said the prices he received for his eggplant this year had been poor.

"We've been [harvesting] now for 11 weeks and the first 10 were pretty brutal," he said.

Mr Richardson said growers were feeling the repercussions of the rising costs that had flowed in the wake of the war in Iran and the closing of the Strait of Hormuz.

"It's something you don't really expect … all of a sudden all your inputs have doubled and that takes a real hit," he said.

David Richardson says prices have been "brutal". (ABC News: Brooke Tindall)

The planting period in autumn was an uncertain time for growers who were trying to source what they needed to get their seedlings in the ground.

"Even for plastic and trickle tape, the wait times were dragged right out, so you had to make sure you had ordered stuff nearly three months in advance," Mr Richardson said.

Eggplant farmers have been receiving lower prices for their produce, despite quality being high. (ABC News: Brooke Tindall)

In a year with good consumer demand, he would receive $16-$20 for a carton of eggplant.

This year, he's been making just $8-$10 per carton.

Consumers feeling the pinch

Jenn Honnery is the CEO of North Queensland Farmers, a collective of growers from Bowen through to Townsville.

She said growers of various produce were in the same boat as Mr Richardson.

David Richardson grows sweet peppers in Bowen. (ABC News: Brooke Tindall)

"A ballpark figure is around a 30 per cent increase in costs, but that's variable depending on your business," Ms Honnery said.

"It's the perfect storm. Prices have gone up to plant, pick, pack and send.

"And then, when they get to market and they're not getting the prices that they need to cover their costs, it just doesn't make the business feasible."

She said while prices for other grocery items had increased, the same could not be said for fruit and vegetables.

Jenn Honnery says farmers are struggling to recoup the costs of production. (Supplied: North Queensland Farmers)

"Fresh produce has a shelf life, and it's got to be sold within a short amount of time, and if people aren't buying it, then it's got to be discounted to move it," Ms Honnery said.

Although fuel prices had lowered, she said consumers were still buying less.

"Prices for everything have gone up dramatically," she said.

"We all see it when we go shopping, we see it at the fuel bowser and interest rates have gone up.

"So, they're buying a little bit less and we're seeing the impact of that back here in our region."

Produce 'looking really good', great value

Despite prices being low, the quality of the region's produce has been anything but.

"It's been a great season so far, good growing conditions, and you'll see that on the supermarket shelf, the produce is looking really good," Ms Honnery said.

Farmers say the quality of their produce is high but so are the costs. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

AUSVEG, the peak industry body representing Australian vegetable growers, conducted a survey on input costs in May.

Spokesperson Andrew MacDonald said the results showed costs had increased by an average of 28 per cent and, for some growers, as high as 79 per cent since the start of the Iran war.

"That has made turning profits to stay viable increasingly challenging," he said, adding that Australians eating fewer vegetables to save money was concerning for the industry.

"We've seen some ABS data that came out earlier this month showing less than 5 per cent of Australians are meeting the recommended five serves a day.

"Despite the major increases we've seen in production costs, vegetables have remained great value."

Mr Richardson said consumers could play their part by buying more fresh, local produce.

"Just try and buy fresh fruit and vegetables that are Australian grown," he said.

"That would really help a farmer out."

World.title: The UK is banning high-caffeine drinks for under-16s. How does coffee compare?
World.content:
The British government wants to ban the sale of high-caffeine energy drinks to people under the age of 16.

The ban would cover drinks, other than tea or coffee, containing more than 150 milligrams of caffeine per litre.

Supporters of the ban say these kinds of drinks have been linked to sleep disruption, anxiety and poor concentration in children and teenagers.

But how do they compare to coffee, tea and other beverages many people regularly consume?

And what's the situation here in Australia?

How much caffeine is in an energy drink?

It can vary depending on the brand and the size of the can or bottle.

However, the Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code says formulated caffeinated beverages, otherwise known as energy drinks, can't contain more than 320 milligrams of caffeine per litre.

That works out to be 80 milligrams for a 250 millilitre can or 160 milligrams in a 500 millilitre can.

How much caffeine is in coffee?

It depends on the type of coffee you're drinking and how long it has been brewed for.

"As a rule of thumb, longer brewing times increase the caffeine concentration," the European Food Information Council's (EUFIC) website says.

The council compiled a list of the caffeine concentrations in food and beverages based on a paper published in the European Food Safety Authority Journal in 2015.

It's important to note how average milligrams of caffeine in a product varies from the amount of caffeine per serving — for example, the 53 milligrams of caffeine in dark chocolate might seem alarming until it's compared to the 7 milligrams in a typical serving size.

Item Average milligrams of caffeine per 100ml or 100mg Milligrams of caffeine per average serving size Espresso coffee 134 80 (60ml) Dark chocolate 53 7 (two squares) Filtered coffee 45 90 (200 ml) Instant coffee 45 90 (200ml) Black tea 22 55 (250ml) Milk chocolate 17 2 (two squares) Chocolate milk (based on cocoa powder) 17 34 (200ml) Green tea 15 38 (250ml) Cola 11 37 (355ml) Decaffeinated tea 3 8 (250ml) Decaffeinated coffee 2 4 (250ml)

Source: European Food Safety Authority

Why is caffeine bad for children?

Caffeine is a central nervous system stimulant.

"Stimulants directly affect the brain," Gina Trapp, a professor of food and nutrition environment at Edith Cowan University, said.

"Energy drinks are inappropriate for children because of their lower physical tolerance for stimulants.

"In other words, the same amount of caffeine is likely to have a more marked effect on a child and teenager than an adult."

Professor Trapp has a lot of experience researching energy drinks and young people, having co-authored several papers on the topic.

She also said the high caffeine content in energy drinks made them addictive.

"Children have a smaller body mass, meaning they can experience higher concentrations of caffeine per kilogram of body weight," Jane Martin, the executive director of the Food for Health Alliance, said.

The Food for Health Alliance is an advocacy body that works to improve diets and prevent obesity in Australia and is partnered with Cancer Council Victoria, Deakin University, VicHealth and Western Australia's Healthway.

"The high caffeine content and other stimulants in energy drinks can impact both physical and mental health," Ms Martin said.

"Energy drinks affect the nervous system and are associated with adverse effects including heart palpitations, sleep disruption, anxiety, restlessness and irritability.

"Sleep is particularly important during adolescence because young people require more sleep than adults to support growth, learning and mental wellbeing."

Espresso coffees have a higher caffeine concentration to filtered or instant coffees. (ABC News: Sam Ikin)

Does Australia have a youth energy drink ban?

No.

There are no federal laws restricting the sale of high-caffeine drinks to children in Australia.

The extent of limitations on energy drinks for children are warning labels on packaging and advice for tuckshops.

"Australia already has measures in place aimed at protecting children from high-caffeine products," a spokesperson from the federal health department said.

"Energy drinks sold in Australia must carry a mandatory advisory statement that they are not recommended for children, pregnant or lactating women, or individuals sensitive to caffeine.

"Recent changes to the Food Standards Code have strengthened controls on caffeine in foods and beverages, including restrictions on the retail sale of pure caffeine as a food and additional controls on other high-caffeine products.

"The National Healthy School Canteens Guidelines advise against the sale of energy drinks in school canteens."

The Australian Dietary Guidelines, published by the federal health department in 2013, say energy drinks are "not suitable for children".

Does that go far enough?

Ms Martin said Australia already recognised that energy drinks were "not appropriate" for children.

"Restricting the sales of these products to young people and children will offer much better protection than the current scenario of providing advice on the packaging and relying on young people to voluntarily avoid these drinks," she said.

"There is growing evidence supporting restricting sales of energy drinks to children and adolescents.

"But introducing an age-based sales ban in Australia would likely require separate Commonwealth or state and territory legislation."

And energy drink manufacturers might complicate matters.

Last year, a Coca-Cola Europacific Partners media release said Australia's energy drink sector was "booming".

"The energy drinks category is growing in volume by 19.6 per cent year-on-year, with this strong trajectory expected to continue over the medium term," the company said.

"The pressure of industry opposition … around actions that will curtail sales and profits from this category may act as a barrier for governments to implement a ban," Ms Martin said.

The ABC has contacted Coca-Cola and Monster Energy for comment.

Loading...

Australian Beverages Council chief executive officer Geoff Parker opposed the idea of a ban.

The council includes Monster Energy, Coca-Cola Australia and PepsiCo Australia and New Zealand as members.

Its website says its members voluntarily have agreed not to direct advertising for energy drinks towards children or sell energy drinks at schools.

However, Professor Trapp argued energy drinks were "aggressively" marketed towards young people.

Mr Parker said restricting the sale of energy drinks for under-16-year-olds would be a "quick headline".

"[It] does not reflect the long-standing evidence and effective local regulatory arrangements designed to inform Australians," Mr Parker said.

"Implementing a ban similar to that proposed in England would not only be disproportionate to the Australian evidence base, it would also present significant practical enforcement challenges across the diverse retail environments in which these products are sold, without clear evidence that it would improve public health outcomes."

Mr Parker said he supported Australia's existing food regulatory system's "strict controls on the manufacturing of beverages including energy drinks".

He pointed to a recent review by Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ) looking into caffeine, which last year approved changes including new labelling restrictions for high-caffeine coffee beverages but did not recommend restrictions on the sale of energy drinks.

The FSANZ report said the most recent safety assessment "did not identify any evidence that the permitted caffeine content of formulated caffeinated beverages [better known as energy drinks] or cola beverages should be changed".

"FSANZ has not identified a risk that would justify amending the provisions for formulated caffeinated beverages."

ABC with Reuters

World.title: Tens of thousands flee fires in France, blazes merge outside Madrid
World.content:
Tens of thousands of people have fled wildfires in southwest France by car and boat and Spain declared a national emergency as huge blazes merged outside Madrid and searing heat left tinder-dry conditions across Europe.

French authorities ordered the total evacuation of the Cap Ferret peninsula, a tourism hotspot on the Atlantic Coast. Two fires merged outside Madrid, and a third was on the verge of joining them, government officials said.

"I had to run from my house. There was a ball of fire. If I'd taken five more minutes, it would have wiped us out," evacuee Enrique Martin said in a shelter in Cebreros, west of Madrid.

Fires burn across the Cap Ferret Peninsula in the south of France. (Reuters :Stephane Mahe)

Both France and Spain sought help from the European Union as the blazes strained firefighting and other emergency services. The national emergency - the first ever issued over a wildfire in Spain - opened up federal funding to tackle the crisis.

"This is the worst wildfire in our region's history," Madrid's regional leader Isabel Diaz Ayuso said after telling reporters the fires had merged.

" It's the perfect storm of very high temperatures and ceaseless winds that aren't letting up. "

In southwest France, authorities sent boats to help the evacuation and a total of about 63,000 people, many of them tourists, were told to get out as two major, separate fires threatened homes and campsites, officials said.

"From our home, we had a view of the fires ... We could see the clouds becoming darker and darker," said Yoan Urien, who left late on Thursday after police told everyone in his neighbourhood in the town of Biscarrosse to leave.

"I was able to find somewhere to take shelter with my pets, but ... it's quite a shock," the 26-year-old said.

France's emergency response resources have been exhausted during the summer heatwave. (AP Photo: Caroline Blumberg)

The other major fire, which began in nearby Saumos, north of Cap Ferret, is threatening to cut off the only road out of the peninsula and is the largest so far this season in France, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told local television.

It has torn through more than 10,000 hectares (24,700 acres) of forest and burned 80 homes, completely destroying about 50 of them, he said.

"It breaks my heart. Because it's such a pleasant place to live, seeing it go up in smoke is truly sad," said family caregiver Corinne Paillaube.

"It's totally apocalyptic," said Ambre Dubos, from the nearby Landes region.

Devastating fire season

In Spain, more than 19,000 people were ordered to evacuate from towns in the mountains west of Madrid, as more than 2,000 personnel and 10 aircraft struggled in vain to prevent the fires converging, Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said.

A short time later another 7,000 people were told to leave from two new localities west of Madrid that were under threat by wildfires.

A third fire in Avila province was on the verge or may have already merged with the two in Madrid, Nicanor Sen, the government representative for the Castile and Leon region, told reporters.

"It is very bad news," Nicanor Sen Velez said.

Fires near Madrid are feared to be the worst in the country's history. (AP Photo: Manu Fernandez)

The area west of Madrid, where many residents from the capital have second homes, is densely populated. In just one development 43 homes had been destroyed, Diaz Ayuso said.

That played a role in the government decision to declare a national emergency, Grande-Marlaska said.

It is the second consecutive year that Spain has faced a particularly destructive fire season.

More than 29 major fires have broken out in Spain so far this year, damaging a surface area five times greater than at the same stage in 2025, when a record area was destroyed, Environment Minister Sara Aagesen said in a social media post.

Spanish police said a man had been arrested and another person was under investigation for allegedly setting off a vast fire in the Madrid region by using a farm vehicle despite a ban in the tinderbox conditions.

Heat hits crops, nuclear plant cooling

Wildfires have burnt more land in Europe already this year than the annual average in the past two decades, data shows as the world's fastest-warming continent has endured three stifling, virtually back-to-back heatwaves so far this year.

Scientists say human-driven climate change is increasing the intensity of heatwaves, droughts and wildfires, while also creating conditions for sudden, destructive storms.

Greece was sending two CL-415 firefighting aircraft to Madrid and will operate across the area of Toledo, the Greek civil protection ministry said.

More than 30,000 people have been evacuated from parts of France due to ongoing fires. (Reuters: Stephane Mahe)

Croatia said it sent on Friday a Canadair CL-415 firefighting aircraft with two crews and 11 Croatian army technical staff to help France battle fires.

After a short reprieve over the weekend, average temperatures in France are expected to rise sharply again next week, according to official weather forecaster Meteo France. The high temperatures are expected to warm French rivers that are used to cool nuclear reactors and could lead to further restrictions, as the reactors reduce output to comply with environmental protection measures.The Golfech 2 nuclear reactor in southern France has remained offline since July 7 due to heat-related restrictions, operator EDF's data showed.

Weeks of hot weather are also taking a toll on the condition of the maize crop in France.

World.title: US and Iran trade strikes after Trump vows 'major military punishment'
World.content:
US missiles have struck targets across Iran, reaching as far as the Caspian coast, as Iran hits US bases across the region and warns of more strikes.

It comes after President Donald Trump vowed "major military punishment" for Tehran and its Houthi allies in Yemen over moves to block a second major international shipping route.

Two weeks after the collapse of an interim truce meant to end the war, Iranian armed forces have responded by firing at US bases in neighbouring countries and warning people there that they may strike non-military buildings used by US personnel.

The Iranian army said Mr Trump's threats only strengthened its resolve, claiming to have attacked US military equipment depots at Al-Adiri, latterly named Camp Buehring, in northern Kuwait, and the positions of US troops at Camp Arifjan and at Camp Doha, near Kuwait City.

Iran warns people to 'move away' from areas used by the US military

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they had also significantly damaged a surveillance tower used by the US in Bahrain.

While Jordan's military said it had intercepted seven missiles and six drones launched by Iran on Friday.

The military said the interceptions, performed by air defence systems and air force planes, "resulted in no casualties or material damage".

The US Central Command says it has carried out strikes on Iranian military targets. (US Central Command)

In exchange, US missiles struck a Revolutionary Guards Navy headquarters in the Ziba Kenar area of the Caspian Sea province of Gilan while also hitting Piranshahr, in West Azerbaijan Province, near Iran's border with Iraq, according to state media.

Four people were killed and five injured in a US missile attack on the Iranian city of Ahvaz, state broadcaster IRIB said.

In a statement read out by Iran's state media, the Revolutionary Guards warned the public in the Gulf countries of potential strikes against US military personnel who may be using "buildings in cities as locations to direct their crimes".

It told people to "immediately move away from areas within a 500 metre radius of covert and hidden locations used by US military personnel".

Red Sea blockade pushes up oil prices

A Yemeni government army officer in Bab el-Mandeb, Yemen, earlier in the war. (Reuters)

The fighting comes after the Houthis, who control northern and western Yemen, said this week they were imposing a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, which has diverted millions of barrels of oil each day by pipeline to the Red Sea to skirt Iran's near-total blockade in the Strait of Hormuz.

The blockade has stoked global inflation and fanned fears of an economic downturn.

Houthis declare maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia In a statement, the Houthis' military spokesperson Yahya Saree says the group will enforce the blockade against its "criminal Saudi enemy", effective immediately.

Houthi fighters struck two Saudi tankers on Thursday in the Red Sea's Bab el-Mandeb strait, pushing oil prices 7 per cent higher to pierce the $100 ($143) per barrel level for the first time since May but fell back under $100 on Friday.

Mr Trump wrote on social media he would hold Iran accountable for any further attacks by the fighters "and major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis, themselves".

He also said that any damage to cargo ships would be paid for with Iranian money, referring to frozen Iranian assets held by the United States, but without specifying how.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi responded with a warning on X, saying no one's assets were safe once governments normalised such confiscation.

"Ensuing chaos will not be pretty or peaceful," he wrote.

Reuters

World.title: Singer Chris Brown pleads guilty to affray over London nightclub incident
World.content:
US singer Chris Brown has pleaded guilty to a charge of affray over what prosecutors described as a bottle attack on a producer in a London nightclub three years ago, with more serious assault charges dropped.

Brown, 37, and his vocal coach Omololu Akinlolu, 40, stood in the dock at London's Southwark Crown Court and spoke only to confirm their names and their guilty pleas over the incident at London's Tape nightclub in February 2023.

The pair had been charged with attempting to inflict grievous bodily harm and a less serious charge of assault causing actual bodily harm to Abraham Diaw, which the pair had denied and were due to go to trial in October.

Co-defendant rapper Omololu Akinlolu, who performs under the name Hoody Baby also pleaded guilty to affray. (Reuters: Jaimi Joy)

Brown and Akinlolu pleaded guilty to the charge of affray, admitting they "used or threatened unlawful violence towards another and their conduct taken together was such as would cause a person of reasonable firmness ... to fear for their personal safety".

Prosecutor Heidi Stonecliffe said the other charges would not proceed to trial and Brown and Akinlolu were granted bail ahead of their sentencing at the same court on October 26.

The maximum sentence for affray is three years' imprisonment and Judge Tony Baumgartner said that "all options" would be open to the court.

Claire Campbell from the Crown Prosecution Service said in a statement: "This was a vicious and unprovoked attack by Brown and Akinlolu in a crowded nightclub where Brown used a glass bottle as a weapon to strike the victim's head twice.

"This kind of violence is entirely unacceptable, and the Crown Prosecution Service will work tirelessly – with the police and partners across the criminal justice system – to pursue cases like this, and prove that no one is above the law."

Prosecutors had alleged Brown launched an "unprovoked attack" on Diaw with a tequila bottle, with Akinlolu and Brown said to have continued to attack Diaw as he tried to flee.

He was arrested in May 2025 having returned to Britain for the first time since the incident and initially denied bail, throwing his worldwide "Breezy Bowl XX" tour into doubt.

But Brown was eventually released after promising to pay a £5 million ($6.66 million) security fee, allowing the tour to go ahead.

The singer left court to cheers from fans chanting "Breezy! Breezy!" before signing autographs and then getting into a waiting car.

World.title: Russian missile strike kills 10 at Ukraine defence industry event
World.content:
A Russian ballistic missile strike has killed 10 people and injured almost 100 others at a defence industry event in Ukraine's Kyiv region, Ukrainian officials say.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that efforts to determine what happened were underway but did not identify the exact target.

"A rescue operation is currently underway in the Kyiv region following a Russian missile strike," he said on Telegram.

The Ukrainian Council of Defence Industry said the missile strike hit a site where representatives were present. (Reuters Photo: State Emergency Service of Ukraine)

Kyiv region acting governor, Ruslan Oliynyk, said preliminary information indicated the missile strike hit a private training ground where events were taking place.

The Ukrainian Council of Defence Industry said that representatives of Ukraine's defence industry were at the site when it was hit, but that it had not organised the event and participants' exact location had not been made public.

Valerii Borovyk, founder of Ukrainian drone company First Contact, told Ukrainian media that a missile struck a training ground where a defence industry exhibition was being held.

Ukraine's prosecutor-general, Ruslan Kravchenko, said that a criminal investigation had been launched into whether officials improperly carried out their duties in organising and conducting the event.

Kremlin says it will pursue 'total victory'

The strike came as the Kremlin said it believed US President Donald Trump was sincere in efforts to end the Ukraine war but would continue fighting while waiting for Washington to present new peace proposals.

"Yes, (fighting) is not the preferred path, but given the absence of prospects for peace, we will see it through to the end, to total victory," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russian state television.

"We will wait for new (US) proposals."

Dmitry Peskov says Moscow will pursue its military objectives in Ukraine while waiting for new US peace proposals. (Sputnik: Gavriil Grigorov/Pool via Reuters)

Mr Peskov said Russia had accepted a previous US proposal, but claimed it had been rejected by Ukraine.

"The Americans — President Trump, his negotiators — are sincere in their desire to formulate options acceptable to everyone," he said.

"The Americans could not persuade the Ukrainians … who were being incited by the Europeans."

Zelenskyy just scored an 'own goal' The Ukrainian president's decision to fire his popular, tech-savvy 35-year-old Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov last week baffled many. Analysts say what happens next could be pivotal to the war.

The last three-way peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US took place in February, shortly before the US and Israel went to war with Iran.

The Kremlin has repeatedly said it hopes US-led mediation will resume once the Middle East crisis has eased.

The top US and Russian diplomats met briefly in Asia this week. Russia has been saying for weeks that it is ready to host Mr Trump's envoys for talks in Moscow, but no date has been announced.

Mr Peskov said Washington's position was ambiguous because it was "continuing to pump Ukraine full of weaponry" while talking about wanting to end the war.

"However, we must leverage this duality in the Trump administration's position wherever it aligns with our interests," he said.

"And their desire to facilitate a peaceful settlement is entirely in line with our interests."

ABC/Wires

World.title: Bali bans two Dutch men alleged to have hosted discriminatory run club
World.content:
Bali's Immigration department has banned two Dutch men from Indonesia for organising a run club event 'fraught with discrimination against local residents'.

It comes after online complaints by Indonesians about the 'Entourage Bali' community went viral.

The organisers of the event have been banend from Indonesia and placed on a travel ban list. (Instagram: @entourage.bali)

In a statement, Bali's Director General of Immigration, Hendarsam Marantoko, said he condemned the event, and that immigration would impose an entry ban on the 'two foreign nationals involved'.

"The Bali Silent Disco running event organised by foreign nationals (is) suspected of violating regulations and being fraught with discrimination against local residents."

" This running event represents a state within a state, "

"I have instructed the Bali immigration team to inspect the event organiser, if any foreign nationals are involved, arrest them immediately."

Immigration officials say the two Dutch men, identified as JAS, 35, and HQV, 37, left Bali for Singapore on Wednesday night.

Officials say they've been slapped with an entry ban and placed on the travel ban list.

"Foreigners must not act as though they can establish their own rules and exclusivity within the jurisdiction of Indonesia," the statement reads.

Immigration officials said foreign nationals were not allowed to manage an event in Indonesia, or act as event organisers.

Alleged bias to western names

A social media post of an Entourage Bali event in May shows a large group of people running through the streets of Canggu, wearing headphones and waving their hands in the air.

On social media, one Indonesian woman said that when she messaged 'Entourage Bali' to join the community, she received a message that her application would be reviewed, while her husband's application with a 'western name and number' was accepted immediately.

The organisers said incorrect automated responses had been sent to some hopeful participants. (Threads: @channisaraa)

In a post on social media, Balinese based Indonesian Senator Niluh Djelantik said "our hospitality should never be mistaken for a license to disrespect us."

On Friday she said she had spoken with immigration officials.

"Utilising public spaces while rejecting local residents is unacceptable," she said.

Senator Niluh Djelantik said the apparent rejection of locals was unacceptable. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

Run club responds

In a statement posted on its social media pages, Entourage Bali said "we are extremely sorry for the people that have been offended and hurt, and we have never meant to be disrespectful or discriminating to anyone".

"Entourage was created as a community for digital nomads in Bali to help people who are new to the island connect with others and do fun activities together during their stay … our community includes members from many countries, including Indonesia."

Entourage Bali said that Indonesians made up "the largest group of participants" in the silent disco run, "representing representing nearly 25% of all tickets sold."

"However, we have made errors in the automated approval process for our WhatsApp groups,

" While we were trying to create a place where digital nomads could meet, a bias was created that some (and not all) +62 numbers / Indonesians were incorrectly rejected. "

"We are pausing all our events and activities for now. We take full accountability for what has happened and promise we will make real changes going forward."

The organisers said 25 per cent of ticket holders were indonesian. (Instagram: @entourage.bali)

The ABC has contacted Entourage Bali for comment.

Visa understanding urged

This blacklisting comes as Bali immigration cracks down on foreign nationals working while on a tourist visa.

On the Australian Smartraveller website it urges Australians to "understand your visa conditions".

“It's illegal to work, conduct research or volunteer if you're on a tourist visa. This includes creating or posting online content for payment or commercial purposes."

"Indonesian authorities may consider it a breach of visa conditions if you create content for commercial purposes while you're on a tourist visa, even if the content is published after you've departed Indonesia."

World.title: Commonwealth Games 2026 LIVE: Pallister wins first gold for Australia as teammate takes 400m freestyle bronze
World.content:
Aussie para-powerlifter Hani Watson has started well, easily clearing her starting weight of 140kg.

Her successful lift briefly puts her first on the leaderboard with two more attempts left.

But moments later Folashade Oluwafemiayo lifts an extraordinary 165kg, setting a new record and putting Watson in second place.

There was unfortunate moment earlier in Group B’s session when Ugandan athlete, Rebecca Zawedde appeared to have an issue with her straps on her first attempt and ran out of time to get to the bar, recording a “no lift”.

For those unfamiliar with Para Powerlifting, athletes have two-minutes to complete their lift from the moment they step on stage. Each lifter gets three regular turns to lift the maximum weight possible.

Some powerlifters prefer to get to the bar as quick as possible, while others like Joyce Wambui Njuguna take a moment to take three deep breath and pauses before beginning their lift.

World.title: By milling its own flour, this local bakery doesn’t just make better bread, it builds stronger communities
World.content:
Review Eating outPerth By milling its own flour, this local bakery doesn’t just make better bread, it builds stronger communities Max Veenhuyzen July 25, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

1 / 3 Apricot bear claws are among the seasonal pastries served at Miller + Baker. Miller + Baker 2 / 3 Pastries and sandwiches constantly rotate throughout the year. Miller + Baker 3 / 3 Golden croissants and viennoiserie are a core part of Miller + Baker’s offering. Miller + Baker Previous Slide Next Slide 14 / 20 How we score Miller + Baker Bakery$$$$ Can a bakery be classified as a restaurant? If you define a restaurant as a place where customers can buy something to eat and drink and there’s somewhere for them to sit down and enjoy their purchase, I think so. Which means that Miller + Baker – a Northbridge bakery-cafe with indoor counter seats plus some tables and chairs scattered across the Lake Street footpath – absolutely fits the description.



But what if you decided to open a bakery that became more than somewhere to eat? I’m not sure if that was Rachel and Mark Taylor’s goal when they opened Miller + Baker in the former home of Italian bakery Casa del Dolce back in 2019, but seven years on, the Taylors’ Little-Corner-Bakery-That-Could feels like more than just somewhere to buy bread. Miller + Baker owners Rachel and Mark Taylor. Max Veenhuyzen Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Inspired by the sourdough and organic food culture the couple enjoyed while living in Copenhagen, the Taylors returned to Perth and were keen to recreate their experience. One such lesson was the deliciousness and nutritional value of sourdough bread made from good wheat. Fate led the Taylors to the Heggarty family, founders of Natural Intelligence Farming and owners of a wheat farm in Mollerin in the Wheatbelt.



The Heggartys’ regenerative agriculture approach – a system that, in a pesticide-free nutshell, eschews chemical inputs in favour of natural approaches that improve soil health – resonated with what the Taylors were looking for. With wheat (and occasionally rye) supply locked in, they set about learning the finer points of the stone mill they bought from America and began turning this single-origin grain into freshly milled flour: more nutritious and better tasting than commercially sold commodity flours. But hey, don’t take my word for it - take home one of the bakery’s Millers sourdough loaves and taste if for yourself. A hefty rugby ball of a loaf that contains more wholewheat flour than any other core Miller + Baker product, its dense crumb is the colour of milky tea and reveals bold flashes of, well, wheaten richness with each chew. This is not a bread one buys if they need a neutral, flavourless medium. Miller + Baker works with a range of different wheat strains. Miller + Baker It’s also not a big seller. Or at least, according to the Taylors, compared to the bakery’s regular classic sourdough that, due to its reduced wholewheat flour ratio, boasts a crumb with more spring and puffier pockets of air.



You can take away loaves of classic sourdough too, but if you felt like enjoying it in situ, there’s a glass cabinet filled with ace pre-made sandwiches that are dying to meet you. While the sangers are based on combinations that should be familiar to most – roast beef, ham and cheese, chicken and salad – little details in the kitchen ensure what guests are eating is less lunch bar and more café. The chook for the chicken salad number, for instance, is roasted in-house and moistened with a salad dressing packing a healthy jolt of acidity. The result is a flavour that’s closer to an Eastern European potato salad. Served in gaseous baguettes that are more chewy than crisp, the roast beef roll is made with the good stuff that’s been slowly poached on-site until soft and yielding. Kelly Bucksley at Miller + Baker. Miller + Baker



To finish: a sprightly chimichurri sauce that had more to say than most of the lacklustre versions served around town. The top half of the ham and cheese baguette is dabbed at with hot English mustard while the bottom is primed with thick smears of nutty brown butter. Recent sightings of free agent consultant chef Frankie Dawson treading the boards in the Miller + Baker kitchen can only mean good things for the menu.
