World.title: ‘This is my last decision’: LeBron James to join 76ers for 24th NBA season
World.content:
SportBasketballNBA ‘This is my last decision’: LeBron James to join 76ers for 24th NBA season Frank Pingue July 25, 2026 — 2:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

LeBron James announced his decision on Friday (US time) to join the Philadelphia 76ers for his record-extending 24th NBA season with hopes of helping the franchise snap a 43-year championship drought. The league’s all-time leading scorer spent the last eight seasons of his glittering career with the Los Angeles Lakers, leading them to a title in 2020 after two separate stints with the Cleveland Cavaliers and four years with the Miami Heat. Off to Philadelphia: LeBron James. Getty Images “This is my last decision. I’m not going for money. I’m not going for family. What am I really playing for at this point? I still want to sacrifice. I still want to work. I still want to grind. I still want to compete, to win and to have a chance at the feeling of winning another championship,” James wrote on social media. “I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energise a new fan base and start this incredible journey one last time. Thank you, LA. Miami I’ll forever love and Northeast Ohio will always be home!”



James will join a 76ers team that made the 2026 NBA playoffs by securing the seventh seed through a play-in tournament before falling to the eventual champion New York Knicks in the second round. James did not disclose terms of the deal, but ESPN reported that the four-time champion signed a two-year, $US8 million ($11.5 million) contract with a player option. View post on X A number of teams had been pursuing James, with Cleveland, Miami, the Golden State Warriors and Minnesota Timberwolves all believed to have been interested in the high-profile free agent. The 41-year-old James, who last March surpassed Robert Parish’s record for most career regular-season games played, has continued to perform at an elite level despite his age.



He earned a league-record 22nd consecutive All-Star selection last February during a season in which he averaged 20.9 points, 6.1 rebounds and 7.2 assists over 60 games. His season ended when the Lakers were swept from the second round of the playoffs. Related Article NBA LeBron James is leaving the Lakers. At 41, he plans to play another season “I thought I was done when the season ended. I wasn’t ready to announce it, and I knew I needed some time to really decide, but I was pretty sure I played my last game. I was honest at that last press conference when I said I needed to look at myself and decide if I still love this game. I still truly love this game, and I have more to give,” James said. “The last few weeks have really been special. I’ve never been able to have no clue what to do and take real time to just think. I’ve had an incredible few months with all the people I love trying to figure it all out.” In a testament to his durability, James and his son Bronny became the first father-son duo to play together in a regular-season NBA game in October 2024, fulfilling what he had long said was one of his remaining basketball goals.



James, a four-time NBA Finals Most Valuable Player, joined the Lakers in 2018. He set the league record for the longest career in NBA history last year when he surpassed Vince Carter’s mark of 22 seasons. Loading He was selected with the first pick in the 2003 NBA Draft by his hometown Cavaliers, where he spent seven seasons before announcing during a live TV special titled The Decision that he was leaving for Miami. The announcement damaged James’ public image and led to many people burning his replica No. 23 jerseys on Cleveland’s streets that night. In Miami, James teamed up with Dwyane Wade and Chris Bosh to create an instant powerhouse that won two NBA titles during their four seasons together in South Beach.



Related Article NBA Knicks break their drought and deliver long-awaited sporting glory to New York James returned to Cleveland and in 2016 rallied the team from a 3-1 series deficit in the NBA Finals to stun the Golden State Warriors and make good on his promise to deliver the Cavaliers their first championship. Two years later, James again left his hometown team, where he remains the franchise leader in nearly every major statistical category, to join the Lakers, where for the first time he played in the NBA’s Western Conference. World.title: ‘Of course we can win it’: Defiant Dangerfield backs the Cats to contend again, despite his injury
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Of course we can win it’: Defiant Dangerfield backs the Cats to contend again, despite his injury Sam McClure Updated July 25, 2026 — 12:13am ,first published 10:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Patrick Dangerfield has revealed he will likely need to take a break in the coming weeks to manage a troublesome adductor injury, as Geelong face a delicate balancing act between preserving their captain and maintaining their finals push. The Cats skipper, who battled through obvious discomfort in Friday night’s statement victory over Melbourne after an incident just before half-time, said he would undergo further medical assessment after feeling the problem worsen during the match. Patrick Dangerfield addresses his teammates at the MCG. AFL Photos “I’ll see the doctor Monday and see where it’s at,” Dangerfield told The Age after the Cats’ 18.9 (117) to 14.13 (97) win. The veteran admitted that, ideally, he would be afforded time to rest the injury, but said Geelong’s injury list and precarious ladder position meant that decision would not be straightforward.



“In an ideal scenario there’d probably be time for rest, but we’ve just had injuries at the wrong time. We’ve just got to find a way,” he said. Editor's pick Updated

AFL 2026 Geelong superstar agrees to a deal for 2027, Pendlebury still undecided Dangerfield insisted the issue was different to the significant groin injuries that interrupted previous seasons and believed he could continue to play without causing further damage, despite increasing discomfort. “It’s an injury I’ve actually never done before. It happened changing direction,” he revealed. It cast the only significant shadow over one of Geelong’s most important victories of the season.



The Cats ended Melbourne’s previously undefeated record at the MCG under Steven King and, in the process, delivered another compelling reminder that they remain firmly in the premiership conversation. With just weeks remaining before finals, the Cats appear to be building towards September in familiar fashion. “We can win it – of course we can win it,” Dangerfield said. “It’s about getting your best football going at the most important time of the year and then riding that wave once you’ve built it. “It started a couple of weeks ago. We haven’t executed it every time, but all you can worry about is the next moment and preparing yourself for the next big part.



“There was a lot riding on tonight. It was pretty cool for us to get it right.” That confidence was built on one devastating quarter that completely transformed the contest. Melbourne dominated the opening term and should have established a commanding advantage. The Demons controlled territory, won the contest around the ball and repeatedly generated forward entries, yet their wastefulness in front of goal proved costly. They could easily have been four or five goals in front but failed to convert their dominance into scoreboard pressure. View post on X Geelong punished them.



Chris Scott’s side produced a ferocious second-quarter burst, slamming on seven goals to two with a combination of ruthless efficiency, clean ball movement and relentless pressure that overwhelmed Melbourne. It was football played at premiership level. The Cats sliced through Melbourne’s defence with speed and precision, punished turnovers and suddenly looked every bit the experienced September side that has made a habit of peaking late in seasons. Emerging key forward Shannon Neale was the biggest beneficiary. Shannon Neale was a standout for the Cats against the in-form Demons. AFL Photos



The athletic spearhead proved far too powerful for Melbourne defender Lukas Cooke, who was playing just his second AFL game, kicking five goals — four of them before half-time — in one of the finest performances of his career. Cooke fought gamely but was handed one of the toughest assignments in football and Neale’s combination of strength, reach and finishing proved too much to contain. Geelong also entered the game with a clear tactical plan for Melbourne captain Max Gawn. Tom Stewart had another standout night for Geelong. AFL Photos Rather than allowing the superstar ruckman to drift behind the play and influence contests with his marking, the Cats used Mark Blicavs to shadow Gawn around the ground after stoppages. Blicavs’ athleticism and discipline denied Gawn the freedom he so often enjoys as an intercepting presence and limited one of Melbourne’s greatest weapons.



The Demons refused to surrender. Defender-turned-forward Harrison Petty threatened to drag his side back into the contest with a career-best display in attack, finishing with four goals in a performance that, at times, evoked memories of club great Garry Lyon. Every time Melbourne threatened to mount a charge, Petty provided another contest and another goal. But Geelong always had the answers. View post on X Just as encouraging for the Cats was where those answers came from.



Dangerfield was quick to praise the club’s emerging talent, singling out defender Connor O’Sullivan as one of the brightest young players in the competition. “I think he’s going to be generational,” Dangerfield said. “He’s going to play for another 15 years. He’s an extraordinary athlete. His ability to run is phenomenal, and he reads the game so well. It’s hard to talk about him and not smile because it’s nice to know we’ve got him.” He also highlighted the performances of Mark O’Connor and Ollie Dempsey as further evidence Geelong’s improvement extends well beyond its established stars.



For all the excitement surrounding those emerging players, however, the fitness of Dangerfield looms as Geelong’s biggest watch over the coming days. The 36-year-old has become one of the masters of managing his body through the demands of a long AFL season, but even he conceded the balancing act is becoming increasingly delicate as finals approach. The Cats have often reached this stage of the season with the luxury of managing veterans from a position of ladder security. This year is different. “Finals aren’t guaranteed,” Dangerfield said. “We’re still fighting. We’ve just got to finish as high as we possibly can.”



On the evidence of Friday night’s emphatic victory, the Cats’ charge towards September has gathered genuine momentum. Whether their captain can remain on the park long enough to lead them may prove one of the defining stories of the final month of the home-and-away season. Jye Amiss has kicked five goals and Murphy Reid produced a third-quarter clinic as Fremantle continued their western derby dominance with a 70-point win over West Coast at Optus Stadium.

Murphy Reid had another standout night for the Dockers. AFL Photos

World.title: Grant injured as Rabbitohs all but end Storm’s finals hopes
World.content:
Melbourne captain Harry Grant suffered a hamstring injury in a 28-26 loss to South Sydney that leaves the depleted Storm’s NRL finals aspirations hanging by a thread.

Their hopes of a 16th consecutive finals berth now hinge on five consecutive wins to finish the regular season and even that may not be enough.

Loading

Grant is set to miss at least some of the fight for Melbourne’s season, joining big names Cameron Munster, Xavier Coates, Eli Katoa, Tui Kamikamica and Will Warbrick on the pine.

Harry Grant. Getty Images

The Queensland hooker pulled up sore popping a pass up for Trent Loiero just before half-time in Friday’s clash at Accor Stadium.

He limped to the sidelines and threw his headgear to the ground in frustration.

After a torrid week that claimed David Fifita (suspension), Cam Murray (calf) and Tallis Duncan (hamstring), the Rabbitohs lost their own hooker Brandon Smith (calf) to injury.

But the victory was crucial to South Sydney’s own finals hopes, which had been thrown into jeopardy with two losses from their previous four games.

Souths were staring down the possibility of falling out of the top eight to finish the weekend when Tyran Wishart and Nick Meaney crossed in quick succession during the final 15 minutes.

Right centre Meaney scythed over to give the Storm a two-point lead with 10 minutes to play.

But when fullback Sua Fa’alogo, excellent to that point, fumbled Cody Walker’s 40/20 kick into touch, the home side had the chance to strike back.

Recently re-signed halfback Ashton Ward found Campbell Graham with a beautiful cutout pass on the right side to give Souths a two-point lead that they held.

Rabbitohs winger Campbell Graham scores against Melbourne. NRL Photos

Fa’alogo had been essential as Melbourne, down 8-0 after as many minutes, rallied for a 16-8 half-time lead.

Most memorably, he beat four defenders then turned rival fullback Matt Dufty inside out on an 80-metre tear for the visitor’s third try.

But without Grant patrolling the middle of the park, the Rabbitohs snatched back ascendancy in the second half and began to pick apart the Storm’s edges – a defensive weakness for the Melburnians all year.

Ashley Klein became the most-capped NRL referee, officiating his 444th game.

World.title: Commonwealth Games 2026 LIVE: Pallister wins first gold for Australia as teammate takes 400m freestyle bronze
World.content:
Aussie para-powerlifter Hani Watson has started well, easily clearing her starting weight of 140kg.

Her successful lift briefly puts her first on the leaderboard with two more attempts left.

But moments later Folashade Oluwafemiayo lifts an extraordinary 165kg, setting a new record and putting Watson in second place.

There was unfortunate moment earlier in Group B’s session when Ugandan athlete, Rebecca Zawedde appeared to have an issue with her straps on her first attempt and ran out of time to get to the bar, recording a “no lift”.

For those unfamiliar with Para Powerlifting, athletes have two-minutes to complete their lift from the moment they step on stage. Each lifter gets three regular turns to lift the maximum weight possible.

Some powerlifters prefer to get to the bar as quick as possible, while others like Joyce Wambui Njuguna take a moment to take three deep breath and pauses before beginning their lift.

1 / 3 Apricot bear claws are among the seasonal pastries served at Miller + Baker. Miller + Baker 2 / 3 Pastries and sandwiches constantly rotate throughout the year. Miller + Baker 3 / 3 Golden croissants and viennoiserie are a core part of Miller + Baker’s offering. Miller + Baker Previous Slide Next Slide 14 / 20 How we score Miller + Baker Bakery$$$$ Can a bakery be classified as a restaurant? If you define a restaurant as a place where customers can buy something to eat and drink and there’s somewhere for them to sit down and enjoy their purchase, I think so. Which means that Miller + Baker – a Northbridge bakery-cafe with indoor counter seats plus some tables and chairs scattered across the Lake Street footpath – absolutely fits the description.



But what if you decided to open a bakery that became more than somewhere to eat? I’m not sure if that was Rachel and Mark Taylor’s goal when they opened Miller + Baker in the former home of Italian bakery Casa del Dolce back in 2019, but seven years on, the Taylors’ Little-Corner-Bakery-That-Could feels like more than just somewhere to buy bread. Miller + Baker owners Rachel and Mark Taylor. Max Veenhuyzen Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Inspired by the sourdough and organic food culture the couple enjoyed while living in Copenhagen, the Taylors returned to Perth and were keen to recreate their experience. One such lesson was the deliciousness and nutritional value of sourdough bread made from good wheat. Fate led the Taylors to the Heggarty family, founders of Natural Intelligence Farming and owners of a wheat farm in Mollerin in the Wheatbelt.



The Heggartys’ regenerative agriculture approach – a system that, in a pesticide-free nutshell, eschews chemical inputs in favour of natural approaches that improve soil health – resonated with what the Taylors were looking for. With wheat (and occasionally rye) supply locked in, they set about learning the finer points of the stone mill they bought from America and began turning this single-origin grain into freshly milled flour: more nutritious and better tasting than commercially sold commodity flours. But hey, don’t take my word for it - take home one of the bakery’s Millers sourdough loaves and taste if for yourself. A hefty rugby ball of a loaf that contains more wholewheat flour than any other core Miller + Baker product, its dense crumb is the colour of milky tea and reveals bold flashes of, well, wheaten richness with each chew. This is not a bread one buys if they need a neutral, flavourless medium. Miller + Baker works with a range of different wheat strains. Miller + Baker It’s also not a big seller. Or at least, according to the Taylors, compared to the bakery’s regular classic sourdough that, due to its reduced wholewheat flour ratio, boasts a crumb with more spring and puffier pockets of air.



You can take away loaves of classic sourdough too, but if you felt like enjoying it in situ, there’s a glass cabinet filled with ace pre-made sandwiches that are dying to meet you. While the sangers are based on combinations that should be familiar to most – roast beef, ham and cheese, chicken and salad – little details in the kitchen ensure what guests are eating is less lunch bar and more café. The chook for the chicken salad number, for instance, is roasted in-house and moistened with a salad dressing packing a healthy jolt of acidity. The result is a flavour that’s closer to an Eastern European potato salad. Served in gaseous baguettes that are more chewy than crisp, the roast beef roll is made with the good stuff that’s been slowly poached on-site until soft and yielding. Kelly Bucksley at Miller + Baker. Miller + Baker



To finish: a sprightly chimichurri sauce that had more to say than most of the lacklustre versions served around town. The top half of the ham and cheese baguette is dabbed at with hot English mustard while the bottom is primed with thick smears of nutty brown butter. Recent sightings of free agent consultant chef Frankie Dawson treading the boards in the Miller + Baker kitchen can only mean good things for the menu. You’ll spy other people of interest in the bakery too. Steven Jackson, a Perth cook that owned St Kilda’s Miss Jackson café, has been managing the kitchen for the past two years while baker Emanuele Vittozzi keeps close watch on the ovens. Between them, they ensure that the pork and fennel sausage roll is chunky in the best possible ways; the croissants are a healthy mix of crisp and that cotton-wool softness; and that the two-pastry pies – shortcrust cases, puff pastry lids – have lift-off. Beyond supporting small producers and quietly raising awareness of good farming and food nutrition, Miller + Baker is building communities in other ways too. The Taylors are partners in cheery Parkside Coffee down the road; they’ve opened another outpost on Hobart Street in North Perth; the cheery staff host a run club; plus the space next to the bakery is now The Mill Room Mercantile, a polished homewares store. It’s amazing what you can achieve by rethinking what a bakery can be. I was honest at that last press conference when I said I needed to look at myself and decide if I still love this game. I still truly love this game, and I have more to give,” James said. “The last few weeks have really been special. I’ve never been able to have no clue what to do and take real time to just think. I’ve had an incredible few months with all the people I love trying to figure it all out.” In a testament to his durability, James and his son Bronny became the first father-son duo to play together in a regular-season NBA game in October 2024, fulfilling what he had long said was one of his remaining basketball goals.



James, a four-time NBA Finals Most Valuable Player, joined the Lakers in 2018. He set the league record for the longest career in NBA history last year when he surpassed Vince Carter’s mark of 22 seasons. Loading He was selected with the first pick in the 2003 NBA Draft by his hometown Cavaliers, where he spent seven seasons before announcing during a live TV special titled The Decision that he was leaving for Miami. The announcement damaged James’ public image and led to many people burning his replica No. 23 jerseys on Cleveland’s streets that night. In Miami, James teamed up with Dwyane Wade and Chris Bosh to create an instant powerhouse that won two NBA titles during their four seasons together in South Beach.



Related Article NBA Knicks break their drought and deliver long-awaited sporting glory to New York James returned to Cleveland and in 2016 rallied the team from a 3-1 series deficit in the NBA Finals to stun the Golden State Warriors and make good on his promise to deliver the Cavaliers their first championship. Two years later, James again left his hometown team, where he remains the franchise leader in nearly every major statistical category, to join the Lakers, where for the first time he played in the NBA’s Western Conference. World.title: ‘Of course we can win it’: Defiant Dangerfield backs the Cats to contend again, despite his injury
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Of course we can win it’: Defiant Dangerfield backs the Cats to contend again, despite his injury Sam McClure Updated July 25, 2026 — 12:13am ,first published 10:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Patrick Dangerfield has revealed he will likely need to take a break in the coming weeks to manage a troublesome adductor injury, as Geelong face a delicate balancing act between preserving their captain and maintaining their finals push. The Cats skipper, who battled through obvious discomfort in Friday night’s statement victory over Melbourne after an incident just before half-time, said he would undergo further medical assessment after feeling the problem worsen during the match. Patrick Dangerfield addresses his teammates at the MCG. AFL Photos “I’ll see the doctor Monday and see where it’s at,” Dangerfield told The Age after the Cats’ 18.9 (117) to 14.13 (97) win. The veteran admitted that, ideally, he would be afforded time to rest the injury, but said Geelong’s injury list and precarious ladder position meant that decision would not be straightforward.



“In an ideal scenario there’d probably be time for rest, but we’ve just had injuries at the wrong time. We’ve just got to find a way,” he said. Editor's pick Updated

AFL 2026 Geelong superstar agrees to a deal for 2027, Pendlebury still undecided Dangerfield insisted the issue was different to the significant groin injuries that interrupted previous seasons and believed he could continue to play without causing further damage, despite increasing discomfort. “It’s an injury I’ve actually never done before. It happened changing direction,” he revealed. It cast the only significant shadow over one of Geelong’s most important victories of the season.



The Cats ended Melbourne’s previously undefeated record at the MCG under Steven King and, in the process, delivered another compelling reminder that they remain firmly in the premiership conversation. With just weeks remaining before finals, the Cats appear to be building towards September in familiar fashion. “We can win it – of course we can win it,” Dangerfield said. “It’s about getting your best football going at the most important time of the year and then riding that wave once you’ve built it. “It started a couple of weeks ago. We haven’t executed it every time, but all you can worry about is the next moment and preparing yourself for the next big part.



“There was a lot riding on tonight. It was pretty cool for us to get it right.” That confidence was built on one devastating quarter that completely transformed the contest. Melbourne dominated the opening term and should have established a commanding advantage. The Demons controlled territory, won the contest around the ball and repeatedly generated forward entries, yet their wastefulness in front of goal proved costly. They could easily have been four or five goals in front but failed to convert their dominance into scoreboard pressure. View post on X Geelong punished them.



Chris Scott’s side produced a ferocious second-quarter burst, slamming on seven goals to two with a combination of ruthless efficiency, clean ball movement and relentless pressure that overwhelmed Melbourne. It was football played at premiership level. The Cats sliced through Melbourne’s defence with speed and precision, punished turnovers and suddenly looked every bit the experienced September side that has made a habit of peaking late in seasons. Emerging key forward Shannon Neale was the biggest beneficiary. Shannon Neale was a standout for the Cats against the in-form Demons. AFL Photos



The athletic spearhead proved far too powerful for Melbourne defender Lukas Cooke, who was playing just his second AFL game, kicking five goals — four of them before half-time — in one of the finest performances of his career. Cooke fought gamely but was handed one of the toughest assignments in football and Neale’s combination of strength, reach and finishing proved too much to contain. Geelong also entered the game with a clear tactical plan for Melbourne captain Max Gawn. Tom Stewart had another standout night for Geelong. AFL Photos Rather than allowing the superstar ruckman to drift behind the play and influence contests with his marking, the Cats used Mark Blicavs to shadow Gawn around the ground after stoppages. Blicavs’ athleticism and discipline denied Gawn the freedom he so often enjoys as an intercepting presence and limited one of Melbourne’s greatest weapons.



The Demons refused to surrender. Defender-turned-forward Harrison Petty threatened to drag his side back into the contest with a career-best display in attack, finishing with four goals in a performance that, at times, evoked memories of club great Garry Lyon. Every time Melbourne threatened to mount a charge, Petty provided another contest and another goal. But Geelong always had the answers. View post on X Just as encouraging for the Cats was where those answers came from.



Dangerfield was quick to praise the club’s emerging talent, singling out defender Connor O’Sullivan as one of the brightest young players in the competition. “I think he’s going to be generational,” Dangerfield said. “He’s going to play for another 15 years. He’s an extraordinary athlete. His ability to run is phenomenal, and he reads the game so well. It’s hard to talk about him and not smile because it’s nice to know we’ve got him.” He also highlighted the performances of Mark O’Connor and Ollie Dempsey as further evidence Geelong’s improvement extends well beyond its established stars.



For all the excitement surrounding those emerging players, however, the fitness of Dangerfield looms as Geelong’s biggest watch over the coming days. The 36-year-old has become one of the masters of managing his body through the demands of a long AFL season, but even he conceded the balancing act is becoming increasingly delicate as finals approach. The Cats have often reached this stage of the season with the luxury of managing veterans from a position of ladder security. This year is different. “Finals aren’t guaranteed,” Dangerfield said. “We’re still fighting. We’ve just got to finish as high as we possibly can.”



On the evidence of Friday night’s emphatic victory, the Cats’ charge towards September has gathered genuine momentum. Whether their captain can remain on the park long enough to lead them may prove one of the defining stories of the final month of the home-and-away season. World.title: Cats flip the script to snap Melbourne’s MCG winning streak
World.content:
Jye Amiss has kicked five goals and Murphy Reid produced a third-quarter clinic as Fremantle continued their western derby dominance with a 70-point win over West Coast at Optus Stadium.

The Dockers led by just eight points at half-time of Friday night’s match before kicking 11 goals to one in the second half to race out easy 16.16 (112) to 6.6 (42) winners.

Amiss took seven marks inside 50m on the way to 5.1, while last year’s Rising Star winner Murphy Reid (26 disposals, one goal) snared the Glendinning-Allan Medal as best afield after turning the contest on its head with a mesmerising nine-possession third quarter.

Murphy Reid had another standout night for the Dockers. AFL Photos

Matthew Johnson (29 disposals, six clearances) and Caleb Serong (26 disposals, seven clearances) also had big games in front of 56,616 fans – a record home crowd for a Fremantle home-and-away-season game.

World.title: Grant injured as Rabbitohs all but end Storm’s finals hopes
World.content:
Melbourne captain Harry Grant suffered a hamstring injury in a 28-26 loss to South Sydney that leaves the depleted Storm’s NRL finals aspirations hanging by a thread.

Their hopes of a 16th consecutive finals berth now hinge on five consecutive wins to finish the regular season and even that may not be enough.

Loading

Grant is set to miss at least some of the fight for Melbourne’s season, joining big names Cameron Munster, Xavier Coates, Eli Katoa, Tui Kamikamica and Will Warbrick on the pine.

Harry Grant. Getty Images

The Queensland hooker pulled up sore popping a pass up for Trent Loiero just before half-time in Friday’s clash at Accor Stadium.

He limped to the sidelines and threw his headgear to the ground in frustration.

After a torrid week that claimed David Fifita (suspension), Cam Murray (calf) and Tallis Duncan (hamstring), the Rabbitohs lost their own hooker Brandon Smith (calf) to injury.

But the victory was crucial to South Sydney’s own finals hopes, which had been thrown into jeopardy with two losses from their previous four games.

Souths were staring down the possibility of falling out of the top eight to finish the weekend when Tyran Wishart and Nick Meaney crossed in quick succession during the final 15 minutes.

Right centre Meaney scythed over to give the Storm a two-point lead with 10 minutes to play.

But when fullback Sua Fa’alogo, excellent to that point, fumbled Cody Walker’s 40/20 kick into touch, the home side had the chance to strike back.

Recently re-signed halfback Ashton Ward found Campbell Graham with a beautiful cutout pass on the right side to give Souths a two-point lead that they held.

Rabbitohs winger Campbell Graham scores against Melbourne. NRL Photos

Fa’alogo had been essential as Melbourne, down 8-0 after as many minutes, rallied for a 16-8 half-time lead.

Most memorably, he beat four defenders then turned rival fullback Matt Dufty inside out on an 80-metre tear for the visitor’s third try.

But without Grant patrolling the middle of the park, the Rabbitohs snatched back ascendancy in the second half and began to pick apart the Storm’s edges – a defensive weakness for the Melburnians all year.

Ashley Klein became the most-capped NRL referee, officiating his 444th game.

AAP

World.title: Green Party determined to return to government benches, co-leader says
World.content:
Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson says the party is determined to return to the government benches, ahead of its annual general meeting.

Party members, delegates, MPs, and candidates have gathered in South Auckland to prepare for the campaign ahead.

Ahead of the AGM, Davidson told RNZ the Greens were committed to "getting rid of this government," and having a strong influence on the next one.

The party has already rolled out its tax policy, as well as its policies for water and energy.

Co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick is set to announce a further policy on Sunday afternoon, with the rest of her speech focusing on rallying the membership for the campaign ahead.

Davidson will deliver a speech focused on the party's values and release the party's election manifesto.

The manifesto, which is developed by the wider party membership, contains the party's broader priorities.

This year, Davidson said there had been a large uptick in volunteers, phone calls, and door knocks, compared to this stage of previous election years.

"There's energy there that I don't think even we were expecting, all due to the sort of vision and solutions that the Greens have been putting out."

Unlike New Zealand First, which opens up its remit sessions to the media, or ACT, which promotes its AGM as more of a public rally, the Green Party's meetings are more like a conclave.

The notoriously closed-door meetings have been full of drama in recent years, from the decision to vacate James Shaw's position as co-leader in 2022, to the agonising over Darleen Tana in 2024 that led to three Pasifika members leaving the party.

Compared to the Greens' tumultuous first year back in opposition, the party goes into the election more cohesive and relaxed.

Davidson said there had been aspects of the last few years that had been "traumatising," but the party was stronger for it.

"No doubt we have gone through a lot this term, and even into last term. We've come through more than a lot, actually. Let's be straight up. So to have come through that and know you can make it through to the light, the members are just really focused now on this election."

While constitutional matters and remits are left for the other years, the membership will still vote on the party's leadership.

Both co-leaders are set to be re-confirmed, but Davidson was not taking anything for granted.

"We have that yearly confirmation for a reason, because our members really do decide if we get the privilege of serving year after year. So I can't rule out anything, but we're hoping that we have good relationships across the party, and we will be campaigning hard to keep the roles that we're going after."

The party was on 10.3 percent in the latest RNZ-Reid Research poll, up 0.2 points from the previous poll, but still a slight dip on the 11.6 percent the Greens got at the 2023 election.

It would give the Greens 13 seats in the House, two down from its current total.

The party's final list, was published in April.

While current polling would see much of the current crop of MPs return, Scott Willis (15th) and Mike Davidson (20th) are in danger of losing their spots, and the highest-ranked new face is Tania Waikato, in 13th.

But Davidson was not deterred.

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Kiwi swimmers to contend for medals after qualifiers
World.content:
New Zealand swimmers have made a flying start in the pool at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, putting themselves in contention for medals on opening day.

Erika Fairweather posted the fastest time of the 400 metre freestyle heats, qualifying first in a time of 4 minutes 6.42 seconds, with team-mate Caitlin Deans qualifying third in the same race on Friday (NZT).

The Kiwi pair were separated by Australian Amelia Weber in second.

Fairweather would look to go one better at Glasgow after narrowly missing the podium in the 400 metre freestyle final at Birmingham.

Eve Thomas also placed third in her heat for the same event, behind Australian pair Lani Pallister and Jenna Forrester.

The trio of New Zealand women would face off in the 400 metre freestyle final due to happen about 6.05am Saturday morning (NZT).

Meanwhile, Lewis Clareburt, who clinched double gold and bronze at Birmingham in 2022, qualified second in the 200 metre individual medley, behind Englishman Thomas Dean.

Clareburt's qualifying time was 1.2 seconds shy of his bronze-medal performance at Birmingham.

The 27-year-old would vie for a fifth Commonwealth Games medal in the 200 metre medley final about 6.15am Saturday (NZT).

Hazel Ouwehand also booked a final berth finishing second in a tightly-contested 50 metre butterfly heat.

The 26-year-old's time of 26.4 seconds was 0.16 seconds behind Jessica Thompson, of South Africa.

Zoe Pedersen also finished second in her 50 metre butterfly heat, completing the swim in 26.6 seconds, 1.05 seconds behind Australian Alex Perkins.

World.title: Respected public servant Dame Helene Quilter dies
World.content:
Dame Helene Quilter, who was honoured for her work in the public service over 45 years, has died.

The Public Service Commissioner, Sir Brian Roche, said Dame Helene died overnight.

Dame Helene served as Secretary of Defence, Deputy Commissioner of the State Services Commission and, most recently, as Deputy Public Service Commissioner at the Public Service Commission Te Kawa Mataaho.

She retired as deputy Public Service commissioner in February 2023.

She was recognised as a Dame Companion of the New Zealand Order of Merit in 2023 for services to the public service and the arts.

Her citation noted her advocacy for diversity and inclusion in public sector appointments, her leadership in strengthening public service capability, and her commitment to serving New Zealand through some of its most important institutions.

Sir Brian said Dame Helene was one of New Zealand's most respected and influential public servants.

"Over a career spanning 45 years, she dedicated herself to strengthening the institutions that serve New Zealanders and to upholding the values of integrity, professionalism and public service," Sir Brian said.

He said she played a central role in the appointment and development of Public Service chief executives, championed greater diversity in leadership, supported the public service through the Covid-19 response, and brought extraordinary wisdom and judgement to some of the most important issues facing government.

"She combined intellectual rigour with humanity, integrity with courage, and a deep understanding of what it means to serve the public good," Sir Brian said.

"Throughout her career, she helped shape the modern public service and was a trusted adviser, mentor and leader to countless public servants. She believed strongly in developing people, building diverse leadership, and leaving our institutions stronger than she found them.

"Those who worked with Helene knew her as someone of immense capability, wisdom and generosity. She challenged us to be better, supported others to succeed, and never lost sight of the purpose of public service - improving the lives of New Zealanders."

World.title: Battle lines drawn over proposed LNG facility
World.content:
Proposed LNG import terminal unlikely to cause disruption Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Port Taranaki has reassured nearby residents that initial assessments of a proposed LNG import terminal indicate it is unlikely "risk management zones" will impact on the community or popular recreational areas like Ngāmotu Beach and Breakwater Bay.

In a letter sent to hundreds of local properties, port chief executive Simon Craddock confirmed both shortlisted proposals involved a ship being moored alongside the Main Breakwater.

Opponents of the project argue Port Taranaki is the wrong place for a liquid natural gas (LNG) import facility.

Former oil and gas industry project manager Rob Green's home on Port View Crescent overlooks Port Taranaki.

"I can look straight down on the port, all the ships at anchor here, and I can see all the logs and so on. So, I'm looking straight down on the port at the Main Breakwater and all those berthing possibilities for ships," he said.

"It's very close, all the noises from the port operations I can hear. I'm looking straight at it."

Green was not convinced the port, about 1km from his apartment, was the right place for an LNG import facility.

"I keep hearing that safety is the top priority, but quite frankly I won't believe it until I can see the risk assessment analysis for myself.

"Here we are bulldozing on to a contract the government seems totally committed to regardless to the concerns of the neighbourhood."

Port Taranaki's letter and an article on the Ministry of Business Innovation and Employment's LNG webpage explain that the vessel to be moored at the Main Breakwater would store LNG and be capable of regasifying it and distributing it into existing transmission pipelines.

Other vessels from suppliers overseas would deliver LNG - which was frozen - to the moored vessel.

The Main Breakwater was about 200m away from popular recreational areas at Ngāmotu Beach, Breakwater Bay and the Lee Breakwater, where recreational fishers both surfcasted and launched boats.

Port Taranaki referred questions about the safety assessment to MBIE, which was managing the procurement process.

In a statement, MBIE said safety was the bottom-line and the plant would not get built if it could not meet safety standards.

"An initial safety evaluation has been undertaken as part of both of the providers' feasibility work, and detailed health and safety assessments will be carried out through the Safety Case process under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 once the preferred provider is contracted," it said in a statement.

"This includes a quantitative risk assessment which is location-specific and will cover the facility and all phases of its operation, as well as generating risk contour lines (or 'buffer zones') to keep the community safe."

MBIE said it was inappropriate to make the initial safety assessment public as it was commercially sensitive.

In statement, WorkSafe said it had no role in the choice of location, but it would work with the preferred provider on the more detailed Safety Case.

"Before the facility can be built and operated, the preferred provider must submit both a design notice and a Safety Case to WorkSafe.

WorkSafe would assess these to determine whether the facility could comply with major hazard facility requirements and that risks had been identified and appropriately managed.

"WorkSafe will either accept or decline the Safety Case. If it is declined, the facility will not go ahead."

The regulator said it didn't publish safety cases in full.

However, if the LNG project was designated a major hazard facility, prescribed information must be published on the WorkSafe website.

This would include an explanation of activities undertaken at the facility, hazard classifications of substances that could cause or contribute to a major incident, and the characteristics of those substances that made them dangerous.

General information about how the public would be warned in the event of a major incident would also be published, and information on how the public should act and what precautionary steps they should take if a major incident occurred.

Taranaki Energy Watch's Sarah Roberts RNZ / Robin Martin

Taranaki Energy Watch spokesperson Sarah Roberts said that would be a case of too little too late.

"What we're saying is this location is not the right place for an LNG import terminal. We know that there's a known potential worst case fatality distance to approximately 2km from these types of facilities. There are thousands of people and a number of schools in this area."

Roberts said right from the outset former Minister of Energy Simon Watts talked about working alongside the Port Kembla Energy Terminal in New South Wales.

"Over there, they have built a new terminal and they have the 2km separation distance between the terminal itself and the nearest residence."

Roberts worried people in the area surrounding Port Taranaki would be hurt if something went wrong.

"We feel like they're purposely avoiding the RMA and Fast Track legislation to get something through that should have been looked at primarily at the beginning. Looking at the location, seeing if there's any alternatives, and making it publicly available, making the safety assessments publicly available."

MBIE said the exact size and details of the safety buffer zones around the LNG import facility at Port Taranaki would be determined independently to the procurement process, once it had been completed.

"It is inappropriate to estimate the exact size of the buffer zones ahead of this detailed Safety Case process. Until the Safety Case is accepted, the import facility will not be built."

People walking along Ngāmotu Beach and at Breakwater Bay had mixed views on the LNG proposal.

Kevin said he accepted it was necessary: "I suppose we have to have the gas to run the country. There's no great place to put it. Everyone wants it somewhere else, but Taranaki has had all the gas and gas production over the years."

His mate, Denis, wasn't so keen: "I'm not really in favour of the whole thing. It's all imported fossil fuels and a bit close to a residential area."

Don had an alternative idea and reckoned the infrastructure was mostly already in place: "Pipe it in, which would eliminate any need for changes around the harbour area."

Robyn was willing to put her trust in the process: "They've got very stringent safety things, that's the big thing with oil and gas."

Grant worried about access to recreational areas: "Not very happy at all.

"There's a lot of people who use this area here. So, is there going to be an exclusion zone for people walking around here? And what about the cafes here, are they going to remove those?"

Graham said he could see both sides of the dilemma: "It's probably no more dangerous than anything else, but it is an unnecessary addition to danger, and the actual plant itself is unnecessary."

Bernard's home was within 2km of the proposed site: "I think it is a bit risky. It is a highly volatile thing and that. I would prefer them going back to Marsden Point and doing it there."

World.title: No bridge too far for man behind new Aoraki Mt Cook bridge
World.content:
No bridge too far for man behind new Hooker Valley bridge Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

There is virtually no bridge too far for the man behind the new Hooker Valley suspension bridge at Aoraki Mount Cook.

The marvel of design and modern engineering is due to open next week and replaces the old one that closed due to erosion caused by storms in April last year.

It spans 189 metres across the Hooker River, making it the longest suspension bridge in the country.

The new 189m long Hooker Valley suspension bridge at Aoraki Mount Cook. Supplied

Construction started in August last year, and since then workers have faced the challenge of gales and snowfall during construction.

The man behind the design, bridge architect and engineer, Dan Crocker told Checkpoint that he feels amazed seeing the bridge in its finished form.

"It's been a lot of work getting to this point, but you know, one of the things is when you arrive on site and everything fits and you've got that beautiful scenery, it just looks right."

Bridge engineer Dan Crocker (right) Supplied

As the longest footbridge in Aotearoa, Crocker said it had been no easy feat getting to this point, with the remote site adding an extra layer of challenges.

"Conventionally with a bridge, you might roll up with a crane and concrete trucks. You can't do that in this environment, everything comes in via helicopter."

"You have to work backwards from what you can get to site and working in these challenging environments. It's a very different type of bridge construction in these remote areas"

The bridge will open to the public on 28 July. Supplied / Department of Conservation

Wild weather at the remote site had also presented issues.

"The contractor brings excavators and containers to site, the winds picked up and brought all the gravel with it and it ended up stripping the paint off the excavators and the containers."

"You can only imagine how much of a severe environment that is to work in... it's not much fun, but on the other days when it's beautiful sunshine and you can see the mountains it makes it worth it."

Unlike a traditional suspension bridge, the new structure lacks what gave the 'swing bridge' its name, so those taking on the near 200m journey don't have to worry about losing their footing.

"Some people are comfortable with moving structures and heights, but a lot of people aren't. So what we try and do is make it as stable as possible while still maintaining that lightweight kind of appearance."

"There is a little bit of movement, but it's definitely suppressed compared to what you would normally have."

While the Hooker Valley bridge may be the longest, it is certainly not the first pedestrian bridge Crocker has designed.

"We wake up every morning, jump out of bed ready to design bridges, that's all we do here."

"Generally we focus on cycle bridges, pedestrian bridges, the kind of bridges people want to come and see and want to visit."

The Hooker Valley bridge is the country's longest suspension bridge. Supplied

Crocker said for him, bridges serve as more than a way to get from A to B.

"They connect communities, they connect different areas that people want to visit, but I like to think of them as also placemakers and wayfinders."

"We've got some little bridges here in Cambridge that I've designed - they're wayfinders in Cambridge itself with a little blue pedestrian bridge.. everybody uses it... 'go past the blue bridge and turn left.'"

Crocker said he also loves the way he's seen his bridges instil a sense of community pride, something he's seen in Westport with the Toki Poutangata bridge, inspired by the area's pounamu.

World.title: Installation features 'forbidden' medicines denied to New Zealanders
World.content:
Locked up medicines on display to highlight unfunded treatments Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Patients waiting for life-changing medicines to be funded say people should not have to fundraise, go into debt, or travel overseas for treatments and therapies that could be administered here.

More than a dozen patient organisations are hosting the Forbidden Pharmacy, online, and this weekend at Auckland's Shed 10.

Supplied/ Forbidden Pharmacy

It's an installation that shows shelves of white medicine packets and bottles locked behind doors - representing what people may need but can't access, because they are not funded by Pharmac.

When Jemma Gerring was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer in late 2023 she had no symptoms till the day she went to the doctor thinking she might have appendicitis.

"It was surreal. It was just like being hit by a freight train. It took a long time to process what that meant," she said.

"You start off really optimistic about, okay, that's great, we'll have treatment and be all better. Very quickly you start looking at the statistics and realise it's not going to be that easy."

Jemma Gerring RNZ/ Amy Williams

She has health insurance but that has a cap for the unfunded drug that is buying her more time with her family.

It has so far cost her hundreds of thousands of dollars for the drug and life-prolonging surgeries in Australia; something she said is unfair to anyone without such means.

"I think the thing for me is I feel guilty that I can afford to pay for this. It's inconvenient and it costs money, but I can pay for it and I really do credit this drug with making a difference in my life," she said.

"I'm still working full-time, I'm still being a mum full-time."

Supplied/ Forbidden Pharmacy

Gerring drives six hours from New Plymouth to Palmerston North each fortnight to have the drug she pays for, Bevacizumab, administered.

It is funded in other countries, including Australia and the UK.

"It's that sort of continual guilt that you feel too, of 'Am I taking money away from my children's future, from my husband's ability to live when I'm not here?'," she said.

"But I'm literally in the situation of buying time, and I like to think it's worth it.

"It's certainly worth it for me."

Locked up medicines on display to highlight unfunded treatments Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Tim Edmonds RNZ/ Amy Williams

The Forbidden Pharmacy has the medication on a shelf, and spokesperson for the installation, Tim Edmonds, said for patients waiting for medicine to be funded, the cost of living is a burden.

"This is having to make decisions no New Zealander should ever have to make, remortgaging homes, setting up Givealittle pages, moving to another country," he said.

"There is a financial cost, an emotional cost, but actually for many people those aren't options and the cost is going without, worsening health and less time with family and loved ones."

Edmonds is chief executive of Blood Cancer NZ and said a recent international report found patients in New Zealand have the poorest publicly-funded access to modern medicines out of comparable OECD countries and that the majority, 95 percent, of modern medicines don't make it to the shelves here.

"We want the future government to solve this for New Zealand," Edmonds said.

"We want the medicines that Pharmac have recommended to the government to be funded over three years and clear the backlog, and we want to plan for sustained investment so that we stop getting further behind the countries that we like to compare ourselves to."

Bart Schroder RNZ/ Amy Williams

For Bart Schroder, having access to an unfunded cancer medication means he is still alive after being diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer five years ago.

His health insurance has covered the cost since diagnosis, otherwise he would have had a long wait.

"In my case, I'm still here four years later, which is pretty good, and I'm still feeling really good," he said.

"That wouldn't have been the case, because my cancer is very aggressive... it would have taken me out so the standard treatment wouldn't have been very effective."

Schroder would like to see the medicine funded so everyone with his diagnosis can access it early on.

An engineer, he is still working for the company he founded and recently sold, it sells specialised equipment around the world.

"Five good years of working, contributing, selling stuff all over the place is way better than six months in a hospital. Hospital is much more expensive than just looking after me for five good years," he said.

"So why don't they fund it? It makes a lot of sense."

Looking ahead, Gerring wants more life-changing medicines funded so everyone can have the same chance as she has to enjoy more of their life.

"I was sort of told average life expectancy from diagnosis is two and a half years. I'm beyond that now, so... I definitely feel like I'm living on borrowed time, but every extra month I get with my children at this very formative age for them is worth it."

Politicians from National, Labour, ACT and New Zealand First visited the Forbidden Pharmacy today.

World.title: What it feels like to have your sport dumped from the Commonwealth Games
World.content:
As the Commonwealth Games kicked off on its first full day of competition, plenty more sat at at home, many wishing it could be them.

Organisers in 2026 ditched badminton, hockey, wrestling, road cycling, mountain biking, rhythmic gymnastics, rugby sevens, squash, table tennis, triathlon, beach volleyball, cricket and, the most storied of all, diving.

It has been held at every edition since the first Empire Games in 1930, until this year.

Of the 22 Commonwealth Games diving events, Anabelle Smith went to the past four, including Glasgow 2014.

Twelve years ago she won bronze in the women's synchronised 3m springboard with Maddison Keeney, but not in Glasgow like the rest of her team.

This dive for Smith (left) and Keeney was at Glasgow 2014 in name only. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The Scottish capital did not have a facility to allow for diving, so Smith, Keeney and Co were shipped to Edinburgh, the site of the 1970 and 1986 Games.

"[There was] obvious disappointment from the divers … but also an understanding," Smith told ABC Sport.

"It made sense they weren't just gonna ship the divers up to Edinburgh, disappointing but they'll power on and look ahead now."

The 33-year-old had not been planning to defend her 3m synchro gold medal from Birmingham 2022, but is instead attending her fifth Games as a spectator and part of the Australian team's connection and belonging squad.

How we got to Glasgow 2026 The bumpy road to Glasgow 2026 has produced a Commonwealth Games that will look a little different than the ones that came before.

She's joined by other athletes who have seen their sports axed, including beach volleyballer Chris McHugh and Melissa 'Milly' Tapper.

Her sport of table tennis was also axed after being included in six straight Games from 2002 to 2022.

Tapper, an Olympian and Paralympian, embodies the inclusive and integrated nature of the Games perhaps better than anyone.

She won team bronze at Glasgow 2014 and singles gold on home soil on the Gold Coast in 2018, and is still getting the chance to flash her skills in the team lounge at the decked-out Glasgow Argyle Hotel.

Loading Instagram content

"I've got a little bit of a call-up having the table tennis table in there," she said.

"We've had plenty of athletes and even some staff come through and challenge. Being around athletes everyone's competitive. It's a lot of fun.

"So even though table tennis isn't technically in the Games, it's still a part of the Games."

Table tennis was a "core sport" for the Commonwealth Games and falls into the category of many of the 2026 events, in that it could be held in existing halls.

Melissa Tapper has represented Australia at the Olympics, Paralympics and Commonwealth Games. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Field hockey, however, requires a bit more space and bespoke facilities. Its history in the Commonwealth Games is not quite as long as diving's, but it had an elevated status as a "core sport".

In 2014, it was held at the Glasgow National Hockey Centre, which remains operational and is located along the River Clyde, within the 13-kilometre corridor of the pared-back 2026 Games.

When cuts were being made for 2026, the International Hockey Federation (FIH) and Commonwealth member nations lobbied for the sport's inclusion, but they missed out as organisers opted largely for indoor sports with athletics the only outdoor event.

Glasgow 2026 events 3x3 basketball/wheelchair basketball

Artistic gymnastics

Athletics

Bowls

Boxing

Judo

Netball

Para powerlifting and weightlifting

Swimming

Track cycling

The Kookaburras have won all seven men's gold medals since 1998, while the Hockeyroos have also never missed the podium, boasting four gold, two silver and a bronze.

Kookaburras captain Eddie Ockenden carried the flag in the Birmingham 2022 opening ceremony, as evidence of the sport's standing in Australia's Commonwealth Games movement, so Hockey Australia was "naturally disappointed" to miss out in 2026.

"Our national teams only play a finite number of international tournaments, making every opportunity to compete in one incredibly valuable," high performance director Bernard Savage said.

"The Commonwealth Games have always been one of those opportunities that our teams have genuinely looked forward to. Beyond the competition itself, the Commonwealth Games provide a unique multi-sport environment that our athletes look forward to and aspire to be a part of.

"The broader interest in the Games has provided an opportunity for our athletes and teams to inspire the next generation of hockey players across Australia and the Commonwealth.

"While this has been disappointing news, our focus remains firmly on our preparation for the 2026 FIH Hockey World Cup."

The World Cup will be played in Belgium and The Netherlands from August 15-30, shortly after the end of the Glasgow Games.
